Through theoretical analysis of these two metrics, we show that the evolution of features follows a simple and quantitative pattern from shallow to deep layers when the input data is nearly orthogonal and the network weights are minimum-norm, balanced, and approximate low-rank: Each layer of the linear network progressively compresses within-class features at a geometric rate and discriminates between-class features at a linear rate with respect to the number of layers that data have passed through. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first quantitative characterization of feature evolution in hierarchical representations of deep linear networks. Empirically, our extensive experiments not only validate our theoretical results numerically but also reveal a similar pattern in deep nonlinear networks which aligns well with recent empirical studies. Moreover, we demonstrate the practical implications of our results in transfer learning. Our code is available at https://github.com/Heimine/PNC_DLN.

papers.title: All Bark and No Bite: Rogue Dimensions in Transformer Language Models Obscure Representational Quality
papers.research_question: How informative are standard similarity measures (cosine similarity, Euclidean distance) in contextualized language models, and how do rogue dimensions dominate these measures, obscuring representational quality?
papers.core_contribution: Standard similarity measures in contextual language models are dominated by a small number of rogue dimensions, and simple postprocessing techniques like standardization can correct for this, revealing underlying representational quality that is preserved across all layers.
papers.conclusion: Standard similarity measures are not informative for contextual language models due to rogue dimensions, and accounting for these dimensions (e.g., via standardization) is essential for any similarity-based analysis.
papers.key_findings:
A small number of rogue dimensions (1-5) dominate cosine similarity and Euclidean distance in contextual language models.
Rogue dimensions are centered far from the origin and have disproportionately high variance.
The rogue dimensions that dominate similarity measures do not dominate model behavior; ablating them has little effect on the language modeling distribution.
Rogue dimensions are often correlated with specific tokens (e.g., punctuation) and positions (e.g., position zero).
After postprocessing (e.g., standardization), representational quality (correlation with human similarity judgments) improves and is preserved across all layers, contrary to previous claims of degradation in later layers.
future_direction: Designing and implementing language models that do not develop rogue dimensions in the first place.
Understanding how rogue dimensions arise over time during pretraining.
Using the MultiBERT checkpoints to study whether rogue dimensions are coincidental or requisite for good performance, and how they emerge.
papers.abstract: Similarity measures are a vital tool for understanding how language models represent and process language. Standard representational similarity measures such as cosine similarity and Euclidean distance have been successfully used in static word embedding models to understand how words cluster in semantic space. Recently, these measures have been applied to embeddings from contextualized models such as BERT and GPT-2. In this work, we call into question the informativity of such measures for contextualized language models. We find that a small number of rogue dimensions, often just 1-3, dominate these measures. Moreover, we find a striking mismatch between the dimensions that dominate similarity measures and those which are important to the behavior of the model. We show that simple postprocessing techniques such as standardization are able to correct for rogue dimensions and reveal underlying representational quality. We argue that accounting for rogue dimensions is essential for any similarity-based analysis of contextual language models.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: Convergent Learning: Do different neural networks learn the same representations?
papers.research_question: Do different neural networks with the same architecture trained from different random initializations learn the same representations (i.e., exhibit convergent learning)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces methods to compare neural network representations and shows that networks exhibit partial convergent learning, with some features learned reliably across networks and others not, and that representations are a mix of local and slightly distributed codes.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks exhibit convergent learning to some extent, and the introduced methods are effective for understanding and comparing the representations they learn.
papers.key_findings:
Some features are learned reliably in multiple networks, yet other features are not consistently learned.
Units learn to span low-dimensional subspaces and, while these subspaces are common to multiple networks, the specific basis vectors learned are not.
The representation codes show evidence of being a mix between a local (single unit) code and slightly, but not fully, distributed codes across multiple units.
The average activation values of neurons vary considerably within a network, yet the mean activation values across different networks converge to an almost identical distribution.
Features learned in different networks are most convergent on the first convolutional layer (conv1) and least convergent on the fourth (conv4).
papers.limitation: Mapping layers for higher layers (conv3-conv5) showed poor performance, and the reasons are not fully understood.
future_direction: Investigate different architectures, training algorithms, and hyperparameters.
Train more powerful predictive models for higher layers with different hyperparameters or architectures.
papers.abstract: Recent success in training deep neural networks have prompted active investigation into the features learned on their intermediate layers. Such research is difficult because it requires making sense of non-linear computations performed by millions of parameters, but valuable because it increases our ability to understand current models and create improved versions of them. In this paper we investigate the extent to which neural networks exhibit what we call convergent learning, which is when the representations learned by multiple nets converge to a set of features which are either individually similar between networks or where subsets of features span similar low-dimensional spaces. We propose a specific method of probing representations: training multiple networks and then comparing and contrasting their individual, learned representations at the level of neurons or groups of neurons. We begin research into this question using three techniques to approximately align different neural networks on a feature level: a bipartite matching approach that makes one-to-one assignments between neurons, a sparse prediction approach that finds one-to-many mappings, and a spectral clustering approach that finds many-to-many mappings. This initial investigation reveals a few previously unknown properties of neural networks, and we argue that future research into the question of convergent learning will yield many more. The insights described here include (1) that some features are learned reliably in multiple networks, yet other features are not consistently learned; (2) that units learn to span low-dimensional subspaces and, while these subspaces are common to multiple networks, the specific basis vectors learned are not; (3) that the representation codes show evidence of being a mix between a local code and slightly, but not fully, distributed codes across multiple units.

papers.title: On the Behavior of Convolutional Nets for Feature Extraction
papers.research_question: How do individual CNN features from all layers behave for feature extraction and transfer learning, and can both presence and absence of feature activations be informative?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a statistical analysis of individual CNN features for feature extraction, showing that features can be discriminative by both presence and absence, and that convolutional layers are more general and discriminant than previously thought, enabling their use for knowledge representation.
papers.conclusion: The study provides insights into the behavior of CNN features for feature extraction, showing that both presence and absence of features are informative, and that convolutional layers are more general than previously thought, which can be exploited for knowledge representation and reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Features can be characteristic of a class by their absence, providing a different information modality, especially in fine-grained datasets.
Features from the last convolutional layer and fully connected layers are highly specific, while other convolutional layers convey more variate information.
For certain tasks, convolutional features outperform fully-connected features at discriminating labels, indicating low-level layers are more general and discriminant.
Low and middle level features have similar behavior across datasets, suggesting they can be used for knowledge representation without fine-tuning.
The relevance of fully-connected features is strongly related to the similarity of the task with the original training task and the width of the task spectrum.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are representation learning techniques. During training, a deep net is capable of generating a descriptive language of unprecedented size and detail in machine learning. Extracting the descriptive language coded within a trained CNN model (in the case of image data), and reusing it for other purposes is a field of interest, as it provides access to the visual descriptors previously learnt by the CNN after processing millions of images, without requiring an expensive training phase. Contributions to this field (commonly known as feature representation transfer or transfer learning) have been purely empirical so far, extracting all CNN features from a single layer close to the output and testing their performance by feeding them to a classifier. This approach has provided consistent results, although its relevance is limited to classification tasks. In a completely different approach, in this paper we statistically measure the discriminative power of every single feature found within a deep CNN, when used for characterizing every class of 11 datasets. We seek to provide new insights into the behavior of CNN features, particularly the ones from convolutional layers, as this can be relevant for their application to knowledge representation and reasoning. Our results confirm that low and middle level features may behave differently to high level features, but only under certain conditions. We find that all CNN features can be used for knowledge representation purposes both by their presence or by their absence, doubling the information a single CNN feature may provide. We also study how much noise these features may include, and propose a thresholding approach to discard most of it. All these insights have a direct application to the generation of CNN embedding spaces.

papers.title: Feature learning is decoupled from generalization in high capacity neural networks
papers.research_question: Do current theories of feature learning measure the quality of learned features (which impacts generalization) or just the strength of representation changes?
papers.core_contribution: Current feature learning theories measure the strength of representation changes (FL strength) but not the quality of features, and these are decoupled. The paper introduces the FL gap to measure feature quality and shows that FL strength does not predict generalization.
papers.conclusion: Current theories of feature learning do not predict generalization because they measure strength rather than quality, indicating the need for a more comprehensive FL theory.
papers.key_findings:
The feature learning gap (∆NT) quantifies the performance improvement of neural networks over kernel methods.
Current FL definitions (NTK-based, CK-based, superposition-based) measure FL strength, not feature quality.
FL strength metrics (e.g., SNT, SCK) fail to distinguish between networks trained on true vs. shuffled labels, indicating decoupling from generalization.
The NTK-based FL strength can be manipulated by output scaling without affecting generalization.
CK-based cumulative utility does not differentiate between shuffled and non-shuffled data.
future_direction: Developing a more comprehensive feature learning theory that links feature learning to generalization.
papers.abstract: Neural networks outperform kernel methods, sometimes by orders of magnitude, e.g. on staircase functions. This advantage stems from the ability of neural networks to learn features, adapting their hidden representations to better capture the data. We introduce a concept we call feature quality to measure this performance improvement. We examine existing theories of feature learning and demonstrate empirically that they primarily assess the strength of feature learning, rather than the quality of the learned features themselves. Consequently, current theories of feature learning do not provide a sufficient foundation for developing theories of neural network generalization.

papers.title: Filtering with Self-Attention and Storing with MLP: One-Layer Transformers Can Provably Acquire and Extract Knowledge
papers.research_question: How do transformers acquire knowledge during pre-training via next-token prediction and extract it after fine-tuning? Under what conditions can pre-trained transformers perform out-of-distribution generalization after full and low-rank fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a theoretical framework for one-layer transformers that shows they can achieve near-optimal pre-training loss and post-fine-tuning out-of-distribution generalization under certain conditions, and explains the roles of self-attention and MLP in knowledge acquisition and extraction.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework provides convergence and generalization guarantees for one-layer transformers, elucidating the mechanisms of knowledge acquisition and extraction and the conditions for successful out-of-distribution generalization after fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can achieve near-optimal pre-training loss during pre-training, demonstrating effective knowledge acquisition.
Given a sufficiently large fine-tuning dataset and appropriate data multiplicity conditions, transformers achieve low generalization error on factual knowledge acquired during pre-training but not revisited in fine-tuning, indicating robust knowledge extraction.
Violation of these conditions leads to elevated generalization error, manifesting as hallucinations.
Self-attention learns to filter out noise tokens and focus on subject and relation tokens, enabling the MLP to learn balanced features for subjects and relations.
Low-rank fine-tuning is effective because the fine-tuning gradients closely approximate their best rank-1 form, with the right singular vector aligning with the Q&A format embedding.
papers.limitation: Uses orthogonal embeddings and simplified architecture, which may not fully capture real-world complexity.
future_direction: Analysis of random embeddings instead of orthogonal embeddings.
papers.abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) demonstrate exceptional performance on knowledge-intensive tasks, yet the theoretical mechanisms underlying knowledge acquisition (storage and memorization) during pre-training and extraction (retrieval and recall) during inference after fine-tuning remain poorly understood. Although prior theoretical studies have explored these processes through analyses of training dynamics, they overlook critical components essential for a comprehensive theory: (1) the multi-layer perceptron (MLP), empirically identified as the primary module for knowledge storage; (2) out-of-distribution (OOD) adaptivity, which enables LLMs to generalize to unseen scenarios post-pre-training; and (3) next-token prediction, the standard autoregressive objective that encodes knowledge as conditional probabilities. In this work, we introduce, to the best of our knowledge, the first theoretical framework that addresses these limitations by examining the training dynamics of one-layer transformers. Under regularity assumptions, we establish that: (i) transformers attain near-optimal training loss during pre-training, demonstrating effective knowledge acquisition; (ii) given a sufficiently large fine-tuning dataset and appropriate data multiplicity conditions, transformers achieve low generalization error on factual knowledge acquired during pre-training but not revisited in fine-tuning, indicating robust knowledge extraction; and (iii) violation of these conditions leads to elevated generalization error, manifesting as hallucinations. Our analysis encompasses both full fine-tuning and low-rank fine-tuning, yielding insights into the efficacy of practical low-rank adaptation methods. We validate our theoretical findings through experiments on synthetic datasets and the real-world PopQA benchmark, employing GPT-2 and Llama-3.2-1B models.

papers.title: Inference-Time Intervention: Eliciting Truthful Answers from a Language Model
papers.research_question: How can we enhance the truthfulness of large language models by intervening on their activations during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a minimally invasive technique that shifts activations along truthful directions in attention heads during inference to improve model truthfulness.
papers.conclusion: ITI is a promising, efficient method for improving truthfulness in LLMs, suggesting that models internally represent truth which can be elicited through activation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
ITI significantly improves truthfulness on the TruthfulQA benchmark, e.g., increasing Alpaca's truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness that can be balanced by tuning intervention strength.
ITI is data-efficient, requiring only a few hundred examples to find truthful directions.
ITI generalizes to other question-answering benchmarks (Natural Questions, TriviaQA, MMLU) with smaller improvements.
LLMs appear to have an internal representation of truth even when generating falsehoods.
papers.limitation:
ITI is not sufficient for ensuring truthful answers from LLMs and should be part of a more comprehensive approach.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness; increasing truthfulness may reduce informativeness.
future_direction: Test ITI on a wider variety of benchmarks beyond TruthfulQA.
Investigate the mechanistic understanding of what ITI does to internal representations.
papers.abstract: We introduce Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a technique designed to enhance the "truthfulness" of large language models (LLMs). ITI operates by shifting model activations during inference, following a set of directions across a limited number of attention heads. This intervention significantly improves the performance of LLaMA models on the TruthfulQA benchmark. On an instruction-finetuned LLaMA called Alpaca, ITI improves its truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%. We identify a tradeoff between truthfulness and helpfulness and demonstrate how to balance it by tuning the intervention strength. ITI is minimally invasive and computationally inexpensive. Moreover, the technique is data efficient: while approaches like RLHF require extensive annotations, ITI locates truthful directions using only few hundred examples. Our findings suggest that LLMs may have an internal representation of the likelihood of something being true, even as they produce falsehoods on the surface.

papers.title: When Representations Align: Universality in Representation Learning Dynamics
papers.research_question: What universal behaviors exist in representation learning dynamics across different neural network architectures? The paper derives an effective theory to describe these dynamics.
papers.core_contribution: Derives an effective theory of representation learning dynamics that exhibits universal behavior across architectures, with two regimes (rich and lazy) depending on initialization.
papers.conclusion: Representation learning dynamics exhibit universal behaviors across architectures when models are sufficiently flexible, and the effective theory captures these behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
The effective theory matches the representation learning dynamics of various architectures (fully connected, convolutional, skip connections, etc.).
Two regimes emerge: at small initial weights, representations are structured by the data (rich regime); at large initial weights, representations retain random initialization structure (lazy regime).
The theory predicts the final representational distance for pairs of datapoints, validated on synthetic datasets.
Experiments on toy datasets (XOR, orthogonal features) and MNIST show the theory's predictions hold for expressive architectures.
The theory breaks down for shallow networks, highlighting the importance of model expressivity.
papers.limitation:
The theory is only valid for expressive architectures and for pairs of datapoints; it does not account for inductive biases.
The linear approximation may break down for datapoints that are not close in representation space.
future_direction: Extend the theory to multi-point interactions.
Incorporate inductive biases of architectures into the theory.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks come in many sizes and architectures. The choice of architecture, in conjunction with the dataset and learning algorithm, is commonly understood to affect the learned neural representations. Yet, recent results have shown that different architectures learn representations with striking qualitative similarities. Here we derive an effective theory of representation learning under the assumption that the encoding map from input to hidden representation and the decoding map from representation to output are arbitrary smooth functions. This theory schematizes representation learning dynamics in the regime of complex, large architectures, where hidden representations are not strongly constrained by the parametrization. We show through experiments that the effective theory describes aspects of representation learning dynamics across a range of deep networks with different activation functions and architectures, and exhibits phenomena similar to the "rich" and "lazy" regime. While many network behaviors depend quantitatively on architecture, our findings point to certain behaviors that are widely conserved once models are sufficiently flexible.

papers.title: Inspecting and Editing Knowledge Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we map natural language statements to fact encodings in an LM's internal representations to enable editing and probing of knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: REMEDI is a method that learns to map natural language statements to fact encodings in LM representations, enabling both editing of knowledge (by adding vectors to hidden representations) and probing of existing knowledge.
papers.conclusion: REMEDI links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.
papers.key_findings:
REMEDI can patch errors made by an LM and insert new facts with or without context provided in the prompt.
REMEDI can help detect errors before generation by comparing edit vectors to unedited representations.
REMEDI increases accuracy on occupation classification and factual editing tasks compared to prompting baselines.
REMEDI generalizes from out-of-context training to in-context editing, suggesting unified representation of background and contextual knowledge.
REMEDI edits preserve correlations between features (e.g., adding 'made of metal' increases probability of 'shiny').
papers.limitation:
REMEDI can occasionally lead to disfluent or incorrect generations.
REMEDI sometimes damages the essence of the entity (e.g., making Wiener schnitzel an anime instead of a food).
REMEDI can also cause unrelated facts to change (e.g., changing the air dates of a TV show).
future_direction: Developing controlled generation interfaces that allow direct steering of model behavior in representation space.
Building tools for monitoring and controlling language generation by directly specifying facts and situations in an LM's native encoding scheme.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) represent facts about the world described by text. Sometimes these facts derive from training data (in most LMs, a representation of the word "banana" encodes the fact that bananas are fruits). Sometimes facts derive from input text itself (a representation of the sentence "I poured out the bottle" encodes the fact that the bottle became empty). We describe REMEDI, a method for learning to map statements in natural language to fact encodings in an LM's internal representation system. REMEDI encodings can be used as knowledge editors: when added to LM hidden representations, they modify downstream generation to be consistent with new facts. REMEDI encodings may also be used as probes: when compared to LM representations, they reveal which properties LMs already attribute to mentioned entities, in some cases making it possible to predict when LMs will generate outputs that conflict with background knowledge or input text. REMEDI thus links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.

papers.title: Network Transplanting
papers.research_question: How to transplant a pre-trained network module to a generic modular network with minimal supervision, i.e., with few or no training samples.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes network transplanting, a method to merge pre-trained networks into a generic modular network with minimal supervision, and introduces the back-distillation algorithm to overcome optimization challenges.
papers.conclusion: Network transplanting is a promising approach for building generic modular networks, and the back-distillation algorithm effectively addresses the space-projection problem, significantly reducing the need for training samples.
papers.key_findings:
Back-distillation enables network transplanting with few or no training samples.
The method physically avoids catastrophic forgetting by only training adapters and freezing category and task modules.
In classification experiments, back-distillation with no training samples outperformed a baseline trained with 100 samples.
For segmentation, back-distillation yielded higher pixel accuracy than baselines across different numbers of training samples.
The method allows incremental addition of new categories without affecting representations of existing categories.
papers.limitation: Given a few samples, whether an additional fine-tuning will increase or decrease the generality of the transplant net is a difficult question, and it requires sophisticated analysis in the future.
future_direction: Analysis of fine-tuning task modules with few samples to increase generality
papers.abstract: This paper focuses on a new task, i.e., transplanting a category-and-task-specific neural network to a generic, modular network without strong supervision. We design an functionally interpretable structure for the generic network. Like building LEGO blocks, we teach the generic network a new category by directly transplanting the module corresponding to the category from a pre-trained network with a few or even without sample annotations. Our method incrementally adds new categories to the generic network but does not affect representations of existing categories. In this way, our method breaks the typical bottleneck of learning a net for massive tasks and categories, i.e. the requirement of collecting samples for all tasks and categories at the same time before the learning begins. Thus, we use a new distillation algorithm, namely back-distillation, to overcome specific challenges of network transplanting. Our method without training samples even outperformed the baseline with 100 training samples.

papers.title: Clustering units in neural networks: upstream vs downstream information
papers.research_question: How can we define and quantify modularity in neural networks? The paper investigates this by comparing upstream and downstream methods for measuring functional similarity between hidden units.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that dropout increases modularity by making hidden units redundant, and that upstream and downstream definitions of functional similarity yield different clusters, indicating a misalignment between input-driven and output-driven neural representations.
papers.conclusion: The study concludes that upstream and downstream ways of thinking about neural representations are not necessarily aligned, which has implications for representation learning and the definition of modularity.
papers.key_findings:
Dropout dramatically increases modularity, contrary to the initial hypothesis that it would decrease modularity.
L2 regularization also increases modularity, while L1 regularization has a more modest effect.
Upstream and downstream methods for measuring functional similarity agree within their families but disagree across families, leading to different cluster assignments.
The redundancy-inducing effect of dropout increases the clusterability of units.
Training increases cluster-similarity among upstream methods but not downstream methods.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to feedforward networks on MNIST, which may not have a meaningful modular solution.
Pairwise independence does not guarantee groupwise independence, which could be a limitation of the method.
future_direction: Applying the methods to larger networks trained on more structured data, and to recurrent networks.
Evaluating the effect of maximizing modularity during training to see if it leads to performance benefits.
papers.abstract: It has been hypothesized that some form of "modular" structure in artificial neural networks should be useful for learning, compositionality, and generalization. However, defining and quantifying modularity remains an open problem. We cast the problem of detecting functional modules into the problem of detecting clusters of similar-functioning units. This begs the question of what makes two units functionally similar. For this, we consider two broad families of methods: those that define similarity based on how units respond to structured variations in inputs ("upstream"), and those based on how variations in hidden unit activations affect outputs ("downstream"). We conduct an empirical study quantifying modularity of hidden layer representations of simple feedforward, fully connected networks, across a range of hyperparameters. For each model, we quantify pairwise associations between hidden units in each layer using a variety of both upstream and downstream measures, then cluster them by maximizing their "modularity score" using established tools from network science. We find two surprising results: first, dropout dramatically increased modularity, while other forms of weight regularization had more modest effects. Second, although we observe that there is usually good agreement about clusters within both upstream methods and downstream methods, there is little agreement about the cluster assignments across these two families of methods. This has important implications for representation-learning, as it suggests that finding modular representations that reflect structure in inputs (e.g. disentanglement) may be a distinct goal from learning modular representations that reflect structure in outputs (e.g. compositionality).

papers.title: Do Llamas Work in English? On the Latent Language of Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: Do multilingual language models trained on English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual transformers like Llama-2 use English as an internal pivot language, with intermediate layers representing concepts in English before mapping to the target language, indicating an English bias in their internal representations.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual LLMs have an English bias in their internal representations, which may lead to linguistic biases and has implications for equitable AI.
papers.key_findings:
In translation tasks, intermediate layers decode the English version of the correct next token before switching to the target language.
The forward pass goes through three phases: input space, concept space (biased towards English), and output space.
Token energy is low in middle layers, indicating that latents are in a concept space orthogonal to token space.
The English bias is less pronounced for languages with single-token words (like Chinese) in repetition tasks.
The same pattern is observed in Mistral-7B, suggesting generality of the phenomenon.
papers.limitation:
Focus on Llama-2 family, so claims may not generalize to other models.
Tasks are simple and controlled, not real-world.
Limited understanding of the concept space structure.
Logit lens only reveals part of the internal state.
future_direction: Investigate how English bias affects downstream model behavior.
Study how English bias changes with different training data or tokenizers.
Extend to a wider range of tasks and models.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
papers.limitation: Layer removal has a more significant negative effect on generative tasks compared to multiple-choice tasks, especially for smaller models.
future_direction: Exploring post-training to restore performance after pruning
Improving model training efficiency by reducing inherent redundancy
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in performance, their size has escalated significantly, with current LLMs containing billions or even trillions of parameters. However, in this study, we discovered that many layers of LLMs exhibit high similarity, and some layers play a negligible role in network functionality. Based on this observation, we define a metric called Block Influence (BI) to gauge the significance of each layer in LLMs. We then propose a straightforward pruning approach: layer removal, in which we directly delete the redundant layers in LLMs based on their BI scores. Experiments demonstrate that our method, which we call ShortGPT, significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in model pruning. Moreover, ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization-like methods, enabling further reduction in parameters and computation. The ability to achieve better results through simple layer removal, as opposed to more complex pruning techniques, suggests a high degree of redundancy in the model architecture.

papers.title: Representations Shape Weak-to-Strong Generalization: Theoretical Insights and Empirical Predictions
papers.research_question: What intrinsic properties of weak and strong models enable weak-to-strong generalization, and how can we characterize their interaction through representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a theoretical framework for weak-to-strong generalization based on the overlap between the principal representations of weak and strong models, and introduces a representation-based metric that predicts W2SG performance without ground truth labels.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the interaction between weak and strong models' representations determines W2SG, and their representation-based metric effectively predicts performance, offering insights for managing W2SG.
papers.key_findings:
W2SG is characterized by the overlap between what the weak model cannot learn and what the strong model can learn using their principal representations.
The projection of labels onto this overlap space quantifies how much the strong model falls short of its full potential due to weak supervision (PredGap).
The theory explains benign overfitting in W2SG, where the strong model overfits weak supervision but still generalizes well.
A representation-based metric derived from the theory strongly correlates with W2SG performance across diverse datasets and models.
The metric predicts W2SG trends without requiring ground truth labels and is robust to hyperparameter choices.
papers.limitation: Using activation maps as representations is a simple heuristic; more principled methods for extracting representations could improve results.
future_direction: Explore more principled methods for defining and extracting representations from LLMs.
Apply the metric to topic-specific representations to predict W2SG for tasks within specific domains.
papers.abstract: Weak-to-Strong Generalization (W2SG), where a weak model supervises a stronger one, serves as an important analogy for understanding how humans might guide superhuman intelligence in the future. Promising empirical results revealed that a strong model can surpass its weak supervisor. While recent work has offered theoretical insights into this phenomenon, a clear understanding of the interactions between weak and strong models that drive W2SG remains elusive. We investigate W2SG through a theoretical lens and show that it can be characterized using kernels derived from the principal components of weak and strong models' internal representations. These kernels can be used to define a space that, at a high level, captures what the weak model is unable to learn but is learnable by the strong model. The projection of labels onto this space quantifies how much the strong model falls short of its full potential due to weak supervision. This characterization also provides insights into how certain errors in weak supervision can be corrected by the strong model, regardless of overfitting. Our theory has significant practical implications, providing a representation-based metric that predicts W2SG performance trends without requiring labels, as shown in experiments on molecular predictions with transformers and 5 NLP tasks involving 52 LLMs.

papers.title: How a student becomes a teacher: learning and forgetting through Spectral methods
papers.research_question: Can an invariant subnetwork be identified in an overparameterized student network that mimics a teacher network, and can a spectral optimization method achieve this?
papers.core_contribution: A spectral training method that, with regularization, identifies an invariant subnetwork within an overparameterized student network that mirrors the teacher's structure and retains full performance when pruned.
papers.conclusion: The spectral training method enables identification of a minimal, efficient subnetwork that retains performance and recovers the teacher's topological features, outperforming conventional weight decay and parametrization.
papers.key_findings:
The spectral method with regularization identifies an invariant subnetwork in the student that matches the teacher's size.
Pruning based on eigenvalue magnitude does not degrade performance until the invariant core is removed, exhibiting a phase-transition-like behavior.
The path distribution of the pruned student matches that of the teacher, unlike conventionally trained networks.
The method generalizes to various datasets (e.g., MNIST, CIFAR-100) and architectures (e.g., ResNet50).
The spectral parametrization yields a node importance ranking via eigenvalues, enabling effective structural pruning.
papers.limitation:
Experiments employ straightforward student network architectures; more complex architectures need to be tested for general conclusions.
The method has been validated on relatively simple datasets; generalization to more complex, real-world datasets is an open question.
The analysis focuses on ranking nodes in hidden layers; input neurons are not included, which could provide insights on relevant features.
future_direction: Extending the parametrization techniques to more advanced network architectures.
Testing the proposed techniques on larger and more complex real-world datasets.
Including input neurons in the analysis to identify key relevant features.
papers.abstract: In theoretical ML, the teacher-student paradigm is often employed as an effective metaphor for real-life tuition. The above scheme proves particularly relevant when the student network is overparameterized as compared to the teacher network. Under these operating conditions, it is tempting to speculate that the student ability to handle the given task could be eventually stored in a sub-portion of the whole network. This latter should be to some extent reminiscent of the frozen teacher structure, according to suitable metrics, while being approximately invariant across different architectures of the student candidate network. Unfortunately, state-of-the-art conventional learning techniques could not help in identifying the existence of such an invariant subnetwork, due to the inherent degree of non-convexity that characterizes the examined problem. In this work, we take a leap forward by proposing a radically different optimization scheme which builds on a spectral representation of the linear transfer of information between layers. The gradient is hence calculated with respect to both eigenvalues and eigenvectors with negligible increase in terms of computational and complexity load, as compared to standard training algorithms. Working in this framework, we could isolate a stable student substructure, that mirrors the true complexity of the teacher in terms of computing neurons, path distribution and topological attributes. When pruning unimportant nodes of the trained student, as follows a ranking that reflects the optimized eigenvalues, no degradation in the recorded performance is seen above a threshold that corresponds to the effective teacher size. The observed behavior can be pictured as a genuine second-order phase transition that bears universality traits.

papers.title: Pretraining with Artificial Language: Studying Transferable Knowledge in Language Models
papers.research_question: What kind of structural knowledge learned in neural network encoders is transferable to processing natural language?
papers.core_contribution: Pretraining with an artificial language that has a nesting dependency structure provides transferable knowledge to natural language tasks, and the transferred knowledge is related to position-aware context dependence.
papers.conclusion: The transferable knowledge in pretrained encoders can be characterized as position-aware context dependence, meaning tokens in a sequence can be characterized by their neighbor tokens at specific positions.
papers.key_findings:
Pretraining with an artificial language that models statistical dependency within a sentence (Log-linear) provides a useful inductive bias for natural language modeling.
A nesting head-to-tail dependency structure is more beneficial for transfer than a flat structure.
Encoders pretrained on languages with nesting dependency structures are better at capturing local contextual information, which is important for tasks like dependency parsing.
The amount of contextual information encoded by the pretrained encoder (as measured by a probing task) correlates with its transfer performance in some cases.
The Uniform and Zipf languages, which lack token dependencies, degrade encoder performance compared to random initialization.
papers.limitation: The knowledge of position-aware context dependence may not explain every aspect of the success of cross-lingual transfer.
future_direction: Investigate how model size affects the transferability of the encoder.
Investigate if there is any difference in the knowledge transferred among different downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: We investigate what kind of structural knowledge learned in neural network encoders is transferable to processing natural language. We design artificial languages with structural properties that mimic natural language, pretrain encoders on the data, and see how much performance the encoder exhibits on downstream tasks in natural language. Our experimental results show that pretraining with an artificial language with a nesting dependency structure provides some knowledge transferable to natural language. A follow-up probing analysis indicates that its success in the transfer is related to the amount of encoded contextual information and what is transferred is the knowledge of position-aware context dependence of language. Our results provide insights into how neural network encoders process human languages and the source of cross-lingual transferability of recent multilingual language models.

papers.title: Representation Convergence: Mutual Distillation is Secretly a Form of Regularization
papers.research_question: What hinders reinforcement learning agents from generalizing like humans? How can we enable them to learn robust representations that drive human-like generalization behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that mutual distillation between reinforcement learning policies acts as an implicit regularization by improving policy robustness to irrelevant features, which leads to better generalization performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that mutual distillation is a form of implicit regularization that improves generalization in reinforcement learning by enhancing policy robustness to irrelevant features and promoting invariant representations.
papers.key_findings:
Theoretically, improving policy robustness to irrelevant features enhances generalization performance.
Empirically, mutual distillation (DML) improves generalization performance across Procgen environments.
DML leads to more robust representations that are invariant to irrelevant features, as visualized by t-SNE.
The proposed MDPO algorithm consistently outperforms the PPO baseline in generalization.
Ablation studies indicate the improvement is due to regularization against irrelevant features, not merely additional information sharing.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we argue that mutual distillation between reinforcement learning policies serves as an implicit regularization, preventing them from overfitting to irrelevant features. We highlight two separate contributions: (i) Theoretically, for the first time, we prove that enhancing the policy robustness to irrelevant features leads to improved generalization performance. (ii) Empirically, we demonstrate that mutual distillation between policies contributes to such robustness, enabling the spontaneous emergence of invariant representations over pixel inputs. Ultimately, we do not claim to achieve state-of-the-art performance but rather focus on uncovering the underlying principles of generalization and deepening our understanding of its mechanisms.

papers.title: Contextures: The Mechanism of Representation Learning
papers.research_question: What representations do foundation models learn, and why are these representations useful for a variety of downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation establishes the contexture theory, which characterizes representation learning as learning the association between input X and a context variable A, and proves that learning the top singular functions of this association yields optimal representations for downstream tasks compatible with the context.
papers.conclusion: The contexture theory provides a unified framework for understanding representation learning, showing that representations are learned from associations with context variables, and that improving contexts is key for advancing foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
Representations are learned from the association between the input X and a context variable A, termed the contexture.
Learning the top singular functions of the expectation operator induced by the context yields optimal representations for tasks compatible with that context.
Scaling up model size alone leads to diminishing returns; further improvement requires better contexts.
A context is most useful when the association between X and A is neither too strong nor too weak, leading to a moderate decay rate of singular values.
Multiple contexts can be mixed (via convolution, convex combination, or concatenation) to create better contexts from existing ones.
papers.abstract: This dissertation establishes the contexture theory to mathematically characterize the mechanism of representation learning, or pretraining. Despite the remarkable empirical success of foundation models, it is not very clear what representations they learn, and why these representations are useful for various downstream tasks. A scientific understanding of representation learning is critical, especially at this point when scaling up the model size is producing diminishing returns, and designing new pretraining methods is imperative for further progress. Prior work treated different representation learning methods quite differently, whereas the contexture theory provides a unified framework for analyzing these methods. The central argument is that a representation is learned from the association between the input X and a context variable A. We prove that if an encoder captures the maximum information of this association, in which case we say that the encoder learns the contexture, then it will be optimal on the class of tasks that are compatible with the context. We also show that a context is the most useful when the association between X and A is neither too strong nor too weak. The important implication of the contexture theory is that increasing the model size alone will achieve diminishing returns, and further advancements require better contexts. We demonstrate that many pretraining objectives can learn the contexture, including supervised learning, self-supervised learning, generative models, etc. Then, we introduce two general objectives -- SVME and KISE, for learning the contexture. We also show how to mix multiple contexts together, an effortless way to create better contexts from existing ones. Then, we prove statistical learning bounds for representation learning. Finally, we discuss the effect of the data distribution shift from pretraining to the downstream task.

papers.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 3.1, Knowledge Storage and Extraction
papers.research_question: How do language models memorize knowledge during training, and extract it later to answer questions or perform logical reasoning during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that knowledge augmentation (e.g., paraphrasing, sentence shuffling) in pretraining data is crucial for reliable knowledge extraction via instruction fine-tuning, and introduces linear probing techniques to explain this phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes with practical recommendations for LLM pretraining: data rewriting (augmentation) is important, and including instruction-like data in pretraining is beneficial.
papers.key_findings:
Mixed training (pretraining on both biographies and QA data) enables knowledge extraction, but the model learns in an abnormal way (first from QA then correlates with BIO).
Without knowledge augmentation in pretraining, instruction fine-tuning fails to extract knowledge (0% accuracy).
Knowledge augmentation (e.g., paraphrasing, sentence shuffling, translations) during pretraining enables knowledge extraction after fine-tuning.
Linear probing shows that knowledge augmentation causes knowledge to be linearly encoded in the hidden embeddings of entity names, whereas without augmentation it is distributed across tokens.
Including celebrity data (with augmentation) in pretraining improves knowledge extraction for minority data (without augmentation).
future_direction: Studying logical reasoning and knowledge manipulation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can store a vast amount of world knowledge, often extractable via question-answering (e.g., "What is Abraham Lincoln's birthday?"). However, do they answer such questions based on exposure to similar questions during training (i.e., cheating), or by genuinely learning to extract knowledge from sources like Wikipedia? In this paper, we investigate this issue using a controlled biography dataset. We find a strong correlation between the model's ability to extract knowledge and various diversity measures of the training data. $\textbf{Essentially}$, for knowledge to be reliably extracted, it must be sufficiently augmented (e.g., through paraphrasing, sentence shuffling, translations) $\textit{during pretraining}$. Without such augmentation, knowledge may be memorized but not extractable, leading to 0% accuracy, regardless of subsequent instruction fine-tuning. To understand why this occurs, we employ (nearly) linear probing to demonstrate a strong connection between the observed correlation and how the model internally encodes knowledge -- whether it is linearly encoded in the hidden embeddings of entity names or distributed across other token embeddings in the training text. This paper provides $\textbf{several key recommendations for LLM pretraining in the industry}$: (1) rewrite the pretraining data -- using small, auxiliary models -- to provide knowledge augmentation, and (2) incorporate more instruction-finetuning data into the pretraining stage before it becomes too late.

papers.title: The Internal State of an LLM Knows When It's Lying
papers.research_question: Can the internal state of an LLM be used to reveal the truthfulness of statements, both provided to and generated by the LLM?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that LLM internal activations contain information about statement truthfulness and introduces SAPLMA, a classifier that uses these activations to detect false statements with higher accuracy than baselines like few-shot prompting.
papers.conclusion: SAPLMA leverages LLM hidden activations to predict statement truthfulness, offering a way to filter false information and increase trust in LLM-generated content.
papers.key_findings:
SAPLMA achieves accuracy between 60% to 80% on specific topics with OPT-6.7b and 70% to 90% with LLAMA2-7b, outperforming few-shot prompting which maxes at 56% accuracy.
The optimal hidden layer for SAPLMA varies between models, e.g., 20th layer for OPT-6.7b and middle layer for LLAMA2-7b.
Sentence probability assigned by the LLM is not a reliable indicator of truthfulness due to dependencies on sentence length and word frequencies.
SAPLMA can classify both externally provided statements and those generated by the LLM itself.
The method does not require fine-tuning the LLM, using only a trained classifier on frozen activations.
papers.limitation:
The method detects binary true/false, but in practice, detecting uncertainty or confidence levels might be more useful.
Tested only in English; applicability to multilingual settings is not verified.
For longer responses, activation values might need decoupling to isolate the most recent statement.
future_direction: Apply SAPLMA to larger LLMs and conduct human interaction experiments.
Study how activations develop over time as additional words are generated.
Extend to multilingual input and test cross-language applicability.
papers.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown exceptional performance in various tasks, one of their most prominent drawbacks is generating inaccurate or false information with a confident tone. In this paper, we provide evidence that the LLM's internal state can be used to reveal the truthfulness of statements. This includes both statements provided to the LLM, and statements that the LLM itself generates. Our approach is to train a classifier that outputs the probability that a statement is truthful, based on the hidden layer activations of the LLM as it reads or generates the statement. Experiments demonstrate that given a set of test sentences, of which half are true and half false, our trained classifier achieves an average of 71\% to 83\% accuracy labeling which sentences are true versus false, depending on the LLM base model. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between our classifier's performance and approaches based on the probability assigned to the sentence by the LLM. We show that while LLM-assigned sentence probability is related to sentence truthfulness, this probability is also dependent on sentence length and the frequencies of words in the sentence, resulting in our trained classifier providing a more reliable approach to detecting truthfulness, highlighting its potential to enhance the reliability of LLM-generated content and its practical applicability in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: How Large Language Models Encode Context Knowledge? A Layer-Wise Probing Study
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode context knowledge across different layers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a layer-wise probing framework to study how LLMs encode context knowledge, finding that more context knowledge is encoded in upper layers and that knowledge-related entity tokens encode knowledge earlier, with knowledge spreading to other tokens via attention.
papers.conclusion: Proposes a novel layer-wise probing framework for explaining how LLMs encode context knowledge, demonstrating that LLMs encode more knowledge in upper layers and transfer knowledge from entity tokens to other tokens, with retention diminishing with irrelevant evidence.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs prefer to encode more context knowledge in the upper layers.
LLMs primarily encode context knowledge within knowledge-related entity tokens at lower layers while progressively expanding more knowledge within other tokens at upper layers.
LLMs gradually forget the earlier context knowledge retained within the intermediate layers when provided with irrelevant evidence.
Base models have lower capability to encode knowledge through prompting compared to chat models.
The long-term memory capability of LLMs degrades when irrelevant evidence is introduced.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical mechanism behind the observed phenomena remains an open issue.
Experiments are limited to LLaMA 2 models, ignoring other SOTA models.
future_direction: Mathematical understanding of the role of self-attention in knowledge transfer.
Experiments on more PLMs (e.g., PaLM, OPT, Pythia).
papers.abstract: Previous work has showcased the intriguing capability of large language models (LLMs) in retrieving facts and processing context knowledge. However, only limited research exists on the layer-wise capability of LLMs to encode knowledge, which challenges our understanding of their internal mechanisms. In this paper, we devote the first attempt to investigate the layer-wise capability of LLMs through probing tasks. We leverage the powerful generative capability of ChatGPT to construct probing datasets, providing diverse and coherent evidence corresponding to various facts. We employ $\mathcal V$-usable information as the validation metric to better reflect the capability in encoding context knowledge across different layers. Our experiments on conflicting and newly acquired knowledge show that LLMs: (1) prefer to encode more context knowledge in the upper layers; (2) primarily encode context knowledge within knowledge-related entity tokens at lower layers while progressively expanding more knowledge within other tokens at upper layers; and (3) gradually forget the earlier context knowledge retained within the intermediate layers when provided with irrelevant evidence. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/Jometeorie/probing_llama.

papers.title: Birds have four legs?! NumerSense: Probing Numerical Commonsense Knowledge of Pre-trained Language Models
papers.research_question: Does and to what extent do pre-trained language models capture numerical commonsense knowledge, and how robust is this knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a probing task and dataset (NumerSense) to evaluate numerical commonsense knowledge in pre-trained language models, finding that models perform poorly and are brittle to adversarial perturbations.
papers.conclusion: Powerful pre-trained models such as BERT and RoBERTa perform surprisingly poorly on numerical commonsense knowledge even after fine-tuning, and the introduced dataset provides a basis for future improvement.
papers.key_findings:
BERT and RoBERTa perform poorly on numerical commonsense knowledge without fine-tuning.
Fine-tuning with distant supervision improves performance but still far from human performance.
Models are brittle to adversarial examples (e.g., inserting adjectives).
Attention analysis shows that important words for numerical commonsense (subject/object) receive low attention weights.
Open-domain QA models also perform poorly on 'how-many' questions derived from NumerSense.
future_direction: Improving PTLMs' abilities to faithfully capture (numerical) commonsense.
Populating numerical facts in current commonsense knowledge bases.
Improving open-domain QA for 'how-many' questions.
Incorporating more structured inductive biases (e.g., dependencies and semantic roles) in pre-training.
Controlling bias in masked language modeling.
papers.abstract: Recent works show that pre-trained language models (PTLMs), such as BERT, possess certain commonsense and factual knowledge. They suggest that it is promising to use PTLMs as "neural knowledge bases" via predicting masked words. Surprisingly, we find that this may not work for numerical commonsense knowledge (e.g., a bird usually has two legs). In this paper, we investigate whether and to what extent we can induce numerical commonsense knowledge from PTLMs as well as the robustness of this process. To study this, we introduce a novel probing task with a diagnostic dataset, NumerSense, containing 13.6k masked-word-prediction probes (10.5k for fine-tuning and 3.1k for testing). Our analysis reveals that: (1) BERT and its stronger variant RoBERTa perform poorly on the diagnostic dataset prior to any fine-tuning; (2) fine-tuning with distant supervision brings some improvement; (3) the best supervised model still performs poorly as compared to human performance (54.06% vs 96.3% in accuracy).

papers.title: Network Transplanting (extended abstract)
papers.research_question: How to merge several pre-trained convolutional networks for different categories and tasks into a generic, modular neural network with few or no additional training annotations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes network transplanting, a method to merge pre-trained networks into a modular transplant net with minimal data, and introduces back-distillation to optimize adapters without fine-tuning existing modules.
papers.conclusion: Network transplanting is an effective method for building generic neural networks by merging pre-trained modules, and back-distillation significantly reduces the need for training samples.
papers.key_findings:
Network transplanting with back-distillation achieves lower error rates in classification compared to baselines, even without training samples.
In segmentation, back-distillation improves pixel accuracy by 10-12% over direct learning with few samples.
The method allows sequential absorption of category modules without catastrophic forgetting.
Back-distillation enables learning adapters with few or no annotations, reducing start-up cost.
papers.abstract: This paper focuses on a new task, i.e., transplanting a category-and-task-specific neural network to a generic, modular network without strong supervision. We design a functionally interpretable structure for the generic network. Like building LEGO blocks, we teach the generic network a new category by directly transplanting the module corresponding to the category from a pre-trained network with a few or even without sample annotations. Our method incrementally adds new categories to the generic network but does not affect representations of existing categories. In this way, our method breaks the typical bottleneck of learning a net for massive tasks and categories, i.e., the requirement of collecting samples for all tasks and categories at the same time before the learning begins. Thus, we use a new distillation algorithm, namely back-distillation, to overcome specific challenges of network transplanting. Our method without training samples even outperformed the baseline with 100 training samples.

papers.title: Concept Distillation: Leveraging Human-Centered Explanations for Model Improvement
papers.research_question: If CAVs can identify and quantify sensitivity to concepts, can they also be used to improve the model? Can we learn less biased and more human-centered models?
papers.core_contribution: Extends Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) from post-hoc analysis to ante-hoc model improvement via a concept loss and concept distillation using a teacher model, enabling model debiasing and prior knowledge induction.
papers.conclusion: Concept distillation and concept loss provide a framework for improving model interpretability, reducing biases, and inducing prior knowledge by leveraging human-centered explanations.
papers.key_findings:
Concept-sensitive training with a concept loss can debias models on synthetic (ColorMNIST, DecoyMNIST, TextureMNIST) and real-world (BFFHQ) datasets.
Using a large pre-trained teacher model (DINO) for concept distillation improves concept learning and debiasing performance compared to using the student model alone.
Extending CAV sensitivity calculation to intermediate layers via class prototypes enhances the method's effectiveness.
The method can induce human-centered concepts as priors in non-classification tasks, demonstrated on Intrinsic Image Decomposition (IID).
The approach is zero-shot and does not require architectural changes or direct concept supervision.
papers.abstract: Humans use abstract concepts for understanding instead of hard features. Recent interpretability research has focused on human-centered concept explanations of neural networks. Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) estimate a model's sensitivity and possible biases to a given concept. In this paper, we extend CAVs from post-hoc analysis to ante-hoc training in order to reduce model bias through fine-tuning using an additional Concept Loss. Concepts were defined on the final layer of the network in the past. We generalize it to intermediate layers using class prototypes. This facilitates class learning in the last convolution layer, which is known to be most informative. We also introduce Concept Distillation to create richer concepts using a pre-trained knowledgeable model as the teacher. Our method can sensitize or desensitize a model towards concepts. We show applications of concept-sensitive training to debias several classification problems. We also use concepts to induce prior knowledge into IID, a reconstruction problem. Concept-sensitive training can improve model interpretability, reduce biases, and induce prior knowledge. Please visit https://avani17101.github.io/Concept-Distilllation/ for code and more details.

papers.title: Factorizing Knowledge in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can a pretrained neural network be decomposed into task-wise disentangled factor networks that can be assembled without fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Knowledge Factorization (KF), a method to decompose a pretrained teacher network into task-disentangled factor networks, each with a shared common-knowledge module and task-specific module, enabling plug-and-play assembly without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge Factorization effectively decomposes a pretrained teacher into task-disentangled factor networks that are modular, interpretable, and readily integratable, demonstrating strong performance and transferability.
papers.key_findings:
Factor networks achieve competitive or better predictive performance compared to knowledge distillation baselines on dedicated tasks.
Factor networks exhibit disentangled representations, as measured by various disentanglement metrics and representation similarity analysis.
The common-knowledge module learned via KF benefits transfer learning to unseen downstream tasks.
KF resolves the negative transfer problem in multi-task learning by structurally and representationally separating task-specific knowledge.
KF provides modularity and scalability, allowing the construction of combined-task networks by assembling factor networks without retraining.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we explore a novel and ambitious knowledge-transfer task, termed Knowledge Factorization~(KF). The core idea of KF lies in the modularization and assemblability of knowledge: given a pretrained network model as input, KF aims to decompose it into several factor networks, each of which handles only a dedicated task and maintains task-specific knowledge factorized from the source network. Such factor networks are task-wise disentangled and can be directly assembled, without any fine-tuning, to produce the more competent combined-task networks. In other words, the factor networks serve as Lego-brick-like building blocks, allowing us to construct customized networks in a plug-and-play manner. Specifically, each factor network comprises two modules, a common-knowledge module that is task-agnostic and shared by all factor networks, alongside with a task-specific module dedicated to the factor network itself. We introduce an information-theoretic objective, InfoMax-Bottleneck~(IMB), to carry out KF by optimizing the mutual information between the learned representations and input. Experiments across various benchmarks demonstrate that, the derived factor networks yield gratifying performances on not only the dedicated tasks but also disentanglement, while enjoying much better interpretability and modularity. Moreover, the learned common-knowledge representations give rise to impressive results on transfer learning. Our code is available at https://github.com/Adamdad/KnowledgeFactor.

papers.title: Understanding and Leveraging the Learning Phases of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What are the learning dynamics of neural networks, specifically the existence of phases in reconstruction loss during training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper empirically and theoretically demonstrates the existence of three phases in reconstruction loss during neural network training (near constant, decrease, increase) and shows that for transfer learning, pre-training should stop before optimal performance on the pre-training task.
papers.conclusion: The work highlights the existence of multiple phases in reconstruction loss during learning, providing insight that can be used to improve transfer learning via early stopping in pre-training.
papers.key_findings:
Empirical evidence shows three phases in reconstruction loss: near constant, decrease, and increase during training.
Theoretical proof for the existence of these phases in a single-layer linear classifier with a derived data model.
Reconstruction loss is minimal when the classifier is not yet fully optimized, indicating a trade-off between discriminative performance and input information retention.
For transfer learning, stopping pre-training early (when reconstruction loss is minimal) improves downstream task performance.
The phases are most pronounced in the last layers of the network, where features become more discriminative.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical analysis relies on assumptions about the data model and shallow networks (single dense layer and softmax layer).
The phases are most notable for the last layers of a network.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to deeper networks.
Investigating the prevalence of these phases in other architectures like RNNs and transformers.
papers.abstract: The learning dynamics of deep neural networks are not well understood. The information bottleneck (IB) theory proclaimed separate fitting and compression phases. But they have since been heavily debated. We comprehensively analyze the learning dynamics by investigating a layer's reconstruction ability of the input and prediction performance based on the evolution of parameters during training. We empirically show the existence of three phases using common datasets and architectures such as ResNet and VGG: (i) near constant reconstruction loss, (ii) decrease, and (iii) increase. We also derive an empirically grounded data model and prove the existence of phases for single-layer networks. Technically, our approach leverages classical complexity analysis. It differs from IB by relying on measuring reconstruction loss rather than information theoretic measures to relate information of intermediate layers and inputs. Our work implies a new best practice for transfer learning: We show empirically that the pre-training of a classifier should stop well before its performance is optimal.

papers.title: High-level features for resource economy and fast learning in skill transfer
papers.research_question: How can compact, high-level features be extracted from a neural network's activations in a task-agnostic way to enable effective and resource-efficient skill transfer to new tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that applying Slow Feature Analysis (SFA) to the last hidden layer activations of a trained network generates compact, interpretable features that are more effective for skill transfer than using the full layer or PCA features, offering better performance and resource economy.
papers.conclusion: SFA provides a principled, unsupervised method for transferring knowledge from a trained network to new problems, offering resource economy and generating quasi-symbolic, interpretable features useful for skill transfer.
papers.key_findings:
Features constructed with SFA are more economical (fewer units) and lead to better skill transfer performance than using the full set of layer activations or PCA features.
PCA is also helpful for resource economy in skill transfer but is not as effective as SFA in terms of success rate.
SFA and PCA capture interpretable high-level features such as joint angles, tip locations, and distance from tip to goal from the network's activation history.
SFA units with the lowest eigenvalues resemble symbolic representations that correlate with high-level task properties.
Transfer learning with SFA features leads to faster learning, especially with fewer training configurations, compared to other methods.
future_direction: Extend the experimental setup to a more continual, open-ended environment to learn representations of progressive complexity.
Integrate the slowness prior into the learning objective to create an end-to-end architecture.
Explore the effectiveness of other dimensionality reduction methods such as independent component analysis for skill transfer.
