papers.abstract: ion is an important aspect of intelligence which enables agents to construct robust representations for effective and efficient decision making. Although, deep neural networks are proven to be effective learning systems due to their ability to form increasingly complex abstractions at successive layers these abstractions are mostly distributed over many neurons, making the re-use of a learned skill costly and blind to the insights that can be obtained on the emergent representations. For avoiding designer bias and unsparing resource use, we propose to exploit neural response dynamics to form compact representations to use in skill transfer. For this, we consider two competing methods based on (1) maximum information compression principle and (2) the notion that abstract events tend to generate slowly changing signals, and apply them to the neural signals generated during task execution. To be concrete, in our simulation experiments, we either apply principal component analysis (PCA) or slow feature analysis (SFA) on the signals collected from the last hidden layer of a deep neural network while it performs a source task, and use these features for skill transfer in a new, target, task. We then compare the generalization and learning performance of these alternatives with the baselines of skill transfer with full layer output and no-transfer settings. Our experimental results on a simulated tabletop robot arm navigation task show that units that are created with SFA are the most successful for skill transfer. SFA as well as PCA, incur less resources compared to usual skill transfer where full layer outputs are used in the new task learning, whereby many units formed show a localized response reflecting end-effector-obstacle-goal relations. Finally, SFA units with the lowest eigenvalues resemble symbolic representations that highly correlate with high-level features such as joint angles and end-effector position which might be thought of as precursors for fully symbolic systems.

papers.title: How Post-Training Reshapes LLMs: A Mechanistic View on Knowledge, Truthfulness, Refusal, and Confidence
papers.research_question: How does post-training affect the internal mechanisms of large language models in terms of knowledge storage, truthfulness, refusal, and confidence?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a mechanistic analysis of how post-training affects LLMs internally, revealing which mechanisms are preserved (e.g., knowledge storage locations, truthfulness direction) and which are altered (e.g., refusal direction), with implications for model steering and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Post-training preserves some internal mechanisms (like knowledge storage and truthfulness direction) and alters others (like refusal direction), providing insights for model steering and future research in interpretability and LLM post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations in LLMs.
Post-training adapts knowledge representations from the base model while also developing new ones.
The truthfulness direction is highly similar between base and post-trained models and is effectively transferable for interventions.
The refusal direction differs between base and post-trained models and shows limited forward transferability.
Differences in confidence between base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons.
papers.limitation: Complex, multi-step processes such as reasoning and instruction-following are not well-captured by current mechanistic interpretability tools, limiting the scope of analysis.
future_direction: Design better post-training methods based on mechanistic insights.
Extend analysis to other capabilities like reasoning and instruction-following.
papers.abstract: Post-training is essential for the success of large language models (LLMs), transforming pre-trained base models into more useful and aligned post-trained models. While plenty of works have studied post-training algorithms and evaluated post-training models by their outputs, it remains understudied how post-training reshapes LLMs internally. In this paper, we compare base and post-trained LLMs mechanistically from four perspectives to better understand post-training effects. Our findings across model families and datasets reveal that: (1) Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations, and it adapts knowledge representations from the base model while developing new knowledge representations; (2) Both truthfulness and refusal can be represented by vectors in the hidden representation space. The truthfulness direction is highly similar between the base and post-trained model, and it is effectively transferable for interventions; (3) The refusal direction is different between the base and post-trained models, and it shows limited forward transferability; (4) Differences in confidence between the base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons. Our study provides insights into the fundamental mechanisms preserved and altered during post-training, facilitates downstream tasks like model steering, and could potentially benefit future research in interpretability and LLM post-training. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/HZD01/post-training-mechanistic-analysis.

papers.title: Knowledge Distillation: Enhancing Neural Network Compression with Integrated Gradients
papers.research_question: How can Integrated Gradients be integrated with Knowledge Distillation to enhance neural network compression while preserving interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a model compression method that integrates Integrated Gradients with Knowledge Distillation, using precomputed IG maps as data augmentation to guide the student model, achieving improved accuracy and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The method balances size reduction, performance preservation, and interpretability, providing a practical pathway for deploying neural networks in resource-constrained environments.
papers.key_findings:
The combined KD and IG method achieves 92.45% accuracy on CIFAR-10, a 1.02 percentage point improvement over the baseline student model.
The method achieves 4.1x compression and 10.8x reduction in inference time (from 140 ms to 13 ms).
Ablation studies show that KD and IG have complementary benefits when combined.
future_direction: Applying the approach to more complex datasets and network architectures.
Integrating other explainable AI techniques into the compression pipeline.
papers.abstract: Efficient deployment of deep neural networks on resource-constrained devices demands advanced compression techniques that preserve accuracy and interoperability. This paper proposes a machine learning framework that augments Knowledge Distillation (KD) with Integrated Gradients (IG), an attribution method, to optimise the compression of convolutional neural networks. We introduce a novel data augmentation strategy where IG maps, precomputed from a teacher model, are overlaid onto training images to guide a compact student model toward critical feature representations. This approach leverages the teacher's decision-making insights, enhancing the student's ability to replicate complex patterns with reduced parameters. Experiments on CIFAR-10 demonstrate the efficacy of our method: a student model, compressed 4.1-fold from the MobileNet-V2 teacher, achieves 92.5% classification accuracy, surpassing the baseline student's 91.4% and traditional KD approaches, while reducing inference latency from 140 ms to 13 ms--a tenfold speedup. We perform hyperparameter optimisation for efficient learning. Comprehensive ablation studies dissect the contributions of KD and IG, revealing synergistic effects that boost both performance and model explainability. Our method's emphasis on feature-level guidance via IG distinguishes it from conventional KD, offering a data-driven solution for mining transferable knowledge in neural architectures. This work contributes to machine learning by providing a scalable, interpretable compression technique, ideal for edge computing applications where efficiency and transparency are paramount.

papers.title: Representations as Language: An Information-Theoretic Framework for Interpretability
papers.research_question: What systematic structures emerge in the representations learned by transformers, and how do they relate to generalization and training dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an information-theoretic framework for interpretability that quantifies structure in representations, identifies two phases of training, and shows how representational structure relates to generalization and model size.
papers.conclusion: The linguistically-motivated approach helps characterize training dynamics and explain generalization, and suggests that intuitions from linguistics and cognitive science about good representations transfer to deep learning models.
papers.key_findings:
Two distinct phases of training: an initial phase of in-distribution learning where representations align with token and part-of-speech information, and a second phase where representations become robust to noise and compress.
Generalization performance improves during the second phase, linking generalization to robustness to noise.
Larger models compress their representations more than smaller models.
The proposed measures (information, variation, regularity, disentanglement) can predict which models will generalize best based on their representational structure.
papers.limitation:
Some results may be particular to the hyperparameters used for training.
The entropy estimation method is an approximation and makes minimal assumptions, but is invariant to linear transformations.
future_direction: Apply the analysis to large-scale translation tasks.
Extend the approach to other levels of abstraction and other models.
papers.abstract: Large scale neural models show impressive performance across a wide array of linguistic tasks. Despite this they remain, largely, black-boxes - inducing vector-representations of their input that prove difficult to interpret. This limits our ability to understand what they learn, and when the learn it, or describe what kinds of representations generalise well out of distribution. To address this we introduce a novel approach to interpretability that looks at the mapping a model learns from sentences to representations as a kind of language in its own right. In doing so we introduce a set of information-theoretic measures that quantify how structured a model's representations are with respect to its input, and when during training that structure arises. Our measures are fast to compute, grounded in linguistic theory, and can predict which models will generalise best based on their representations. We use these measures to describe two distinct phases of training a transformer: an initial phase of in-distribution learning which reduces task loss, then a second stage where representations becoming robust to noise. Generalisation performance begins to increase during this second phase, drawing a link between generalisation and robustness to noise. Finally we look at how model size affects the structure of the representational space, showing that larger models ultimately compress their representations more than their smaller counterparts.

papers.title: Analyzing the Inner Workings of Transformers in Compositional Generalization
papers.research_question: What type of syntactic features do Transformer models depend on in tasks requiring compositional generalization, and what internal mechanisms do they employ?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that Transformer models rely on syntactic features for compositional generalization but also develop non-compositional solutions internally; subnetworks with better generalization performance depend on both syntactic and non-syntactic features.
papers.conclusion: Transformer models develop non-compositional solutions internally and fail to generalize compositionally even when generalization performance is decent, suggesting a need for better inductive bias to utilize syntactic features.
papers.key_findings:
The base Transformer model depends on syntactic features (constituency and dependency) to output correct answers in compositional generalization tasks.
A subnetwork with much better generalization performance than the whole model relies on a non-compositional algorithm in addition to syntactic features.
The subnetwork improves its generalization performance relatively slowly during training compared to its in-distribution performance.
The non-compositional solution is acquired in the early stages of training.
The model's reliance on syntactic features varies between machine translation and semantic parsing tasks.
papers.limitation:
The compositional generalization tasks are based on synthetically generated datasets and might not represent the variety in natural language expressions.
The results may not transfer to larger models because the experiments used relatively small models trained on a small synthetic dataset.
future_direction: Consider other generalization patterns or other linguistic features to obtain a more profound insight into the linguistic competence of neural models.
papers.abstract: The compositional generalization abilities of neural models have been sought after for human-like linguistic competence. The popular method to evaluate such abilities is to assess the models' input-output behavior. However, that does not reveal the internal mechanisms, and the underlying competence of such models in compositional generalization remains unclear. To address this problem, we explore the inner workings of a Transformer model by finding an existing subnetwork that contributes to the generalization performance and by performing causal analyses on how the model utilizes syntactic features. We find that the model depends on syntactic features to output the correct answer, but that the subnetwork with much better generalization performance than the whole model relies on a non-compositional algorithm in addition to the syntactic features. We also show that the subnetwork improves its generalization performance relatively slowly during the training compared to the in-distribution one, and the non-compositional solution is acquired in the early stages of the training.

papers.title: Seeking Neural Nuggets: Knowledge Transfer in Large Language Models from a Parametric Perspective
papers.research_question: Whether implicit knowledge stored in the parameters of a larger language model (teacher) can be transferred to a smaller model (student) through a parametric perspective.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a parametric knowledge transfer paradigm that extracts task-specific parameters from a teacher model using sensitivity-based techniques and injects them into a student model via LoRA, demonstrating the transferability of implicit knowledge across LLMs of different scales.
papers.conclusion: Parametric knowledge transfer is feasible and effective; the proposed framework successfully transfers knowledge from larger to smaller LLMs, and the analysis highlights key factors that contribute to successful transfer.
papers.key_findings:
Transferring extracted parameters from a teacher to a student model consistently improves the student's performance across reasoning, professional knowledge, instruction-driven, and open-ended conversation benchmarks.
The structural integrity of the extracted parameters (e.g., preserving submatrices) is crucial for effective transfer, outperforming random or single-weight extraction.
Sensitivity-based parameter extraction outperforms random selection, and the origin of parameters (which modules) matters more than the sheer number of parameters transferred.
Scaling up the teacher model generally leads to better student performance, even when there are architectural differences between models.
The number of seed samples used for sensitivity calculation and the initialization strategy for the LoRA module are important factors influencing transfer efficacy.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) inherently encode a wealth of knowledge within their parameters through pre-training on extensive corpora. While prior research has delved into operations on these parameters to manipulate the underlying implicit knowledge (encompassing detection, editing, and merging), there remains an ambiguous understanding regarding their transferability across models with varying scales. In this paper, we seek to empirically investigate knowledge transfer from larger to smaller models through a parametric perspective. To achieve this, we employ sensitivity-based techniques to extract and align knowledge-specific parameters between different LLMs. Moreover, the LoRA module is used as the intermediary mechanism for injecting the extracted knowledge into smaller models. Evaluations across four benchmarks validate the efficacy of our proposed method. Our findings highlight the critical factors contributing to the process of parametric knowledge transfer, underscoring the transferability of model parameters across LLMs of different scales. Project website: https://maszhongming.github.io/ParaKnowTransfer.

papers.title: A framework for the emergence and analysis of language in social learning agents
papers.research_question: How are internal representations structured and optimized for communication between agents in social learning, and how does language emerge from such interactions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a teacher-student reinforcement learning framework with a sparse autoencoder to study emergent communication, showing that student feedback shapes the language embedding to prioritize policy information, improving task performance and generalization.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides insights into how language emerges from social interactions and how communication constraints shape internal representations, with implications for generalization in cooperative multi-agent systems.
papers.key_findings:
Providing teacher information to the student leads to higher task completion rates and the ability to generalize to unseen tasks.
Optimizing message content with student feedback improves information encoding, altering the latent structure to focus on policy (goal location and initial action) rather than state space (wall position).
The emergent communication exhibits properties of natural language such as compositionality (topographic similarity) and pressure towards entropy minimization.
Feeding back the student's own task information (closing-the-loop) retains some task-relevant information but results in degraded performance and loss of generalization to unknown goals.
Bi-directional communication (with feedback) is critical for transmitting helpful information and enhances the reconstruction capability of the autoencoder.
future_direction: Understanding how social agents reconcile abstractions from their own experience with those acquired through communication.
Achieving a balance between tutoring and learning in multi-task and multi-agent systems to maintain a relevant and generalizable message space.
papers.abstract: Neural systems have evolved not only to solve environmental challenges through internal representations but also, under social constraints, to communicate these to conspecifics. In this work, we aim to understand the structure of these internal representations and how they may be optimized to transmit pertinent information from one individual to another. Thus, we build on previous teacher-student communication protocols to analyze the formation of individual and shared abstractions and their impact on task performance. We use reinforcement learning in grid-world mazes where a teacher network passes a message to a student to improve task performance. This framework allows us to relate environmental variables with individual and shared representations. We compress high-dimensional task information within a low-dimensional representational space to mimic natural language features. In coherence with previous results, we find that providing teacher information to the student leads to a higher task completion rate and an ability to generalize tasks it has not seen before. Further, optimizing message content to maximize student reward improves information encoding, suggesting that an accurate representation in the space of messages requires bi-directional input. These results highlight the role of language as a common representation among agents and its implications on generalization capabilities.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Learning Representations: To What Extent Do\n Different Neural Networks Learn the Same Representation
papers.research_question: How similar are the representations learned by two networks with identical architecture but trained from different initializations?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a theory and efficient algorithms based on neuron activation subspace matches to analyze representation similarity, and finds that representations learned by differently initialized convolutional networks are not as similar as expected.
papers.conclusion: Representations learned by convolutional layers are not as similar as prevalently expected, raising fundamental questions about whether networks learn different representations or if subspace match is an inadequate metric.
papers.key_findings:
For most convolutional layers, the maximum match similarity is very low, indicating low overall similarity of representations.
Layers close to the output sometimes exhibit high similarity, likely due to alignment with the output task.
Layers close to the input show relatively high similarity, likely due to alignment with input data and low-dimensional nature.
Simple matches reveal that very few single neurons or small neuron sets learn similar representations.
The distribution of simple match sizes shows that similarity is not local, even in layers with high overall similarity.
papers.limitation: The result may indicate either that networks learn completely different representations or that the subspace match metric is not suitable for measuring representation similarity.
future_direction: Investigating what is the right metric for similarity of representations.
Systematic and in-depth study of representation similarity in deep learning.
papers.abstract:
It is widely believed that learning good representations is one of the main
reasons for the success of deep neural networks. Although highly intuitive,
there is a lack of theory and systematic approach quantitatively characterizing
what representations do deep neural networks learn. In this work, we move a
tiny step towards a theory and better understanding of the representations.
Specifically, we study a simpler problem: How similar are the representations
learned by two networks with identical architecture but trained from different
initializations. We develop a rigorous theory based on the neuron activation
subspace match model. The theory gives a complete characterization of the
structure of neuron activation subspace matches, where the core concepts are
maximum match and simple match which describe the overall and the finest
similarity between sets of neurons in two networks respectively. We also
propose efficient algorithms to find the maximum match and simple matches.
Finally, we conduct extensive experiments using our algorithms. Experimental
results suggest that, surprisingly, representations learned by the same
convolutional layers of networks trained from different initializations are not
as similar as prevalently expected, at least in terms of subspace match.

papers.title: Weight Space Structure and Internal Representations: A Direct Approach to Learning and Generalization in Multilayer Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How does the geometrical structure of the weight space in multilayer neural networks relate to learning and generalization capabilities for parity and committee machines?
papers.core_contribution: Analytically derives the geometrical structure of weight space in multilayer neural networks and provides exact results for learning and generalization in parity and committee machines, with an interpretation of replica symmetry breaking.
papers.conclusion: The geometrical approach provides insights into learning and generalization in multilayer neural networks, linking weight space structure to internal representations and replica symmetry breaking.
papers.key_findings:
For parity and committee machines, the number of dominant volumes ND and total volumes NR vanish at critical capacities, providing storage limits.
Replica symmetry breaking is geometrically interpreted in terms of weight space structure and internal representations.
In the limit of large hidden units, multilayer neural networks are exactly solvable models.
Generalization error for the parity machine transitions from high to low at α0 = log K / log 2.
For the committee machine, generalization error is smooth near the VC dimension and crosses over at α ~ K.
papers.limitation: Results are exact only in the limit of a large number of hidden units.
future_direction: Extend the calculation to the regime where α is on the order of K for the committee machine.
papers.abstract: We analytically derive the geometrical structure of the weight space in multilayer neural networks in terms of the volumes of couplings associated with the internal representations of the training set. In this framework, focusing on the parity and committee machines, we show how to deduce learning and generalization capabilities, both reinterpreting some known properties and finding new exact results. The relationship between our approach and information theory as well as the Mitchison-Durbin calculation is established. Our results are exact in the limit of a large number $K$ of hidden units, whereas for finite $K$ a complete geometrical interpretation of symmetry breaking is given.

papers.title: Does Deep Learning Learn to Abstract? A Systematic Probing Framework
papers.research_question: Does deep learning learn to abstract? The paper investigates whether pre-trained language models can learn abstract concepts (like grammar) from concrete instances and transfer them to new tasks, rather than just memorizing surface patterns.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a systematic probing framework to investigate abstraction capability in deep learning models and provides strong evidence that pre-trained language models (T5 and GPT2) can learn abstract concepts (like grammar) and transfer them to new tasks, rather than just memorizing surface patterns.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that pre-trained language models do have abstraction capability, as evidenced by the probing framework, and that this capability exhibits specific characteristics such as a two-stage learning process and concentration in middle-layer attention heads.
papers.key_findings:
The training phase exhibits a 'memorize-then-abstract' two-stage process.
The learned abstract concepts are gathered in a few middle-layer attention heads.
Abstraction capability is robust to concept mutations, and more robust to low-level/source-side mutations than high-level/target-side ones.
Generic pre-training is critical to the emergence of abstraction capability, and PLMs exhibit better abstraction with larger model sizes and data scales.
papers.limitation:
Lack of a quantitative metric for abstraction capability
Probing tasks are synthetic and may not fully capture natural language abstraction
papers.abstract: Abstraction is a desirable capability for deep learning models, which means to induce abstract concepts from concrete instances and flexibly apply them beyond the learning context. At the same time, there is a lack of clear understanding about both the presence and further characteristics of this capability in deep learning models. In this paper, we introduce a systematic probing framework to explore the abstraction capability of deep learning models from a transferability perspective. A set of controlled experiments are conducted based on this framework, providing strong evidence that two probed pre-trained language models (PLMs), T5 and GPT2, have the abstraction capability. We also conduct in-depth analysis, thus shedding further light: (1) the whole training phase exhibits a "memorize-then-abstract" two-stage process; (2) the learned abstract concepts are gathered in a few middle-layer attention heads, rather than being evenly distributed throughout the model; (3) the probed abstraction capabilities exhibit robustness against concept mutations, and are more robust to low-level/source-side mutations than high-level/target-side ones; (4) generic pre-training is critical to the emergence of abstraction capability, and PLMs exhibit better abstraction with larger model sizes and data scales.

papers.title: Understanding Learning Dynamics Through Structured Representations
papers.research_question: How do architectural structural choices influence learning dynamics, such as convergence, generalization, and adaptation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a structured neural architecture (PGNN) that decomposes layers into structured transformations and adaptive corrections, providing theoretical and empirical evidence that this design improves training stability, generalization, and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The structured-corrective architecture (PGNN) provides a principled way to embed inductive biases into neural networks, improving stability and generalization while preserving flexibility, offering a new perspective on architectural design.
papers.key_findings:
Structured transformations improve gradient conditioning and reduce vanishing/exploding gradients.
PGNN exhibits smaller generalization gaps across layers, indicating more stable and generalizable internal representations.
The corrective path adaptively compensates for structural deficiencies, allowing a trade-off between structure and flexibility.
Theoretical analysis shows convergence guarantees under Lipschitz conditions for recursive dynamics.
Empirical results show improved robustness, faster convergence under alignment, and reduced sensitivity to initialization and gradient noise.
papers.abstract: While modern deep networks have demonstrated remarkable versatility, their training dynamics remain poorly understood--often driven more by empirical tweaks than architectural insight. This paper investigates how internal structural choices shape the behavior of learning systems. Building on prior efforts that introduced simple architectural constraints, we explore the broader implications of structure for convergence, generalization, and adaptation. Our approach centers on a family of enriched transformation layers that incorporate constrained pathways and adaptive corrections. We analyze how these structures influence gradient flow, spectral sensitivity, and fixed-point behavior--uncovering mechanisms that contribute to training stability and representational regularity. Theoretical analysis is paired with empirical studies on synthetic and structured tasks, demonstrating improved robustness, smoother optimization, and scalable depth behavior. Rather than prescribing fixed templates, we emphasize principles of tractable design that can steer learning behavior in interpretable ways. Our findings support a growing view that architectural design is not merely a matter of performance tuning, but a critical axis for shaping learning dynamics in scalable and trustworthy neural systems.

papers.title: An overview of condensation phenomenon in deep learning
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the condensation phenomenon in neural networks, where neurons in the same layer condense into groups during nonlinear training, and discusses its implications for generalization and reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The condensation phenomenon is a common feature during nonlinear training that provides valuable insights into neural network behavior, from generalization to reasoning, and future work will advance theoretical understanding and practical applications.
papers.key_findings:
During the nonlinear training of neural networks, neurons in the same layer tend to condense into groups with similar outputs.
The number of condensed clusters of neurons in the same layer typically increases monotonically as training progresses.
Neural networks with small weight initializations or Dropout optimization can facilitate this condensation process.
The condensation phenomenon offers valuable insights into the generalization abilities of neural networks.
Condensation correlates to stronger reasoning abilities in transformer-based language models.
papers.limitation: The study of condensation is still in its early stages.
future_direction: Theoretical advancements and practical approaches to harness the condensation effect for more effective utilization of neural networks.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we provide an overview of a common phenomenon, condensation, observed during the nonlinear training of neural networks: During the nonlinear training of neural networks, neurons in the same layer tend to condense into groups with similar outputs. Empirical observations suggest that the number of condensed clusters of neurons in the same layer typically increases monotonically as training progresses. Neural networks with small weight initializations or Dropout optimization can facilitate this condensation process. We also examine the underlying mechanisms of condensation from the perspectives of training dynamics and the structure of the loss landscape. The condensation phenomenon offers valuable insights into the generalization abilities of neural networks and correlates to stronger reasoning abilities in transformer-based language models.

papers.title: Decoding In-Context Learning: Neuroscience-inspired Analysis of Representations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context learning, and how do these changes mediate improvement in behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired framework using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and Attention Ratio Analysis (ARA) to show that in-context learning improves task-critical representations and attention allocation, which correlate with behavioral gains.
papers.conclusion: ICL improves task-critical representations and attention allocation to relevant content in the prompt, and these representational changes are correlated with behavioral gains.
papers.key_findings:
ICL leads to changes in prompt embedding similarity matrices to better encode task-critical information, which in turn improves behavior.
ICL increases the decodability of task-critical information (e.g., line slope) from embeddings via probing classifiers.
ICL shifts attention to relevant content in the prompt (increased attention ratio to informative parts), which correlates with behavioral improvement.
These representational changes are consistent across multiple layers (except the first) in both Llama-2 and Vicuna models.
The proposed methods (RSA and ARA) provide scalable tools for analyzing latent representations in large language models.
future_direction: Study the effects of ICL on improving planning behavior in LLMs by analyzing latent representations before and after ICL in planning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable performance improvement through in-context learning (ICL) by leveraging task-specific examples in the input. However, the mechanisms behind this improvement remain elusive. In this work, we investigate how LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context-learning, and how these changes mediate improvement in behavior. We employ neuroscience-inspired techniques such as representational similarity analysis (RSA) and propose novel methods for parameterized probing and measuring ratio of attention to relevant vs. irrelevant information in Llama-2 70B and Vicuna 13B. We designed two tasks with a priori relationships among their conditions: linear regression and reading comprehension. We formed hypotheses about expected similarities in task representations and measured hypothesis alignment of LLM representations before and after ICL as well as changes in attention. Our analyses revealed a meaningful correlation between improvements in behavior after ICL and changes in both embeddings and attention weights across LLM layers. This empirical framework empowers a nuanced understanding of how latent representations shape LLM behavior, offering valuable tools and insights for future research and practical applications.

papers.title: Representational Distance Learning for Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can a student deep neural network learn from the internal representational spaces of a teacher model by matching their representational distance matrices (RDMs)?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Representational Distance Learning (RDL), a stochastic gradient descent method that uses auxiliary error functions to pull a student network's representational distance matrices (RDMs) toward those of a teacher network, enabling transfer learning even with architectural differences.
papers.conclusion: RDL is a promising method for transferring knowledge from a teacher model to a student DNN by matching their internal representational spaces, and may be used in the future to train DNNs using brain-activity measurements (e.g., fMRI-based RDMs) to build more realistic models of biological brains.
papers.key_findings:
RDL significantly improved visual classification performance on MNIST and CIFAR-100 compared to baseline networks without transfer learning.
RDL was competitive with other transfer learning techniques (finetuning, deep supervision, hints) on MNIST.
On CIFAR-100, RDL outperformed finetuning and performed comparably to deep supervision and hints.
Multidimensional scaling (MDS) visualizations showed that RDL pulled the student's RDMs toward the teacher's RDMs, especially at deeper layers.
RDL allows a student network to learn similar sequential transformations to those learned by a teacher network.
future_direction: Train DNNs using fMRI-based RDMs from the human visual ventral stream to build more realistic models of biological brains.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) provide useful models of visual representational transformations. We present a method that enables a DNN (student) to learn from the internal representational spaces of a reference model (teacher), which could be another DNN or, in the future, a biological brain. Representational spaces of the student and the teacher are characterized by representational distance matrices (RDMs). We propose representational distance learning (RDL), a stochastic gradient descent method that drives the RDMs of the student to approximate the RDMs of the teacher. We demonstrate that RDL is competitive with other transfer learning techniques for two publicly available benchmark computer vision datasets (MNIST and CIFAR-100), while allowing for architectural differences between student and teacher. By pulling the student's RDMs toward those of the teacher, RDL significantly improved visual classification performance when compared to baseline networks that did not use transfer learning. In the future, RDL may enable combined supervised training of deep neural networks using task constraints (e.g., images and category labels) and constraints from brain-activity measurements, so as to build models that replicate the internal representational spaces of biological brains.

papers.title: Mind Scramble: Unveiling Large Language Model Psychology Via Typoglycemia
papers.research_question: Does LLM possess human-like cognitive processes and mechanisms in reading and comprehending? The paper uses Typoglycemia to explore this.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces LLM Psychology, a framework that uses Typoglycemia experiments to study cognitive behaviors of LLMs. It finds that LLMs exhibit human-like behaviors but are fundamentally data-driven, and each LLM has a unique cognitive pattern.
papers.conclusion: The study advances research on aligning LLMs with human cognition and provides evidence that LLMs' abilities are data-driven, offering a case for LLM Psychology.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as slightly lower task accuracy with consuming more tokens and time.
Different LLMs show varying degrees of robustness to scrambled input, making it a democratized benchmark for model evaluation.
The impact of different task types varies, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) in scrambled format being more challenging.
LLMs' emergent human-like abilities are fundamentally statistical and data-driven, rather than genuinely resembling human cognition.
Each LLM exhibits its unique and consistent 'cognitive pattern' across various tasks, unveiling a general mechanism in its psychology process.
papers.abstract: Research into the external behaviors and internal mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) has shown promise in addressing complex tasks in the physical world. Studies suggest that powerful LLMs, like GPT-4, are beginning to exhibit human-like cognitive abilities, including planning, reasoning, and reflection. In this paper, we introduce a research line and methodology called LLM Psychology, leveraging human psychology experiments to investigate the cognitive behaviors and mechanisms of LLMs. We migrate the Typoglycemia phenomenon from psychology to explore the "mind" of LLMs. Unlike human brains, which rely on context and word patterns to comprehend scrambled text, LLMs use distinct encoding and decoding processes. Through Typoglycemia experiments at the character, word, and sentence levels, we observe: (I) LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as lower task accuracy and higher token/time consumption; (II) LLMs exhibit varying robustness to scrambled input, making Typoglycemia a benchmark for model evaluation without new datasets; (III) Different task types have varying impacts, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) being more challenging in scrambled form; (IV) Each LLM has a unique and consistent "cognitive pattern" across tasks, revealing general mechanisms in its psychology process. We provide an in-depth analysis of hidden layers to explain these phenomena, paving the way for future research in LLM Psychology and deeper interpretability.

papers.title: Talking Heads: Understanding Inter-layer Communication in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How is information represented and routed between layers in transformer language models, specifically through low-rank communication channels?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer LMs use low-rank subspaces (communication channels) in the residual stream to pass information between layers; these channels can be identified via SVD of weight matrices and are causally important for model behaviors.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn intricately structured representations through pretraining, and the discovered communication channels provide a mechanistic explanation for some prompt sensitivities, enabling improved model performance and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer LMs use low-rank (1D or 2D) subspaces in the residual stream for inter-layer communication.
These communication channels can be identified by applying SVD to weight matrices (OV and QK) and computing composition scores on the rank-1 components.
The identified channels are causally important for model behaviors, such as inhibition in the IOI task.
The model's sensitivity to item order in a list (Laundry List task) is explained by the limited capacity of these low-rank channels.
Model editing (zeroing or scaling components) based on these channels can significantly improve performance on the Laundry List task.
papers.limitation:
The method does not work for key composition (Appendix B).
Analysis is limited to two small models (GPT-2 small and Pythia 160m).
Difficulty in controlling all variables in the available data (Section 7).
future_direction: Future work in static weight analysis more generally.
More rigorous analysis of interactions between specific heads (e.g., 8.3 and 9.9).
Extending the method to analyze more complex behaviors.
papers.abstract: Although it is known that transformer language models (LMs) pass features from early layers to later layers, it is not well understood how this information is represented and routed by the model. We analyze a mechanism used in two LMs to selectively inhibit items in a context in one task, and find that it underlies a commonly used abstraction across many context-retrieval behaviors. Specifically, we find that models write into low-rank subspaces of the residual stream to represent features which are then read out by later layers, forming low-rank communication channels (Elhage et al., 2021) between layers. A particular 3D subspace in model activations in GPT-2 can be traversed to positionally index items in lists, and we show that this mechanism can explain an otherwise arbitrary-seeming sensitivity of the model to the order of items in the prompt. That is, the model has trouble copying the correct information from context when many items ``crowd" this limited space. By decomposing attention heads with the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), we find that previously described interactions between heads separated by one or more layers can be predicted via analysis of their weight matrices alone. We show that it is possible to manipulate the internal model representations as well as edit model weights based on the mechanism we discover in order to significantly improve performance on our synthetic Laundry List task, which requires recall from a list, often improving task accuracy by over 20%. Our analysis reveals a surprisingly intricate interpretable structure learned from language model pretraining, and helps us understand why sophisticated LMs sometimes fail in simple domains, facilitating future analysis of more complex behaviors.

papers.title: VISIT: Visualizing and Interpreting the Semantic Information Flow of Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we interpret and visualize the semantic information flow inside transformer language models, particularly focusing on attention heads and memory values?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a tool for visualizing the semantic information flow in transformer language models as an interactive flow graph, and provides new insights into layer norms as semantic filters and the existence of regularization neurons.
papers.conclusion: The work introduces a tool to visualize the semantic information flow in transformers using the logit lens, demonstrates its utility by revealing insights about layer norms and regularization neurons, and validates the approach by supporting other analyses.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads' semantics can be projected via the OV circuit, and only the heads with the largest norms dominate the block's output.
Memory values with the highest attention scores capture the semantics of their corresponding attention head.
Layer normalization layers act as semantic filters, demoting function words and promoting content words in the residual stream.
Regularization neurons exist that are consistently highly activated, have high entropy, and may serve as a constant bias or regularization term.
The flow-graph visualization tool can qualitatively replicate mechanistic analyses, such as indirect object identification, and reveal internal information flow patterns.
papers.limitation:
Limited to English language models, particularly GPT models with multi-head attention, and insights might not generalize to other languages or datasets.
Projection methods and the intersection score Ik have limitations in capturing semantic connections between different tokens with the same meaning.
Pruning based on the assumption that the most activated neurons determine the final prediction might be misleading as less activated neurons could also be relevant.
The methods are not causal and do not employ interventions, so further investigation is needed to fully understand the mechanisms.
future_direction: Apply causal interventions to verify the findings.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in interpretability suggest we can project weights and hidden states of transformer-based language models (LMs) to their vocabulary, a transformation that makes them more human interpretable. In this paper, we investigate LM attention heads and memory values, the vectors the models dynamically create and recall while processing a given input. By analyzing the tokens they represent through this projection, we identify patterns in the information flow inside the attention mechanism. Based on our discoveries, we create a tool to visualize a forward pass of Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPTs) as an interactive flow graph, with nodes representing neurons or hidden states and edges representing the interactions between them. Our visualization simplifies huge amounts of data into easy-to-read plots that can reflect the models' internal processing, uncovering the contribution of each component to the models' final prediction. Our visualization also unveils new insights about the role of layer norms as semantic filters that influence the models' output, and about neurons that are always activated during forward passes and act as regularization vectors.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: How Do the Architecture and Optimizer Affect Representation Learning? On the Training Dynamics of Representations in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do the architecture and optimizer affect the evolution of representations in various DNN layers during training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper elucidates the training dynamics of representations in deep neural networks using CKA similarity and a new decision regions similarity (DRS) approach, showing how architecture (ResNet vs. ViT) and optimizer (Adam vs. SGD) affect representation learning.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides detailed insights into representation learning dynamics, highlighting dependencies on architecture and optimizer, and proposes new analysis tools for future studies.
papers.key_findings:
Training phases are more distinguishable in SGD training than in Adam training, and for ViT than for ResNet.
ViT layers have synchronized dynamics of representation learning, unlike ResNet.
In Adam training, first-layer representations in convolutional networks become more similar to random representations in the perfect fitting regime.
Decision regions of deeper layers and DNN output become more fragmented during memorization phases, especially in ViT.
The implicit regularization of Adam affects representation learning dynamics, depending on DNN width and architecture.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we elucidate how representations in deep neural networks (DNNs) evolve during training. Our focus is on overparameterized learning settings where the training continues much after the trained DNN starts to perfectly fit its training data. We examine the evolution of learned representations along the entire training process. We explore the representational similarity of DNN layers, each layer with respect to its own representations throughout the training process. For this, we use two similarity metrics: (1) The centered kernel alignment (CKA) similarity; (2) Similarity of decision regions of linear classifier probes that we train for the DNN layers. We visualize and analyze the decision regions of the DNN output and the layer probes during the DNN training to show how they geometrically evolve. Our extensive experiments discover training dynamics patterns that can emerge in layers depending on the relative layer-depth, architecture and optimizer. Among our findings: (i) The training phases, including those related to memorization, are more distinguishable in SGD training than in Adam training, and for Vision Transformer (ViT) than for ResNet; (ii) Unlike ResNet, the ViT layers have synchronized dynamics of representation learning.

papers.title: The Knowledge Microscope: Features as Better Analytical Lenses than Neurons
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether features (obtained via Sparse Autoencoders) are better analytical units than neurons for understanding the mechanisms of factual knowledge in language models, addressing challenges of limited knowledge expression, poor interpretability, polysemanticity, and performance in downstream tasks like privacy erasure.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that features extracted via Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are superior analytical units to neurons for studying factual knowledge in language models, exhibiting stronger impact on knowledge expression, better interpretability, stronger monosemanticity, and enabling more effective privacy erasure through the proposed FeatureEdit method.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that features are better analytical units than neurons for understanding factual knowledge in language models, and the proposed FeatureEdit method effectively leverages features for privacy erasure.
papers.key_findings:
SAE is effective in decomposing neurons into features for studying factual knowledge mechanisms.
Features, especially post-MLP features, have a stronger impact on knowledge expression than neurons.
Features demonstrate superior interpretability compared to neurons.
Features exhibit stronger monosemanticity, with clear activation patterns for related facts and inactivity for unrelated ones.
The proposed feature-based editing method, FeatureEdit, outperforms neuron-based methods in erasing privacy-sensitive knowledge while maintaining better generalization and causing less damage to general model capabilities.
papers.limitation:
The mapping from features back to weights is indirect and sub-optimal, requiring reconstruction.
The clustering phenomenon of SAE features and their stability across different numbers of features require further investigation.
future_direction: Investigate the inherent stable structure of SAE feature space and whether it is truly insensitive to the number of features.
Improve the mapping from features back to weights for more direct model editing.
papers.abstract: Previous studies primarily utilize MLP neurons as units of analysis for understanding the mechanisms of factual knowledge in Language Models (LMs); however, neurons suffer from polysemanticity, leading to limited knowledge expression and poor interpretability. In this paper, we first conduct preliminary experiments to validate that Sparse Autoencoders (SAE) can effectively decompose neurons into features, which serve as alternative analytical units. With this established, our core findings reveal three key advantages of features over neurons: (1) Features exhibit stronger influence on knowledge expression and superior interpretability. (2) Features demonstrate enhanced monosemanticity, showing distinct activation patterns between related and unrelated facts. (3) Features achieve better privacy protection than neurons, demonstrated through our proposed FeatureEdit method, which significantly outperforms existing neuron-based approaches in erasing privacy-sensitive information from LMs.Code and dataset will be available.

papers.title: Toward Causal Representation Learning
papers.research_question: How can causality contribute to modern machine learning research, particularly in addressing transfer learning, generalization, and robustness? What is the problem of causal representation learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reviews and synthesizes fundamental concepts of causal inference and relates them to open problems in machine learning, arguing that causality can help address limitations in transfer learning, generalization, and robustness, and introduces the problem of causal representation learning.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that causality can significantly contribute to machine learning by providing a framework for robust and generalizable models, and that causal representation learning is a key research area at the intersection of both fields.
papers.key_findings:
Causality provides a framework for modeling interventions and distribution shifts, which can improve robustness and generalization in machine learning.
Causal representation learning, the discovery of high-level causal variables from low-level observations, is a central problem for AI and causality.
The independent causal mechanism (ICM) principle and the sparse mechanism shift (SMS) hypothesis are key for learning causal models.
Causal models can answer interventional and counterfactual questions, going beyond statistical associations.
Combining causality with machine learning can lead to more versatile AI systems.
future_direction: Causal representation learning: discovering high-level causal variables from low-level observations.
Combining the strengths of causality and machine learning to build more versatile AI.
Developing methods for causal discovery and learning from data with weak assumptions.
papers.abstract: The two fields of machine learning and graphical causality arose and are developed separately. However, there is, now, cross-pollination and increasing interest in both fields to benefit from the advances of the other. In this article, we review fundamental concepts of causal inference and relate them to crucial open problems of machine learning, including transfer and generalization, thereby assaying how causality can contribute to modern machine learning research. This also applies in the opposite direction: we note that most work in causality starts from the premise that the causal variables are given. A central problem for AI and causality is, thus, causal representation learning, that is, the discovery of high-level causal variables from low-level observations. Finally, we delineate some implications of causality for machine learning and propose key research areas at the intersection of both communities.

papers.title: ERNIE-Tiny : A Progressive Distillation Framework for Pretrained Transformer Compression
papers.research_question: How to effectively compress pretrained language models (PLMs) by addressing the pretrain-finetune distillation discrepancy through a smooth transition of teacher, training data, and learning objective?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a four-stage progressive distillation framework (ERNIE-Tiny) that smooths the transition from pretrain to finetune distillation by gradually altering teacher model, training data, and learning objective, introducing a novel general-enhanced distillation stage to improve student generalization.
papers.conclusion: The proposed progressive distillation framework ERNIE-Tiny effectively compresses pretrained language models, maintaining high performance while significantly reducing model size and inference time, and demonstrates improved generalization.
papers.key_findings:
A 4-layer ERNIE-Tiny student maintains over 98% of its 12-layer teacher BERTbase performance on the GLUE benchmark with 9.4x faster inference speed.
The general-enhanced distillation stage, which uses a finetuned teacher on general data, improves the student model's generalization, especially on low-resource tasks.
The task-adaptive distillation stage serves as a crucial bridge, smoothing the transition between general and task-specific data distillation and improving final performance.
ERNIE-Tiny achieves state-of-the-art compression results on both English (GLUE) and Chinese NLP tasks, outperforming the teacher BERTbase on Chinese tasks with 7.5x fewer parameters.
Ablation studies confirm the importance of each distillation stage, with the removal of any stage leading to performance degradation.
papers.limitation: The work did not apply larger unlabeled general data such as C4, leaving more efficient data utilization for future work.
future_direction: Applying larger unlabeled general data (e.g., C4) and exploring more efficient data utilization.
papers.abstract: Pretrained language models (PLMs) such as BERT adopt a training paradigm which first pretrain the model in general data and then finetune the model on task-specific data, and have recently achieved great success. However, PLMs are notorious for their enormous parameters and hard to be deployed on real-life applications. Knowledge distillation has been prevailing to address this problem by transferring knowledge from a large teacher to a much smaller student over a set of data. We argue that the selection of thee three key components, namely teacher, training data, and learning objective, is crucial to the effectiveness of distillation. We, therefore, propose a four-stage progressive distillation framework ERNIE-Tiny to compress PLM, which varies the three components gradually from general level to task-specific level. Specifically, the first stage, General Distillation, performs distillation with guidance from pretrained teacher, gerenal data and latent distillation loss. Then, General-Enhanced Distillation changes teacher model from pretrained teacher to finetuned teacher. After that, Task-Adaptive Distillation shifts training data from general data to task-specific data. In the end, Task-Specific Distillation, adds two additional losses, namely Soft-Label and Hard-Label loss onto the last stage. Empirical results demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework and generalization gain brought by ERNIE-Tiny.In particular, experiments show that a 4-layer ERNIE-Tiny maintains over 98.0%performance of its 12-layer teacher BERT base on GLUE benchmark, surpassing state-of-the-art (SOTA) by 1.0% GLUE score with the same amount of parameters. Moreover, ERNIE-Tiny achieves a new compression SOTA on five Chinese NLP tasks, outperforming BERT base by 0.4% accuracy with 7.5x fewer parameters and9.4x faster inference speed.

papers.title: Neural Redshift: Random Networks are not Random Functions
papers.research_question: What are the inductive biases of neural network architectures that contribute to generalization, independent of gradient-based training?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks have an inductive bias towards functions of a particular complexity (Neural Redshift), observable in random-weight networks, which explains generalization independent of gradient descent.
papers.conclusion: The Neural Redshift provides a fresh explanation for generalization in neural networks independent of gradient-based training and points to avenues for controlling inductive biases.
papers.key_findings:
Random-weight neural networks implement functions of biased complexity, depending on architecture components like activations.
ReLU activations, residual connections, and layer normalization contribute to a simplicity bias (low complexity).
The simplicity bias is not universal; it can be modulated by architecture choices (e.g., weight magnitude, alternative activations).
Transformers inherit similar inductive biases from their building blocks, exhibiting simplicity bias in sequence generation.
Matching the preferred complexity of an architecture to the target function's complexity improves generalization.
papers.limitation: The complexity measures used (frequency, polynomial order, compressibility) do not fully capture the inductive biases of architectures.
future_direction: Characterizing fine-grained differences in inductive biases beyond complexity measures.
Controlling inductive biases to improve generalization on complex tasks or mitigate shortcut learning.
papers.abstract: Our understanding of the generalization capabilities of neural networks (NNs) is still incomplete. Prevailing explanations are based on implicit biases of gradient descent (GD) but they cannot account for the capabilities of models from gradient-free methods nor the simplicity bias recently observed in untrained networks. This paper seeks other sources of generalization in NNs. Findings. To understand the inductive biases provided by architectures independently from GD, we examine untrained, random-weight networks. Even simple MLPs show strong inductive biases: uniform sampling in weight space yields a very biased distribution of functions in terms of complexity. But unlike common wisdom, NNs do not have an inherent "simplicity bias". This property depends on components such as ReLUs, residual connections, and layer normalizations. Alternative architectures can be built with a bias for any level of complexity. Transformers also inherit all these properties from their building blocks. Implications. We provide a fresh explanation for the success of deep learning independent from gradient-based training. It points at promising avenues for controlling the solutions implemented by trained models.

papers.title: Encouraging an Appropriate Representation Simplifies Training of Neural\n Networks
papers.research_question: Can encouraging an appropriate internal representation simplify training and improve generalization in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Encouraging neural networks to learn specific internal representations, such as digit-wise one-hot encoding, can simplify training and improve generalization on tasks where conventional training fails.
papers.conclusion: Integrating domain knowledge by encouraging neural networks to learn human-like concepts can be beneficial for generalization and interpretability, especially in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
Conventional training of TraNet fails to achieve any correct translations or transcriptions on the benchmark tasks.
When the digit-wise one-hot encoding is encouraged by training encoder and decoder separately, TraNet achieves 95.8% accuracy on translation and 74.9% on transcription.
The encouraged model is more understandable to humans, as the internal representations correspond to human-interpretable concepts.
Encouraging appropriate representations can integrate domain knowledge and improve model trust and debuggability.
papers.limitation: The tasks considered are simple and can be solved by other means, such as using deeper networks or formal language techniques.
future_direction: Applying the idea of encouraging human-like concepts to other applications, such as credit scoring or medical diagnosis.
Using encouraged models together with conventional models in critical applications to handle disagreements.
papers.abstract:
A common assumption about neural networks is that they can learn an
appropriate internal representations on their own, see e.g. end-to-end
learning. In this work we challenge this assumption. We consider two simple
tasks and show that the state-of-the-art training algorithm fails, although the
model itself is able to represent an appropriate solution. We will demonstrate
that encouraging an appropriate internal representation allows the same model
to solve these tasks. While we do not claim that it is impossible to solve
these tasks by other means (such as neural networks with more layers), our
results illustrate that integration of domain knowledge in form of a desired
internal representation may improve the generalization ability of neural
networks.

papers.title: Network Dynamics-Based Framework for Understanding Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can deep neural networks be understood through a dynamical systems framework that defines neuron-level transformation modes and attraction basins to explain learning dynamics and phenomena like grokking?
papers.core_contribution: A theoretical framework that redefines linearity and nonlinearity in neural networks at the neuron level through order-preserving and non-order-preserving transformations, and introduces attraction basins in sample and weight spaces to analyze learning dynamics, generalization, and phenomena like grokking.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework of transformation modes and attraction basins provides a transparent, multi-scale view of deep neural network dynamics, offering principled guidance for optimizing architectures and training strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Distinct learning phases emerge during training, characterized by the distribution of OPT and NPT neurons across layers, which are linked to network performance.
Phase transitions in learning dynamics, often induced by batch normalization in evaluation mode, are a prerequisite for the grokking phenomenon in deep networks.
The attraction basins in sample space and weight space vary independently; their balance determines optimal network depth and width for generalization and stability.
The Rank Probability Distribution (RPD) gradient, especially in the first hidden layer, quantifies the proportion of OPT/NPT neurons and indicates the network's information extraction capability.
Grokking in shallow networks arises from an abrupt expansion of attraction basins, representing a shift from memorization to generalization, while in deep networks it stems from statistical mismatches introduced by batch normalization during phase transitions.
future_direction: Applying the framework to optimize weight initialization, particularly for large language models like Transformers.
Using the framework to quickly assess hyperparameter settings to avoid grokking and achieve optimal performance efficiently, reducing computational cost.
papers.abstract: Advancements in artificial intelligence call for a deeper understanding of the fundamental mechanisms underlying deep learning. In this work, we propose a theoretical framework to analyze learning dynamics through the lens of dynamical systems theory. We redefine the notions of linearity and nonlinearity in neural networks by introducing two fundamental transformation units at the neuron level: order-preserving transformations and non-order-preserving transformations. Different transformation modes lead to distinct collective behaviors in weight vector organization, different modes of information extraction, and the emergence of qualitatively different learning phases. Transitions between these phases may occur during training, accounting for key phenomena such as grokking. To further characterize generalization and structural stability, we introduce the concept of attraction basins in both sample and weight spaces. The distribution of neurons with different transformation modes across layers, along with the structural characteristics of the two types of attraction basins, forms a set of core metrics for analyzing the performance of learning models. Hyperparameters such as depth, width, learning rate, and batch size act as control variables for fine-tuning these metrics. Our framework not only sheds light on the intrinsic advantages of deep learning, but also provides a novel perspective for optimizing network architectures and training strategies.

papers.title: Disentangling Representations through Multi-task Learning
papers.research_question: Under what conditions do disentangled representations emerge in agents that optimally solve multi-task evidence accumulation classification tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Multi-task learning in evidence accumulation tasks leads to disentangled representations in the latent state of autoregressive models, with theoretical guarantees on emergence conditions.
papers.conclusion: Multi-task learning establishes a formal link between competence at multiple tasks and the formation of disentangled, interpretable world models in both biological and artificial systems, explaining their generalization capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Theoretical guarantees show that any optimal multi-task classifier must encode a maximum likelihood estimate of the ground truth in its latent state, leading to abstract and disentangled representations as the number of tasks increases.
RNNs trained on multi-task classification learn disentangled representations in the form of continuous attractors, enabling zero-shot out-of-distribution generalization.
Transformers are particularly suited for disentangling representations, achieving orthogonality even with fewer tasks compared to RNNs.
Noise in observations is necessary for disentangled representations to emerge, as it prevents saturation and preserves distance information.
The framework is robust to various manipulations including correlated inputs, non-linear decision boundaries, and free reaction-time tasks.
future_direction: Characterizing representation learning with multiple manifold decision boundaries
Exploring interplay between task diversity, energy constraints, and the emergence of shared representations
papers.abstract: Intelligent perception and interaction with the world hinges on internal representations that capture its underlying structure (''disentangled'' or ''abstract'' representations). Disentangled representations serve as world models, isolating latent factors of variation in the world along approximately orthogonal directions, thus facilitating feature-based generalization. We provide experimental and theoretical results guaranteeing the emergence of disentangled representations in agents that optimally solve multi-task evidence accumulation classification tasks, canonical in the neuroscience literature. The key conceptual finding is that, by producing accurate multi-task classification estimates, a system implicitly represents a set of coordinates specifying a disentangled representation of the underlying latent state of the data it receives. The theory provides conditions for the emergence of these representations in terms of noise, number of tasks, and evidence accumulation time. We experimentally validate these predictions in RNNs trained to multi-task, which learn disentangled representations in the form of continuous attractors, leading to zero-shot out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization in predicting latent factors. We demonstrate the robustness of our framework across autoregressive architectures, decision boundary geometries and in tasks requiring classification confidence estimation. We find that transformers are particularly suited for disentangling representations, which might explain their unique world understanding abilities. Overall, our framework establishes a formal link between competence at multiple tasks and the formation of disentangled, interpretable world models in both biological and artificial systems, and helps explain why ANNs often arrive at human-interpretable concepts, and how they both may acquire exceptional zero-shot generalization capabilities.

papers.title: Understanding Gated Neurons in Transformers from Their Input-Output Functionality
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between what a neuron reads and what it writes?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a parameter-based method to classify gated neurons in transformers by input-output weight similarity, finding that enrichment neurons dominate early-middle layers while depletion neurons are more common in later layers.
papers.conclusion: The input-output perspective complements activation-dependent analyses and approaches that treat input and output separately, providing insights into how neurons manipulate concepts in the residual stream.
papers.key_findings:
Enrichment neurons dominate in early-middle layers across all 12 models studied, whereas later layers tend more towards depletion neurons.
A large proportion of neurons are input manipulators, with conditional enrichment being the most common class, especially in early-middle layers.
Many neurons exhibit double checking, where gate and input weight vectors are approximately orthogonal but intuitively represent the same concept.
The median cosine similarity between input and output weights is positive in early layers and negative in later layers, indicating a smooth transition in functionality.
Neurons rarely have prototypical weight configurations; instead, they often add novel but related information to the residual stream.
papers.limitation:
The method is parameter-based and therefore limited in scope; it is not designed to replace other neuron analysis methods.
Mathematical similarities of weights may not reflect semantic similarity; orthogonal vectors can represent similar concepts, and similar vectors can represent non-identical concepts.
Case studies of individual neurons may be cherry-picked, focusing on interpretable neurons in later layers, so interpretations may not generalize.
The paper provides only possible interpretations of observed phenomena, not definitive explanations.
future_direction: Extend the method to non-gated activation functions.
Study the evolution of input-output functionalities during model training.
