papers.research_question: To what extent can knowledge distillation transfer debiasing capabilities between models? Can knowledge distillation train less biased models compared to standard training? What internal mechanisms cause the debiasing behavior change after distillation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents the first large-scale study on the effect of knowledge distillation on debiasing capabilities, showing that vanilla KD often fails to preserve debiasing and can increase student bias, and proposes three strategies to improve distillability.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents the first study on the distillability of debiasing capabilities, showing vanilla KD does not consistently preserve debiasing, and proposes three solutions (data augmentation, iterative KD, initialization) that significantly improve distillability.
papers.key_findings:
The debiasing capability of a model is undermined post-KD; students become more biased than teachers.
Training a debiased model does not benefit from injecting teacher knowledge (KD does not improve generalization).
Although overall robustness may remain stable post-distillation, significant variations occur across different bias types.
The effectiveness of debiasing transfer depends on model scale similarity; similar scales lead to better transfer.
Larger teachers do not guarantee more robust students.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are mainly conducted on logit-based knowledge distillation. The effect of other knowledge distillation methods has not been explored.
The work does not explore the scenario where multiple teachers participate in the distillation process.
future_direction: Investigate self-distilled debiasing, where the student iteratively distills knowledge from itself rather than relying on a fixed teacher, and explicitly guide the student using counterfactual data augmentation during distillation.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an effective method for model compression and transferring knowledge between models. However, its effect on model's robustness against spurious correlations that degrade performance on out-of-distribution data remains underexplored. This study investigates the effect of knowledge distillation on the transferability of ``debiasing'' capabilities from teacher models to student models on natural language inference (NLI) and image classification tasks. Through extensive experiments, we illustrate several key findings: (i) overall the debiasing capability of a model is undermined post-KD; (ii) training a debiased model does not benefit from injecting teacher knowledge; (iii) although the overall robustness of a model may remain stable post-distillation, significant variations can occur across different types of biases; and (iv) we pin-point the internal attention pattern and circuit that causes the distinct behavior post-KD. Given the above findings, we propose three effective solutions to improve the distillability of debiasing methods: developing high quality data for augmentation, implementing iterative knowledge distillation, and initializing student models with weights obtained from teacher models. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study on the effect of KD on debiasing and its interenal mechanism at scale. Our findings provide understandings on how KD works and how to design better debiasing methods.

papers.title: On the Impact of Knowledge Distillation for Model Interpretability
papers.research_question: Does knowledge distillation improve model interpretability in addition to model accuracy?
papers.core_contribution: Knowledge distillation improves model interpretability by transferring class-similarity information from teacher to student, making activation maps more object-centric.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge distillation enhances both the accuracy and interpretability of models, and this improvement is consistent across different KD methods, datasets, and notions of interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
KD increases the number of concept detectors (interpretability) compared to training from scratch.
KD improves interpretability by transferring class-similarity information, while label smoothing reduces interpretability.
The interpretability of student models improves as the amount of class-similarity information they learn increases.
Various KD methods (vanilla KD, AT, FT, CRD, SSKD, self-KD) all improve model interpretability.
KD improves interpretability across different datasets (ImageNet, CIFAR, MNIST, SST) and different interpretability measures (concept detectors, five-band-scores, DiffROAR, loss gradients).
future_direction: Determine whether KD can yield other useful results (e.g., model robustness).
Explore whether additional metrics can be used to measure model interpretability.
papers.abstract: Several recent studies have elucidated why knowledge distillation (KD) improves model performance. However, few have researched the other advantages of KD in addition to its improving model performance. In this study, we have attempted to show that KD enhances the interpretability as well as the accuracy of models. We measured the number of concept detectors identified in network dissection for a quantitative comparison of model interpretability. We attributed the improvement in interpretability to the class-similarity information transferred from the teacher to student models. First, we confirmed the transfer of class-similarity information from the teacher to student model via logit distillation. Then, we analyzed how class-similarity information affects model interpretability in terms of its presence or absence and degree of similarity information. We conducted various quantitative and qualitative experiments and examined the results on different datasets, different KD methods, and according to different measures of interpretability. Our research showed that KD models by large models could be used more reliably in various fields.

papers.title: Latent Neural Representations Analysis and Distillation for Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we effectively distill Transformer models when there is a dimensionality mismatch between teacher and student, and how can analysis of latent neural representations (like outlier dimensions) inform better distillation algorithms?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces two novel distillation methods: Attention Map Alignment Distillation (AMAD) for handling mismatched attention heads between teacher and student models, and Emergent Outlier Focused Distillation (EOFD) which prioritizes critical outlier dimensions in latent representations. It also provides the first systematic analysis of emergent outlier dimensions in Encoder-Decoder T5 and instruction-finetuned Flan-T5 models.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methods for analyzing and distilling latent neural representations advance the understanding and acceleration of Transformer inference, with AMAD and EOFD demonstrating state-of-the-art distillation performance and generalization across architectures.
papers.key_findings:
AMAD enables effective distillation between teacher and student Transformers with different numbers of attention heads, outperforming conventional methods on vision-language tasks like VQA and captioning.
Outlier dimensions in T5 and Flan-T5 models, identified by unusually large activation magnitudes, are critical for zero-shot performance and are shared across layers within the encoder or decoder, but differ between encoder and decoder.
EOFD, which focuses distillation loss on these outlier dimensions, achieves state-of-the-art performance on the GLUE benchmark and generalizes across BERT, GPT-2, and T5 architectures.
Distillation with AMAD can compensate for the absence of vision-language pre-training, and in some cases, distilled students outperform pre-trained and fine-tuned teachers.
The growth of outlier magnitude in T5 models is more correlated with increasing layer depth rather than overall model size, contrary to findings in GPT models.
papers.limitation: In some cases, a Teacher attention head may not be similar to any Student head after AMAD distillation, indicating a potential failure mode for knowledge transfer.
papers.abstract: Transformer-backed Large Language Models and Large Vision-Language Models are among the most widely used machine learning models recently. However, due to their enormous size, their behaviors and dynamics become difficult to understand and explain, and their inference speed and cost become slow and forbidding. Therefore, understanding their latent neural patterns and distilling their latent neural representations into smaller, cheaper, and faster models are vital for creating more explainable, accessible, and sustainable machine intelligence. However, knowledge distillation algorithms face an inherent challenge in minimizing the divergence between the neural activation representations of a teacher Transformer and a student Transformer: The latent representation spaces of the smaller Student always have lower dimensionality than those of the larger Teacher. We will address this Transformer distillation dimensionality mismatch or reduction problem by analyzing the neural activation patterns within these latent representation spaces and by proposing corresponding novel algorithms for distilling each group of components of Transformers. Our ultimate goal is to advance the field of understanding and accelerating the inference process of large Transformers by studying their latent neural representations.Specifically, we first develop novel algorithms for aligning the heads within the Multi-Head Attention components of these Transformers for latent neural representation distillation. We propose a new Attention Map Alignment Distillation (AMAD) method for Transformers with multi-head attention, which, unlike previous literature, can work for a Teacher and a Student with mismatched dimensionalities in terms of the numbers of attention heads. Specifically, we soft-align different heads in Teacher and Student attention maps using a cosine similarity weighting. The Teacher head contributes more to the Student heads for which it has a higher similarity weight. Each Teacher head contributes to all the Student heads by minimizing the divergence between the attention latent neural activation distributions for the soft-aligned heads.We then advance the understanding and distillation of the latent neural representations of the Feed Forward Network and Layer Normalization components of these Transformers. Previous literature shows that a small subset of dimensions within the high-dimensional latent neural representation spaces of language Transformers emerge as “outliers”, with weights or latent neuron activations of unusually large magnitudes—several standard deviations from the mean—during pretraining, and seem to encode critical linguistic knowledge in a sparse way. We systematically extend these previous findings on emergent outliers to Encoder-Decoder Transformers and instruction-finetuned models at scale, for the first time. We show that emergent outlier dimensions of the Transformer latent neural representations contribute significantly more to zero-shot performance than non-outlier dimensions. Leveraging our findings, we further propose the Emergent Outlier Focused Distillation (EOFD) method, which prioritizes these critical outlier latent dimensions to address the trade-off among these representation dimensions during distillation. Specifically, we propose a weighted MSE loss to place greater emphasis on the emergent outlier dimensions of the latent neural representations, which are identified by the standard deviations of neuron activation magnitudes.We demonstrate that our AMAD and EOFD distillation algorithms achieve state-of-the-art performance empirically and generalize well to different Transformer architectures. Specifically, for AMAD, we experiment on distilling VL-T5 and BLIP and apply the AMAD loss to their T5, BERT, and ViT sub-modules. We show that, under vision-language settings, AMAD outperforms conventional distillation methods on the VQA-2.0, COCO captioning, and Multi30K translation datasets. We further show that even without VL pre-training, the distilled VL-T5 models outperform corresponding VL pre-trained VL-T5 models that are further fine-tuned by ground-truth signals, and that fine-tuning distillation can also compensate to some degree for the absence of VL pre-training in BLIP models. As for EOFD, we empirically show that it outperforms state-of-the-art distillation methods on the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark. We further demonstrate that EOFD generalizes well across Encoder-only BERT, Decoder-only GPT-2, and Encoder-Decoder T5 architectures.

papers.title: A Closer Look at Deep Learning Heuristics: Learning rate restarts, Warmup and Distillation
papers.research_question: Why do heuristics such as cosine annealing (SGDR), learning rate warmup, and knowledge distillation improve the convergence and performance of deep learning models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses mode connectivity and canonical correlation analysis (CCA) to empirically investigate the reasons behind the success of deep learning heuristics like cosine annealing, learning rate warmup, and knowledge distillation.
papers.conclusion: The empirical analysis using mode connectivity and CCA sheds light on the heuristics of cosine annealing, warmup, and distillation, suggesting that common explanations are oversimplified and opening new questions for deeper exploration.
papers.key_findings:
The reasons often quoted for the success of cosine annealing (e.g., escaping local minima) are not evidenced in practice; iterates move over barriers after restarts but this is an oversimplification.
The effect of learning rate warmup is to prevent the deeper layers (e.g., fully-connected stack) from creating training instability; freezing these layers achieves similar outcomes.
In knowledge distillation, the latent knowledge shared by the teacher is primarily disbursed to the deeper layers of the student network.
Mode connectivity is a robust framework for connecting optima obtained from vastly different training schemes (e.g., different optimizers, batch sizes, regularization).
For SGDR, the path found by mode connectivity corresponds to lower training loss but higher validation loss than the iterates, suggesting a generalization gap.
papers.abstract: The convergence rate and final performance of common deep learning models have significantly benefited from heuristics such as learning rate schedules, knowledge distillation, skip connections, and normalization layers. In the absence of theoretical underpinnings, controlled experiments aimed at explaining these strategies can aid our understanding of deep learning landscapes and the training dynamics. Existing approaches for empirical analysis rely on tools of linear interpolation and visualizations with dimensionality reduction, each with their limitations. Instead, we revisit such analysis of heuristics through the lens of recently proposed methods for loss surface and representation analysis, viz., mode connectivity and canonical correlation analysis (CCA), and hypothesize reasons for the success of the heuristics. In particular, we explore knowledge distillation and learning rate heuristics of (cosine) restarts and warmup using mode connectivity and CCA. Our empirical analysis suggests that: (a) the reasons often quoted for the success of cosine annealing are not evidenced in practice; (b) that the effect of learning rate warmup is to prevent the deeper layers from creating training instability; and (c) that the latent knowledge shared by the teacher is primarily disbursed to the deeper layers.

papers.title: Improved Feature Distillation via Projector Ensemble
papers.research_question: What is the effect of the feature projector in knowledge distillation, and can an ensemble of projectors improve feature distillation performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates the role of the projector in feature distillation, hypothesizing it prevents overfitting to teacher features, and proposes a simple yet effective method using an ensemble of projectors to improve student network performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates the positive effect of a projector in feature distillation and shows that an ensemble of projectors can further improve student network performance on image classification tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Adding a projector improves distillation performance even when student and teacher feature dimensions are identical, by disentangling the tasks of feature extraction for classification and feature matching for distillation.
Training a student without a projector leads to overfitting to the teacher's feature distribution, resulting in less discriminative features for classification.
An ensemble of projectors further improves student performance by providing diverse transformed features and improving generalization.
The proposed method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art feature distillation methods on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet across various teacher-student pairs.
Simply increasing the depth or width of a single projector does not improve performance and can degrade it, whereas a horizontal ensemble of shallow projectors is effective.
papers.limitation: The proposed method is only evaluated on image classification tasks; its application to other downstream tasks (e.g., object detection and semantic segmentation) remains for future work.
future_direction: Applying the proposed method to other downstream tasks such as object detection and semantic segmentation.
Exploring how to effectively and efficiently integrate logits and similarity information into the proposed projector ensemble framework.
papers.abstract: In knowledge distillation, previous feature distillation methods mainly focus on the design of loss functions and the selection of the distilled layers, while the effect of the feature projector between the student and the teacher remains under-explored. In this paper, we first discuss a plausible mechanism of the projector with empirical evidence and then propose a new feature distillation method based on a projector ensemble for further performance improvement. We observe that the student network benefits from a projector even if the feature dimensions of the student and the teacher are the same. Training a student backbone without a projector can be considered as a multi-task learning process, namely achieving discriminative feature extraction for classification and feature matching between the student and the teacher for distillation at the same time. We hypothesize and empirically verify that without a projector, the student network tends to overfit the teacher's feature distributions despite having different architecture and weights initialization. This leads to degradation on the quality of the student's deep features that are eventually used in classification. Adding a projector, on the other hand, disentangles the two learning tasks and helps the student network to focus better on the main feature extraction task while still being able to utilize teacher features as a guidance through the projector. Motivated by the positive effect of the projector in feature distillation, we propose an ensemble of projectors to further improve the quality of student features. Experimental results on different datasets with a series of teacher-student pairs illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

papers.title: DistillLens: Symmetric Knowledge Distillation Through Logit Lens
papers.research_question: How can we improve knowledge distillation by aligning the intermediate thought processes of student and teacher models using symmetric divergence objectives?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DISTILLLENS, a knowledge distillation framework that uses Logit Lens and symmetric divergence to align intermediate layer distributions, improving student performance.
papers.conclusion: DISTILLLENS effectively aligns intermediate thought trajectories of student and teacher models, consistently outperforming standard KD and feature-transfer methods across GPT-2 and Llama architectures.
papers.key_findings:
DISTILLLENS outperforms standard KD and feature-transfer baselines on diverse instruction-following benchmarks.
The symmetric divergence objective (JSD) enforces a dual-sided penalty that prevents both overconfidence and underconfidence.
DISTILLLENS reduces exposure bias compared to standard KD without the computational overhead of on-policy methods.
The method is modular and can be combined with existing KD baselines, with the most improvement when combined with mode-seeking objectives like RKL.
Ablation studies show that using 5 interleaved intermediate layers yields the best performance.
papers.limitation: Computational overhead during training due to projecting multiple intermediate layers through the unembedding matrix.
future_direction: Inject complex reasoning capabilities into smaller architectures
Extend to cross-architecture distillation
papers.abstract: Standard Knowledge Distillation (KD) compresses Large Language Models (LLMs) by optimizing final outputs, yet it typically treats the teacher's intermediate layer's thought process as a black box. While feature-based distillation attempts to bridge this gap, existing methods (e.g., MSE and asymmetric KL divergence) ignore the rich uncertainty profiles required for the final output. In this paper, we introduce DistillLens, a framework that symmetrically aligns the evolving thought processes of student and teacher models. By projecting intermediate hidden states into the vocabulary space via the Logit Lens, we enforce structural alignment using a symmetric divergence objective. Our analysis proves that this constraint imposes a dual-sided penalty, preventing both overconfidence and underconfidence while preserving the high-entropy information conduits essential for final deduction. Extensive experiments on GPT-2 and Llama architectures demonstrate that DistillLens consistently outperforms standard KD and feature-transfer baselines on diverse instruction-following benchmarks. The code is available at https://github.com/manishdhakal/DistillLens.

papers.title: On information captured by neural networks: connections with memorization and generalization
papers.research_question: How does the information captured by neural networks during training relate to memorization and generalization?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation develops an information-theoretic framework to understand memorization and generalization in neural networks, introducing methods to control label noise information, measure sample informativeness, and derive nonvacuous generalization bounds.
papers.conclusion: The findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the mechanisms underlying neural network generalization by analyzing the information captured during training.
papers.key_findings:
Limiting label noise information in neural network weights reduces memorization of noisy labels and improves generalization.
The proposed functional sample information (F-SI) measure identifies atypical, ambiguous, or underrepresented examples that are more informative for training.
The f-CMI generalization bounds, based on information in predictions, are nonvacuous and closely track the generalization gap in practical deep learning scenarios.
Knowledge distillation benefits from reducing supervision complexity, which is controlled by teacher accuracy, margin, and the compatibility of teacher and student neural tangent kernels.
Sample-wise information-theoretic generalization bounds have formal limitations, revealing a difference between information-theoretic and PAC-Bayesian perspectives.
papers.limitation: The linearized network approximation used to compute sample information may not be accurate for highly nonlinear networks or when the network is far from its initialization.
future_direction: Extending the sample information measure to other learning settings beyond classification.
Improving the f-CMI-based generalization bounds to be tighter in cases where they currently overestimate the gap.
Further exploration of online knowledge distillation and its theoretical properties.
papers.abstract: Despite the popularity and success of deep learning, there is limited understanding of when, how, and why neural networks generalize to unseen examples. Since learning can be seen as extracting information from data, we formally study information captured by neural networks during training. Specifically, we start with viewing learning in presence of noisy labels from an information-theoretic perspective and derive a learning algorithm that limits label noise information in weights. We then define a notion of unique information that an individual sample provides to the training of a deep network, shedding some light on the behavior of neural networks on examples that are atypical, ambiguous, or belong to underrepresented subpopulations. We relate example informativeness to generalization by deriving nonvacuous generalization gap bounds. Finally, by studying knowledge distillation, we highlight the important role of data and label complexity in generalization. Overall, our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the mechanisms underlying neural network generalization.

papers.title: An Interpretable Neuron Embedding for Static Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How to provide a sample- and class-independent explanation of neurons in a model, and can static knowledge from neuron semantics be used for knowledge distillation without sample-by-sample guidance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a method to embed neurons into semantic vectors for interpretability, enabling static knowledge distillation that performs comparably to existing methods without sample-by-sample teacher guidance.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes neuron embedding for interpretability and static knowledge distillation, demonstrating effective knowledge transfer without instance-specific guidance.
papers.key_findings:
Semantic vectors accurately represent neuron semantics, as shown by similar activation maps for neurons with similar vectors.
The embedding method spontaneously converges to manually annotated semantic vectors without supervision.
Static knowledge distillation achieves performance comparable to or better than existing relation-based knowledge distillation methods.
The method allows for analysis of neuron similar and additive relations.
Without sample-by-sample guidance, SKD is efficient and scalable.
papers.abstract: Although deep neural networks have shown well-performance in various tasks, the poor interpretability of the models is always criticized. In the paper, we propose a new interpretable neural network method, by embedding neurons into the semantic space to extract their intrinsic global semantics. In contrast to previous methods that probe latent knowledge inside the model, the proposed semantic vector externalizes the latent knowledge to static knowledge, which is easy to exploit. Specifically, we assume that neurons with similar activation are of similar semantic information. Afterwards, semantic vectors are optimized by continuously aligning activation similarity and semantic vector similarity during the training of the neural network. The visualization of semantic vectors allows for a qualitative explanation of the neural network. Moreover, we assess the static knowledge quantitatively by knowledge distillation tasks. Empirical experiments of visualization show that semantic vectors describe neuron activation semantics well. Without the sample-by-sample guidance from the teacher model, static knowledge distillation exhibit comparable or even superior performance with existing relation-based knowledge distillation methods.

papers.title: DePass: Unified Feature Attributing by Simple Decomposed Forward Pass
papers.research_question: How can we attribute the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations in a faithful, fine-grained, and unified way without requiring auxiliary training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution in Transformers based on a single decomposed forward pass that freezes attention scores and MLP activations, enabling lossless, additive decomposition and faithful attribution without auxiliary training.
papers.conclusion: DePass is a simple and efficient framework for interpreting Transformer models via a decomposed forward pass, achieving faithful attribution across token-level, component-level, and subspace-level granularities and serving as a general-purpose tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
DePass enables lossless additive decomposition of hidden states throughout the forward pass of Transformer models.
DePass provides more faithful token-level attribution compared to gradient-based and attention-based baseline methods.
DePass can attribute model behavior to specific architectural components (attention heads, MLP neurons) and to arbitrary linear subspaces.
DePass can be combined with Sparse Autoencoders (SAE) for token-level attribution of interpretable features.
DePass is computationally efficient, requiring only a single forward pass and significantly faster than exhaustive ablation methods.
papers.limitation:
DePass only captures information flow through the output-value (OV) circuit and does not explain query-key (QK) circuit interactions.
Decomposing the QK circuit would involve quadratic complexity and remains a challenging open problem.
Practical memory constraints require grouping components for fine-grained analysis, which can increase time costs.
future_direction: Unwrapping the QK circuit to understand its interactions is a key direction for future work.
Releasing a general-purpose toolkit supporting a broad range of Transformer models.
Optimizing computational efficiency and improving hardware deployment strategies to support higher-resolution attribution.
papers.abstract: Attributing the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations is a central challenge in mechanistic interpretability. We introduce DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution based on a single decomposed forward pass. DePass decomposes hidden states into customized additive components, then propagates them with attention scores and MLP's activations fixed. It achieves faithful, fine-grained attribution without requiring auxiliary training. We validate DePass across token-level, model component-level, and subspace-level attribution tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness and fidelity. Our experiments highlight its potential to attribute information flow between arbitrary components of a Transformer model. We hope DePass serves as a foundational tool for broader applications in interpretability.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
papers.research_question: How are factual associations stored and recalled in autoregressive transformer language models, and can they be directly edited?
papers.core_contribution: Factual associations in GPT are stored in mid-layer feed-forward modules and can be directly edited using a rank-one update method (ROME), which achieves strong generalization and specificity.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations in autoregressive transformers are stored in mid-layer MLP modules and can be directly edited via localized weight updates, with ROME providing an effective method for such edits.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals that mid-layer MLP modules at the last subject token are decisive for factual predictions.
The Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method can effectively edit factual associations by updating a single MLP layer with a rank-one weight update.
ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: On Explaining Knowledge Distillation: Measuring and Visualising the Knowledge Transfer Process
papers.research_question: How to explain and quantify the knowledge transfer process in knowledge distillation, specifically visualizing distilled and residual features.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces UniCAM, a gradient-based visual explanation method for knowledge distillation, and two metrics (FSS and RS) to quantify the similarity and relevance of distilled knowledge.
papers.conclusion: UniCAM and the FSS and RS metrics provide valuable insights for explaining the knowledge distillation process, as demonstrated on various datasets.
papers.key_findings:
With Teacher guidance, Student models learn more relevant features and discard irrelevant ones, with distilled features focusing on key object parts and residual features on backgrounds.
UniCAM effectively visualizes distilled and residual features, showing that KD is not simple feature copying but guided training.
The proposed FSS and RS metrics quantify attention pattern similarity and feature relevance, showing higher RS for Students trained with KD.
Capacity gaps between Teacher and Student can impede knowledge transfer, but Teacher assistants can bridge this gap.
Experiments on multiple datasets and KD techniques validate the effectiveness of UniCAM and the metrics.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were exclusively conducted on classification tasks.
Added computational cost from computing pairwise distances, gradients, and metrics.
future_direction: Extend UniCAM to more complex datasets.
Explore applicability to tasks beyond classification.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains challenging due to the opaque nature of the knowledge transfer process from a Teacher to a Student, making it difficult to address certain issues related to KD. To address this, we proposed UniCAM, a novel gradient-based visual explanation method, which effectively interprets the knowledge learned during KD. Our experimental results demonstrate that with the guidance of the Teacher's knowledge, the Student model becomes more efficient, learning more relevant features while discarding those that are not relevant. We refer to the features learned with the Teacher's guidance as distilled features and the features irrelevant to the task and ignored by the Student as residual features. Distilled features focus on key aspects of the input, such as textures and parts of objects. In contrast, residual features demonstrate more diffused attention, often targeting irrelevant areas, including the backgrounds of the target objects. In addition, we proposed two novel metrics: the feature similarity score (FSS) and the relevance score (RS), which quantify the relevance of the distilled knowledge. Experiments on the CIFAR10, ASIRRA, and Plant Disease datasets demonstrate that UniCAM and the two metrics offer valuable insights to explain the KD process.

papers.title: Joint learning of interpretation and distillation
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether a distilled model should give a similar prediction for a similar reason as its teacher model on the same input, and proposes methods to explain the distilled model and use explanation imitation to improve distillation.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a novel explanation solution for the GBDT2NN distilled model by using interpretation vectors from the teacher model, and introduces a joint learning method that uses explanation as an auxiliary task to improve prediction performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that imitating the explanation of the teacher model is an effective means to improve the performance of distillation models and provides interpretability for the distilled model.
papers.key_findings:
The independent interpretable method can generate explanations for GBDT2NN that are highly correlated with the teacher model's explanations, as measured by NDCG and top-k coverage.
The joint method, which incorporates interpretation learning into the distillation process, improves the prediction performance of GBDT2NN on several benchmarks.
The joint method also leads to faster convergence during training compared to the standard GBDT2NN model.
Visual evaluation on MNIST datasets shows the proposed method can accurately identify important features (pixels) for classification.
papers.abstract: The extra trust brought by the model interpretation has made it an indispensable part of machine learning systems. But to explain a distilled model's prediction, one may either work with the student model itself, or turn to its teacher model. This leads to a more fundamental question: if a distilled model should give a similar prediction for a similar reason as its teacher model on the same input? This question becomes even more crucial when the two models have dramatically different structure, taking GBDT2NN for example. This paper conducts an empirical study on the new approach to explaining each prediction of GBDT2NN, and how imitating the explanation can further improve the distillation process as an auxiliary learning task. Experiments on several benchmarks show that the proposed methods achieve better performance on both explanations and predictions.

papers.title: Cross-Model Semantics in Representation Learning
papers.research_question: How do structural constraints affect the compatibility of internal representations across different architectures? To what extent are learned representations tied to specific architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper formalizes representational alignment across architectures and demonstrates that structural regularities induce more stable representational geometry, improving interoperability of learned features.
papers.conclusion: PGNN integrates structural priors to enhance learning efficiency and generalization, and structural constraints can improve representational transferability across models.
papers.key_findings:
PGNN exhibits faster convergence and slightly higher test accuracy compared to baseline MLP.
Ablation shows that removing structural projection in PGNN leads to lower performance, confirming its utility.
PGNN shows similar robustness to initialization noise as MLP, with slight advantages under mild noise.
Representational alignment metrics show that structured representations can be partially aligned across architectures.
The framework enables measurement of alignment using CKA, subspace overlap, and transfer accuracy.
papers.limitation: Extrapolation to more complex datasets like CIFAR-10 did not show a major advantage for PGNN.
future_direction: Adapting and scaling PGNN to broader domains and more complex data distributions.
papers.abstract: The internal representations learned by deep networks are often sensitive to architecture-specific choices, raising questions about the stability, alignment, and transferability of learned structure across models. In this paper, we investigate how structural constraints--such as linear shaping operators and corrective paths--affect the compatibility of internal representations across different architectures. Building on the insights from prior studies on structured transformations and convergence, we develop a framework for measuring and analyzing representational alignment across networks with distinct but related architectural priors. Through a combination of theoretical insights, empirical probes, and controlled transfer experiments, we demonstrate that structural regularities induce representational geometry that is more stable under architectural variation. This suggests that certain forms of inductive bias not only support generalization within a model, but also improve the interoperability of learned features across models. We conclude with a discussion on the implications of representational transferability for model distillation, modular learning, and the principled design of robust learning systems.

papers.title: Optimal transfer protocol by incremental layer defrosting
papers.research_question: How to choose the optimal number of layers to freeze in transfer learning, and how does this optimal transfer depth depend on the amount of training data and the similarity between source and target tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a layer-wise defrosting protocol to identify the optimal transfer depth in transfer learning, showing that the optimal number of layers to freeze depends non-trivially on the target dataset size and source-target task similarity.
papers.conclusion: The layer-wise defrosting protocol can effectively identify the optimal transfer depth, which depends on data size and task similarity, and can significantly improve transfer learning performance.
papers.key_findings:
The optimal transfer depth (number of layers to freeze) depends on the size of the target training set: with more data, it is better to defrost more layers.
The optimal transfer depth depends on the similarity between source and target tasks: more similar tasks allow transferring more layers.
Compliant learning: networks can achieve good accuracy even when early layers are constrained to be close to source weights, indicating degeneracy in parameter space.
Topological similarity of representations (measured by Information Imbalance) can predict transfer effectiveness.
The layer-wise defrosting protocol can yield significant performance gains over vanilla freezing, sometimes more than acquiring more data.
papers.limitation:
The approach lacks strong theoretical foundations.
No practical rule of thumb for identifying the best transfer protocol without explicit cross-validation on a target test set.
future_direction: Develop a training schedule for transfer learning capable of efficiently performing layer-wise defrosting in a fully automatic manner.
Understand how to disentangle input similarity from the labeling rule.
papers.abstract: Transfer learning is a powerful tool enabling model training with limited amounts of data. This technique is particularly useful in real-world problems where data availability is often a serious limitation. The simplest transfer learning protocol is based on ``freezing" the feature-extractor layers of a network pre-trained on a data-rich source task, and then adapting only the last layers to a data-poor target task. This workflow is based on the assumption that the feature maps of the pre-trained model are qualitatively similar to the ones that would have been learned with enough data on the target task. In this work, we show that this protocol is often sub-optimal, and the largest performance gain may be achieved when smaller portions of the pre-trained network are kept frozen. In particular, we make use of a controlled framework to identify the optimal transfer depth, which turns out to depend non-trivially on the amount of available training data and on the degree of source-target task correlation. We then characterize transfer optimality by analyzing the internal representations of two networks trained from scratch on the source and the target task through multiple established similarity measures.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Grokking: An Effective Theory of Representation Learning
papers.research_question: What is the origin of generalization in grokking? Why does the training time needed to generalize diverge as training set size decreases? Under what conditions does delayed generalization occur?
papers.core_contribution: Provides an effective theory and phase diagrams to explain grokking, showing that generalization arises from structured representations and that grokking can be understood as a phase between comprehension and memorization.
papers.conclusion: This study provides intuitive explanations of the origin of grokking and highlights the usefulness of physics-inspired tools, such as effective theories and phase diagrams, for understanding deep learning.
papers.key_findings:
Generalization in grokking originates from structured representations, whose dynamics are predicted by an effective theory.
There are four learning phases: comprehension, grokking, memorization, and confusion, with representation learning occurring only in a 'Goldilocks zone'.
On transformers, the grokking phase stays closer to memorization, leading to delayed generalization.
The critical training set size corresponds to the least amount of data needed to determine a good representation.
Grokking can be remedied with proper hyperparameter tuning, as shown in phase diagrams.
papers.limitation: The effective theory is based on Euclidean distance between embeddings and might not capture other metrics defined by the decoder.
future_direction: Generalizing the effective theory to use metrics beyond Euclidean distance.
Investigating modifications to the effective theory to account for repulsion among different classes in image classification.
papers.abstract: We aim to understand grokking, a phenomenon where models generalize long after overfitting their training set. We present both a microscopic analysis anchored by an effective theory and a macroscopic analysis of phase diagrams describing learning performance across hyperparameters. We find that generalization originates from structured representations whose training dynamics and dependence on training set size can be predicted by our effective theory in a toy setting. We observe empirically the presence of four learning phases: comprehension, grokking, memorization, and confusion. We find representation learning to occur only in a "Goldilocks zone" (including comprehension and grokking) between memorization and confusion. We find on transformers the grokking phase stays closer to the memorization phase (compared to the comprehension phase), leading to delayed generalization. The Goldilocks phase is reminiscent of "intelligence from starvation" in Darwinian evolution, where resource limitations drive discovery of more efficient solutions. This study not only provides intuitive explanations of the origin of grokking, but also highlights the usefulness of physics-inspired tools, e.g., effective theories and phase diagrams, for understanding deep learning.

papers.title: Understanding Deep Representation Learning via Layerwise Feature Compression and Discrimination
papers.research_question: How do deep networks perform hierarchical feature learning across layers? Specifically, how do they transform input data into output across layers in classification tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a theoretical analysis showing that in deep linear networks, each layer progressively compresses within-class features at a geometric rate and discriminates between-class features at a linear rate, which also holds approximately in nonlinear networks.
papers.conclusion: Deep networks hierarchically compress and discriminate features across layers, providing a theoretical explanation for empirical observations of progressive neural collapse and feature learning.
papers.key_findings:
In deep linear networks, the within-class compression metric decays geometrically and the between-class discrimination metric increases linearly with layer depth.
This pattern of progressive feature compression and discrimination also occurs approximately in deep nonlinear networks.
Increasing the depth of deep linear networks improves generalization performance and feature compression.
Linear layers in hybrid networks mimic the feature learning behavior of deep nonlinear layers.
The theoretical results are validated on synthetic and real datasets.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical analysis assumes nearly orthogonal input data and balanced, low-rank weights, which may not always hold in practice.
The theory is developed for deep linear networks and may not fully capture the behavior of nonlinear networks.
future_direction: Extending the theoretical analysis to nonlinear networks.
Investigating the role of depth in other network architectures.
Exploring the implications for transfer learning and architecture design.
papers.abstract: Over the past decade, deep learning has proven to be a highly effective tool for learning meaningful features from raw data. However, it remains an open question how deep networks perform hierarchical feature learning across layers. In this work, we attempt to unveil this mystery by investigating the structures of intermediate features. Motivated by our empirical findings that linear layers mimic the roles of deep layers in nonlinear networks for feature learning, we explore how deep linear networks transform input data into output by investigating the output (i.e., features) of each layer after training in the context of multi-class classification problems. Toward this goal, we first define metrics to measure within-class compression and between-class discrimination of intermediate features, respectively. Through theoretical analysis of these two metrics, we show that the evolution of features follows a simple and quantitative pattern from shallow to deep layers when the input data is nearly orthogonal and the network weights are minimum-norm, balanced, and approximate low-rank: Each layer of the linear network progressively compresses within-class features at a geometric rate and discriminates between-class features at a linear rate with respect to the number of layers that data have passed through. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first quantitative characterization of feature evolution in hierarchical representations of deep linear networks. Empirically, our extensive experiments not only validate our theoretical results numerically but also reveal a similar pattern in deep nonlinear networks which aligns well with recent empirical studies. Moreover, we demonstrate the practical implications of our results in transfer learning. Our code is available at https://github.com/Heimine/PNC_DLN.

papers.title: All Bark and No Bite: Rogue Dimensions in Transformer Language Models Obscure Representational Quality
papers.research_question: How informative are standard similarity measures (cosine similarity, Euclidean distance) in contextualized language models, and how do rogue dimensions dominate these measures, obscuring representational quality?
papers.core_contribution: Standard similarity measures in contextual language models are dominated by a small number of rogue dimensions, and simple postprocessing techniques like standardization can correct for this, revealing underlying representational quality that is preserved across all layers.
papers.conclusion: Standard similarity measures are not informative for contextual language models due to rogue dimensions, and accounting for these dimensions (e.g., via standardization) is essential for any similarity-based analysis.
papers.key_findings:
A small number of rogue dimensions (1-5) dominate cosine similarity and Euclidean distance in contextual language models.
Rogue dimensions are centered far from the origin and have disproportionately high variance.
The rogue dimensions that dominate similarity measures do not dominate model behavior; ablating them has little effect on the language modeling distribution.
Rogue dimensions are often correlated with specific tokens (e.g., punctuation) and positions (e.g., position zero).
After postprocessing (e.g., standardization), representational quality (correlation with human similarity judgments) improves and is preserved across all layers, contrary to previous claims of degradation in later layers.
future_direction: Designing and implementing language models that do not develop rogue dimensions in the first place.
Understanding how rogue dimensions arise over time during pretraining.
Using the MultiBERT checkpoints to study whether rogue dimensions are coincidental or requisite for good performance, and how they emerge.
papers.abstract: Similarity measures are a vital tool for understanding how language models represent and process language. Standard representational similarity measures such as cosine similarity and Euclidean distance have been successfully used in static word embedding models to understand how words cluster in semantic space. Recently, these measures have been applied to embeddings from contextualized models such as BERT and GPT-2. In this work, we call into question the informativity of such measures for contextualized language models. We find that a small number of rogue dimensions, often just 1-3, dominate these measures. Moreover, we find a striking mismatch between the dimensions that dominate similarity measures and those which are important to the behavior of the model. We show that simple postprocessing techniques such as standardization are able to correct for rogue dimensions and reveal underlying representational quality. We argue that accounting for rogue dimensions is essential for any similarity-based analysis of contextual language models.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: Convergent Learning: Do different neural networks learn the same representations?
papers.research_question: Do different neural networks with the same architecture trained from different random initializations learn the same representations (i.e., exhibit convergent learning)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces methods to compare neural network representations and shows that networks exhibit partial convergent learning, with some features learned reliably across networks and others not, and that representations are a mix of local and slightly distributed codes.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks exhibit convergent learning to some extent, and the introduced methods are effective for understanding and comparing the representations they learn.
papers.key_findings:
Some features are learned reliably in multiple networks, yet other features are not consistently learned.
Units learn to span low-dimensional subspaces and, while these subspaces are common to multiple networks, the specific basis vectors learned are not.
The representation codes show evidence of being a mix between a local (single unit) code and slightly, but not fully, distributed codes across multiple units.
The average activation values of neurons vary considerably within a network, yet the mean activation values across different networks converge to an almost identical distribution.
Features learned in different networks are most convergent on the first convolutional layer (conv1) and least convergent on the fourth (conv4).
papers.limitation: Mapping layers for higher layers (conv3-conv5) showed poor performance, and the reasons are not fully understood.
future_direction: Investigate different architectures, training algorithms, and hyperparameters.
Train more powerful predictive models for higher layers with different hyperparameters or architectures.
papers.abstract: Recent success in training deep neural networks have prompted active investigation into the features learned on their intermediate layers. Such research is difficult because it requires making sense of non-linear computations performed by millions of parameters, but valuable because it increases our ability to understand current models and create improved versions of them. In this paper we investigate the extent to which neural networks exhibit what we call convergent learning, which is when the representations learned by multiple nets converge to a set of features which are either individually similar between networks or where subsets of features span similar low-dimensional spaces. We propose a specific method of probing representations: training multiple networks and then comparing and contrasting their individual, learned representations at the level of neurons or groups of neurons. We begin research into this question using three techniques to approximately align different neural networks on a feature level: a bipartite matching approach that makes one-to-one assignments between neurons, a sparse prediction approach that finds one-to-many mappings, and a spectral clustering approach that finds many-to-many mappings. This initial investigation reveals a few previously unknown properties of neural networks, and we argue that future research into the question of convergent learning will yield many more. The insights described here include (1) that some features are learned reliably in multiple networks, yet other features are not consistently learned; (2) that units learn to span low-dimensional subspaces and, while these subspaces are common to multiple networks, the specific basis vectors learned are not; (3) that the representation codes show evidence of being a mix between a local code and slightly, but not fully, distributed codes across multiple units.

papers.title: On the Behavior of Convolutional Nets for Feature Extraction
papers.research_question: How do individual CNN features from all layers behave for feature extraction and transfer learning, and can both presence and absence of feature activations be informative?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a statistical analysis of individual CNN features for feature extraction, showing that features can be discriminative by both presence and absence, and that convolutional layers are more general and discriminant than previously thought, enabling their use for knowledge representation.
papers.conclusion: The study provides insights into the behavior of CNN features for feature extraction, showing that both presence and absence of features are informative, and that convolutional layers are more general than previously thought, which can be exploited for knowledge representation and reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Features can be characteristic of a class by their absence, providing a different information modality, especially in fine-grained datasets.
Features from the last convolutional layer and fully connected layers are highly specific, while other convolutional layers convey more variate information.
For certain tasks, convolutional features outperform fully-connected features at discriminating labels, indicating low-level layers are more general and discriminant.
Low and middle level features have similar behavior across datasets, suggesting they can be used for knowledge representation without fine-tuning.
The relevance of fully-connected features is strongly related to the similarity of the task with the original training task and the width of the task spectrum.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are representation learning techniques. During training, a deep net is capable of generating a descriptive language of unprecedented size and detail in machine learning. Extracting the descriptive language coded within a trained CNN model (in the case of image data), and reusing it for other purposes is a field of interest, as it provides access to the visual descriptors previously learnt by the CNN after processing millions of images, without requiring an expensive training phase. Contributions to this field (commonly known as feature representation transfer or transfer learning) have been purely empirical so far, extracting all CNN features from a single layer close to the output and testing their performance by feeding them to a classifier. This approach has provided consistent results, although its relevance is limited to classification tasks. In a completely different approach, in this paper we statistically measure the discriminative power of every single feature found within a deep CNN, when used for characterizing every class of 11 datasets. We seek to provide new insights into the behavior of CNN features, particularly the ones from convolutional layers, as this can be relevant for their application to knowledge representation and reasoning. Our results confirm that low and middle level features may behave differently to high level features, but only under certain conditions. We find that all CNN features can be used for knowledge representation purposes both by their presence or by their absence, doubling the information a single CNN feature may provide. We also study how much noise these features may include, and propose a thresholding approach to discard most of it. All these insights have a direct application to the generation of CNN embedding spaces.

papers.title: Feature learning is decoupled from generalization in high capacity neural networks
papers.research_question: Do current theories of feature learning measure the quality of learned features (which impacts generalization) or just the strength of representation changes?
papers.core_contribution: Current feature learning theories measure the strength of representation changes (FL strength) but not the quality of features, and these are decoupled. The paper introduces the FL gap to measure feature quality and shows that FL strength does not predict generalization.
papers.conclusion: Current theories of feature learning do not predict generalization because they measure strength rather than quality, indicating the need for a more comprehensive FL theory.
papers.key_findings:
The feature learning gap (∆NT) quantifies the performance improvement of neural networks over kernel methods.
Current FL definitions (NTK-based, CK-based, superposition-based) measure FL strength, not feature quality.
FL strength metrics (e.g., SNT, SCK) fail to distinguish between networks trained on true vs. shuffled labels, indicating decoupling from generalization.
The NTK-based FL strength can be manipulated by output scaling without affecting generalization.
CK-based cumulative utility does not differentiate between shuffled and non-shuffled data.
future_direction: Developing a more comprehensive feature learning theory that links feature learning to generalization.
papers.abstract: Neural networks outperform kernel methods, sometimes by orders of magnitude, e.g. on staircase functions. This advantage stems from the ability of neural networks to learn features, adapting their hidden representations to better capture the data. We introduce a concept we call feature quality to measure this performance improvement. We examine existing theories of feature learning and demonstrate empirically that they primarily assess the strength of feature learning, rather than the quality of the learned features themselves. Consequently, current theories of feature learning do not provide a sufficient foundation for developing theories of neural network generalization.

papers.title: Filtering with Self-Attention and Storing with MLP: One-Layer Transformers Can Provably Acquire and Extract Knowledge
papers.research_question: How do transformers acquire knowledge during pre-training via next-token prediction and extract it after fine-tuning? Under what conditions can pre-trained transformers perform out-of-distribution generalization after full and low-rank fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a theoretical framework for one-layer transformers that shows they can achieve near-optimal pre-training loss and post-fine-tuning out-of-distribution generalization under certain conditions, and explains the roles of self-attention and MLP in knowledge acquisition and extraction.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework provides convergence and generalization guarantees for one-layer transformers, elucidating the mechanisms of knowledge acquisition and extraction and the conditions for successful out-of-distribution generalization after fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can achieve near-optimal pre-training loss during pre-training, demonstrating effective knowledge acquisition.
Given a sufficiently large fine-tuning dataset and appropriate data multiplicity conditions, transformers achieve low generalization error on factual knowledge acquired during pre-training but not revisited in fine-tuning, indicating robust knowledge extraction.
Violation of these conditions leads to elevated generalization error, manifesting as hallucinations.
Self-attention learns to filter out noise tokens and focus on subject and relation tokens, enabling the MLP to learn balanced features for subjects and relations.
Low-rank fine-tuning is effective because the fine-tuning gradients closely approximate their best rank-1 form, with the right singular vector aligning with the Q&A format embedding.
papers.limitation: Uses orthogonal embeddings and simplified architecture, which may not fully capture real-world complexity.
future_direction: Analysis of random embeddings instead of orthogonal embeddings.
papers.abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) demonstrate exceptional performance on knowledge-intensive tasks, yet the theoretical mechanisms underlying knowledge acquisition (storage and memorization) during pre-training and extraction (retrieval and recall) during inference after fine-tuning remain poorly understood. Although prior theoretical studies have explored these processes through analyses of training dynamics, they overlook critical components essential for a comprehensive theory: (1) the multi-layer perceptron (MLP), empirically identified as the primary module for knowledge storage; (2) out-of-distribution (OOD) adaptivity, which enables LLMs to generalize to unseen scenarios post-pre-training; and (3) next-token prediction, the standard autoregressive objective that encodes knowledge as conditional probabilities. In this work, we introduce, to the best of our knowledge, the first theoretical framework that addresses these limitations by examining the training dynamics of one-layer transformers. Under regularity assumptions, we establish that: (i) transformers attain near-optimal training loss during pre-training, demonstrating effective knowledge acquisition; (ii) given a sufficiently large fine-tuning dataset and appropriate data multiplicity conditions, transformers achieve low generalization error on factual knowledge acquired during pre-training but not revisited in fine-tuning, indicating robust knowledge extraction; and (iii) violation of these conditions leads to elevated generalization error, manifesting as hallucinations. Our analysis encompasses both full fine-tuning and low-rank fine-tuning, yielding insights into the efficacy of practical low-rank adaptation methods. We validate our theoretical findings through experiments on synthetic datasets and the real-world PopQA benchmark, employing GPT-2 and Llama-3.2-1B models.

papers.title: Inference-Time Intervention: Eliciting Truthful Answers from a Language Model
papers.research_question: How can we enhance the truthfulness of large language models by intervening on their activations during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a minimally invasive technique that shifts activations along truthful directions in attention heads during inference to improve model truthfulness.
papers.conclusion: ITI is a promising, efficient method for improving truthfulness in LLMs, suggesting that models internally represent truth which can be elicited through activation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
ITI significantly improves truthfulness on the TruthfulQA benchmark, e.g., increasing Alpaca's truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness that can be balanced by tuning intervention strength.
ITI is data-efficient, requiring only a few hundred examples to find truthful directions.
ITI generalizes to other question-answering benchmarks (Natural Questions, TriviaQA, MMLU) with smaller improvements.
LLMs appear to have an internal representation of truth even when generating falsehoods.
papers.limitation:
ITI is not sufficient for ensuring truthful answers from LLMs and should be part of a more comprehensive approach.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness; increasing truthfulness may reduce informativeness.
future_direction: Test ITI on a wider variety of benchmarks beyond TruthfulQA.
Investigate the mechanistic understanding of what ITI does to internal representations.
papers.abstract: We introduce Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a technique designed to enhance the "truthfulness" of large language models (LLMs). ITI operates by shifting model activations during inference, following a set of directions across a limited number of attention heads. This intervention significantly improves the performance of LLaMA models on the TruthfulQA benchmark. On an instruction-finetuned LLaMA called Alpaca, ITI improves its truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%. We identify a tradeoff between truthfulness and helpfulness and demonstrate how to balance it by tuning the intervention strength. ITI is minimally invasive and computationally inexpensive. Moreover, the technique is data efficient: while approaches like RLHF require extensive annotations, ITI locates truthful directions using only few hundred examples. Our findings suggest that LLMs may have an internal representation of the likelihood of something being true, even as they produce falsehoods on the surface.

papers.title: When Representations Align: Universality in Representation Learning Dynamics
papers.research_question: What universal behaviors exist in representation learning dynamics across different neural network architectures? The paper derives an effective theory to describe these dynamics.
papers.core_contribution: Derives an effective theory of representation learning dynamics that exhibits universal behavior across architectures, with two regimes (rich and lazy) depending on initialization.
papers.conclusion: Representation learning dynamics exhibit universal behaviors across architectures when models are sufficiently flexible, and the effective theory captures these behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
The effective theory matches the representation learning dynamics of various architectures (fully connected, convolutional, skip connections, etc.).
Two regimes emerge: at small initial weights, representations are structured by the data (rich regime); at large initial weights, representations retain random initialization structure (lazy regime).
The theory predicts the final representational distance for pairs of datapoints, validated on synthetic datasets.
Experiments on toy datasets (XOR, orthogonal features) and MNIST show the theory's predictions hold for expressive architectures.
The theory breaks down for shallow networks, highlighting the importance of model expressivity.
papers.limitation:
The theory is only valid for expressive architectures and for pairs of datapoints; it does not account for inductive biases.
The linear approximation may break down for datapoints that are not close in representation space.
future_direction: Extend the theory to multi-point interactions.
Incorporate inductive biases of architectures into the theory.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks come in many sizes and architectures. The choice of architecture, in conjunction with the dataset and learning algorithm, is commonly understood to affect the learned neural representations. Yet, recent results have shown that different architectures learn representations with striking qualitative similarities. Here we derive an effective theory of representation learning under the assumption that the encoding map from input to hidden representation and the decoding map from representation to output are arbitrary smooth functions. This theory schematizes representation learning dynamics in the regime of complex, large architectures, where hidden representations are not strongly constrained by the parametrization. We show through experiments that the effective theory describes aspects of representation learning dynamics across a range of deep networks with different activation functions and architectures, and exhibits phenomena similar to the "rich" and "lazy" regime. While many network behaviors depend quantitatively on architecture, our findings point to certain behaviors that are widely conserved once models are sufficiently flexible.

papers.title: Inspecting and Editing Knowledge Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we map natural language statements to fact encodings in an LM's internal representations to enable editing and probing of knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: REMEDI is a method that learns to map natural language statements to fact encodings in LM representations, enabling both editing of knowledge (by adding vectors to hidden representations) and probing of existing knowledge.
papers.conclusion: REMEDI links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.
papers.key_findings:
REMEDI can patch errors made by an LM and insert new facts with or without context provided in the prompt.
REMEDI can help detect errors before generation by comparing edit vectors to unedited representations.
REMEDI increases accuracy on occupation classification and factual editing tasks compared to prompting baselines.
REMEDI generalizes from out-of-context training to in-context editing, suggesting unified representation of background and contextual knowledge.
REMEDI edits preserve correlations between features (e.g., adding 'made of metal' increases probability of 'shiny').
papers.limitation:
REMEDI can occasionally lead to disfluent or incorrect generations.
REMEDI sometimes damages the essence of the entity (e.g., making Wiener schnitzel an anime instead of a food).
REMEDI can also cause unrelated facts to change (e.g., changing the air dates of a TV show).
future_direction: Developing controlled generation interfaces that allow direct steering of model behavior in representation space.
Building tools for monitoring and controlling language generation by directly specifying facts and situations in an LM's native encoding scheme.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) represent facts about the world described by text. Sometimes these facts derive from training data (in most LMs, a representation of the word "banana" encodes the fact that bananas are fruits). Sometimes facts derive from input text itself (a representation of the sentence "I poured out the bottle" encodes the fact that the bottle became empty). We describe REMEDI, a method for learning to map statements in natural language to fact encodings in an LM's internal representation system. REMEDI encodings can be used as knowledge editors: when added to LM hidden representations, they modify downstream generation to be consistent with new facts. REMEDI encodings may also be used as probes: when compared to LM representations, they reveal which properties LMs already attribute to mentioned entities, in some cases making it possible to predict when LMs will generate outputs that conflict with background knowledge or input text. REMEDI thus links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.

papers.title: Network Transplanting
papers.research_question: How to transplant a pre-trained network module to a generic modular network with minimal supervision, i.e., with few or no training samples.
