However, existing RAG systems often suffer from an unfaithfulness issue, where the model's response contradicts evidence from the retrieved context. Existing approaches to improving contextual faithfulness largely rely on external interventions, such as prompt engineering, decoding constraints, or reward-based fine-tuning. These works treat the LLM as a black box and overlook a crucial question: how does the LLM internally integrate retrieved evidence with its parametric memory, particularly under knowledge conflicts? To address this gap, we conduct a probing-based analysis of hidden-state representations in LLMs and observe three findings: knowledge integration occurs hierarchically, conflicts manifest as latent signals at the sentence level, and irrelevant context is often amplified when aligned with parametric knowledge. Building on these findings, we propose CLEAR (Conflict-Localized and Enhanced Attention for RAG), a framework that (i) decomposes context into fine-grained sentence-level knowledge, (ii) employs hidden-state probing to localize conflicting knowledge, and (iii) introduces conflict-aware fine-tuning to guide the model to accurately integrate retrieved evidence. Extensive experiments across three benchmarks demonstrate that CLEAR substantially improves both accuracy and contextual faithfulness, consistently outperforming strong baselines under diverse conflict conditions. The related resources are available at https://github.com/LinfengGao/CLEAR.

papers.title: Adaptive Knowledge Distillation for Classification of Hand Images using Explainable Vision Transformers
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the use of vision transformers (ViTs) for classification of hand images and introduces distillation methods that allow a student model to adaptively extract knowledge from a teacher model while learning on data of a different domain to prevent catastrophic forgetting.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes adaptive knowledge distillation methods that enable a vision transformer model to excel in a new domain while retaining knowledge from a source domain without access to the source data, thereby preventing catastrophic forgetting.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of ViT models for hand image classification and shows that the proposed adaptive knowledge distillation methods enable successful domain adaptation without catastrophic forgetting, making them suitable for real-world biometric applications.
papers.key_findings:
ViT models significantly outperform traditional machine learning methods for hand image classification.
The internal states of ViTs, specifically the linear component of the 11th layer and the Norm component, are useful for explaining model outputs.
The proposed adaptive distillation methods achieve excellent performance on both source and target domains, particularly when the two domains are significantly dissimilar.
Distilling knowledge from a prior copy of the student as the teacher is more effective than using an ensemble teacher.
The methods help stabilize the learning process and mitigate catastrophic forgetting during domain adaptation.
future_direction: Develop the proposed methods on other types of data such as fingerprints and iris recognition data for biometric applications.
papers.abstract: Assessing the forensic value of hand images involves the use of unique features and patterns present in an individual's hand. The human hand has distinct characteristics, such as the pattern of veins, fingerprints, and the geometry of the hand itself. This paper investigates the use of vision transformers (ViTs) for classification of hand images. We use explainability tools to explore the internal representations of ViTs and assess their impact on the model outputs. Utilizing the internal understanding of ViTs, we introduce distillation methods that allow a student model to adaptively extract knowledge from a teacher model while learning on data of a different domain to prevent catastrophic forgetting. Two publicly available hand image datasets are used to conduct a series of experiments to evaluate performance of the ViTs and our proposed adaptive distillation methods. The experimental results demonstrate that ViT models significantly outperform traditional machine learning methods and the internal states of ViTs are useful for explaining the model outputs in the classification task. By averting catastrophic forgetting, our distillation methods achieve excellent performance on data from both source and target domains, particularly when these two domains exhibit significant dissimilarity. The proposed approaches therefore can be developed and implemented effectively for real-world applications such as access control, identity verification, and authentication systems.

papers.title: Learning Hierarchically-Structured Concepts II: Overlapping Concepts, and Networks With Feedback
papers.research_question: How can hierarchically structured concepts with limited overlap be represented, recognized, and learned in neural networks that include feedback edges?
papers.core_contribution: Extends previous work by allowing limited overlap between concepts and feedback edges in networks, and provides algorithms for recognition and learning in these more general settings.
papers.conclusion: The paper extends the study of hierarchically structured concepts to allow overlap and feedback, providing recognition and learning algorithms with theoretical guarantees.
papers.key_findings:
For feed-forward networks, robust recognition algorithms are provided that work with approximate weights and scaling.
For networks with feedback, recognition algorithms require only two passes for tree hierarchies but may require more time for general hierarchies with overlap.
Learning algorithms for feed-forward networks are extended to handle overlap using a modified Winner-Take-All assumption.
Learning algorithms for networks with feedback use separate rules for upward and downward edges.
The learning behavior is reformulated in terms of achieving certain ranges of edge weights.
papers.limitation: The learning algorithms depend on Winner-Take-All subnetworks that are treated abstractly and not implemented.
future_direction: Studying recognition after partial learning.
Handling extraneous inputs and stochastic firing.
Implementing Winner-Take-All networks and interleaving learning of children and parents.
papers.abstract: We continue our study from Lynch and Mallmann-Trenn (Neural Networks, 2021), of how concepts that have hierarchical structure might be represented in brain-like neural networks, how these representations might be used to recognize the concepts, and how these representations might be learned. In Lynch and Mallmann-Trenn (Neural Networks, 2021), we considered simple tree-structured concepts and feed-forward layered networks. Here we extend the model in two ways: we allow limited overlap between children of different concepts, and we allow networks to include feedback edges. For these more general cases, we describe and analyze algorithms for recognition and algorithms for learning.

papers.title: Mitigate Position Bias in LLMs via Scaling a Single Hidden States Channel
papers.research_question: How can position bias (lost in the middle) in long-context language models be mitigated by addressing positional information in hidden states?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that positional information in hidden states (besides position embeddings) contributes to position bias in LLMs, and proposes a method to mitigate bias by scaling a single channel of hidden states, improving performance on long-context tasks.
papers.conclusion: Scaling positional hidden states effectively mitigates position bias in LLMs, improving performance on long-context tasks without significant side effects, and the method is generalizable across different model architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights exhibit U-shaped patterns that correlate with position bias.
Positional information in hidden states, generated by the causal mask, is a significant cause of position bias.
Specific channels in hidden states (positional hidden states) show monotonic relationship with token position.
Scaling a single positional hidden state channel can significantly reduce position bias and improve retrieval accuracy.
The proposed method generalizes across different model architectures and tasks with minimal impact on original capabilities.

papers.title: A mathematical theory for understanding when abstract representations emerge in neural networks
papers.research_question: Under what conditions do abstract representations emerge in neural networks? Specifically, the paper investigates whether abstract representations are guaranteed to appear in feedforward networks trained on tasks that depend directly on latent variables.
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mathematical theory proving that abstract representations are guaranteed to emerge in the hidden layer of feedforward nonlinear networks when trained on tasks that depend directly on latent variables, and develops a mean-field optimization framework to analyze such representations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that abstract representations emerge naturally in neural networks trained on tasks with latent variables, providing a mathematical explanation for similar observations in neuroscience and machine learning, and offers a general framework for understanding representation geometry in task-optimized networks.
papers.key_findings:
For whitened and target-aligned inputs, ReLU networks develop abstract representations with parallelism score (PS) equal to 1 at global minima.
The optimal representation kernel takes the form K = a*11^T + b*K_Y, where K_Y is the output kernel.
The emergence of abstract representations is robust to the choice of activation function, holding for two broad classes of nonlinearities: threshold functions and odd functions.
The theory extends to multi-element classes (n ≥ 2) and deep feedforward architectures.
The framework provides a mean-field description where the optimal preactivation distribution satisfies a self-consistent condition.
papers.limitation:
The theory is limited to feedforward networks trained on tasks with binary latent variables and assumes the network reaches a global minimum.
The analysis assumes specific input geometries (whitened or target-aligned inputs) and may not cover all possible input structures.
future_direction: Extend the framework to other architectures such as ResNet and transformer models.
Analyze learning dynamics in networks trained with biological learning rules.
Investigate the Platonic representation hypothesis using the developed mathematical toolkit.
papers.abstract: Recent experiments reveal that task-relevant variables are often encoded in approximately orthogonal subspaces of the neural activity space. These disentangled low-dimensional representations are observed in multiple brain areas and across different species, and are typically the result of a process of abstraction that supports simple forms of out-of-distribution generalization. The mechanisms by which such geometries emerge remain poorly understood, and the mechanisms that have been investigated are typically unsupervised (e.g., based on variational auto-encoders). Here, we show mathematically that abstract representations of latent variables are guaranteed to appear in the last hidden layer of feedforward nonlinear networks when they are trained on tasks that depend directly on these latent variables. These abstract representations reflect the structure of the desired outputs or the semantics of the input stimuli. To investigate the neural representations that emerge in these networks, we develop an analytical framework that maps the optimization over the network weights into a mean-field problem over the distribution of neural preactivations. Applying this framework to a finite-width ReLU network, we find that its hidden layer exhibits an abstract representation at all global minima of the task objective. We further extend these analyses to two broad families of activation functions and deep feedforward architectures, demonstrating that abstract representations naturally arise in all these scenarios. Together, these results provide an explanation for the widely observed abstract representations in both the brain and artificial neural networks, as well as a mathematically tractable toolkit for understanding the emergence of different kinds of representations in task-optimized, feature-learning network models.

papers.title: Pruned Neural Networks are Surprisingly Modular
papers.research_question: What is the modular structure of multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) after training and weight pruning?
papers.core_contribution: Training and weight pruning produce MLPs that are more modular than randomly initialized networks, and dropout during training significantly increases modularity.
papers.conclusion: The process of learning via gradient descent and pruning selects for modularity, and modularity is closely associated with learning.
papers.key_findings:
Pruned neural networks are more modular than random networks with the same sparsity and weight distribution.
Networks trained with dropout are much more modular than those trained without dropout.
Modularity increases as a by-product of learning or memorization, not automatically from SGD or pruning alone.
Lesion experiments show that the identified modules have functional significance for network performance.
The modularity is not just due to topology; the specific weight values also contribute to clusterability.
papers.limitation: The paper provides almost no understanding of the specific function of 'modules', and we are as yet unable to infer any aspects of the behavior of the network from the techniques described.
future_direction: Extending results to larger networks trained on larger datasets.
Developing an appropriate notion of modularity for convolutional neural networks.
Understanding why networks are clusterable and why dropout has the effect it does.
papers.abstract: The learned weights of a neural network are often considered devoid of scrutable internal structure. To discern structure in these weights, we introduce a measurable notion of modularity for multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), and investigate the modular structure of MLPs trained on datasets of small images. Our notion of modularity comes from the graph clustering literature: a "module" is a set of neurons with strong internal connectivity but weak external connectivity. We find that training and weight pruning produces MLPs that are more modular than randomly initialized ones, and often significantly more modular than random MLPs with the same (sparse) distribution of weights. Interestingly, they are much more modular when trained with dropout. We also present exploratory analyses of the importance of different modules for performance and how modules depend on each other. Understanding the modular structure of neural networks, when such structure exists, will hopefully render their inner workings more interpretable to engineers. Note that this paper has been superceded by "Clusterability in Neural Networks", arxiv:2103.03386 and "Quantifying Local Specialization in Deep Neural Networks", arxiv:2110.08058!

papers.title: From Compression to Expression: A Layerwise Analysis of In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How do LLMs extract and differentiate task information from shallow to deep layers during in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers and analyzes the Layerwise Compression-Expression phenomenon in ICL, where early layers compress task information from demonstrations and later layers express it for prediction, with implications for performance and robustness.
papers.conclusion: This work provides a comprehensive analysis of ICL internal dynamics, uncovering the prevalent Layerwise Compression-Expression phenomenon, which deepens understanding of structured representation learning in LLMs and offers practical implications for interpretability, efficiency, and robustness.
papers.key_findings:
The Layerwise Compression-Expression phenomenon is prevalent across diverse model architectures (transformer and state-space) and task domains (symbolic, language, multimodal).
Larger models and more demonstrations lead to more compressed task representations, explaining performance improvements with scale and context length.
Noisy demonstrations result in less compressed representations, but ICL remains robust up to a certain noise ratio due to distinguishable task vectors.
Attention mechanisms contribute to reducing both bias and variance of task representations as the number of demonstrations increases, as shown in a theoretical analysis.
Task-vector contrastive fine-tuning, motivated by the analysis, can further compress task vectors and improve task-vector accuracy.
papers.limitation: The theoretical analysis uses a simplified linear attention model, sharing the same simplifications and limitations as prior work on linear self-attention.
future_direction: Theoretical investigation of the phenomenon in the infinite-sample regime.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables large language models (LLMs) to adapt to new tasks without weight updates by learning from demonstration sequences. While ICL shows strong empirical performance, its internal representational mechanisms are not yet well understood. In this work, we conduct a statistical geometric analysis of ICL representations to investigate how task-specific information is captured across layers. Our analysis reveals an intriguing phenomenon, which we term *Layerwise Compression-Expression*: early layers progressively produce compact and discriminative representations that encode task information from the input demonstrations, while later layers express these representations to incorporate the query and generate the prediction. This phenomenon is observed consistently across diverse tasks and a range of contemporary LLM architectures. We demonstrate that it has important implications for ICL performance -- improving with model size and the number of demonstrations -- and for robustness in the presence of noisy examples. To further understand the effect of the compact task representation, we propose a bias-variance decomposition and provide a theoretical analysis showing how attention mechanisms contribute to reducing both variance and bias, thereby enhancing performance as the number of demonstrations increases. Our findings reveal an intriguing layerwise dynamic in ICL, highlight how structured representations emerge within LLMs, and showcase that analyzing internal representations can facilitate a deeper understanding of model behavior.

papers.title: How Does Gradient Descent Learn Features -- A Local Analysis for Regularized Two-Layer Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Does feature learning only happen in the early stages of gradient training, or can it also occur in the final stage (local convergence)?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that feature learning can occur in the final stage of gradient training (local convergence) through a variant of gradient descent with weight decay, allowing recovery of ground-truth directions in a teacher-student setup.
papers.conclusion: Feature learning not only happens at the initial gradient steps, but can also occur towards the end of training.
papers.key_findings:
Feature learning can occur in the final stage of gradient training (local convergence), not only in early stages.
A variant of gradient descent with weight decay can recover the target network within polynomial time.
Student neurons align with teacher neurons at the end of training, capturing exact ground-truth directions.
The local loss landscape satisfies a Lojasiewicz property, ensuring gradient descent makes progress.
Weight decay helps balance norms between layers and reduces cancellation between neurons with opposite signs.
papers.limitation: Analysis is on population loss; finite-sample analysis is omitted.
future_direction: Proving convergence when training both layers simultaneously beyond early and final stages.
Achieving a tight sample complexity for finite-sample analysis.
papers.abstract: The ability of learning useful features is one of the major advantages of neural networks. Although recent works show that neural network can operate in a neural tangent kernel (NTK) regime that does not allow feature learning, many works also demonstrate the potential for neural networks to go beyond NTK regime and perform feature learning. Recently, a line of work highlighted the feature learning capabilities of the early stages of gradient-based training. In this paper we consider another mechanism for feature learning via gradient descent through a local convergence analysis. We show that once the loss is below a certain threshold, gradient descent with a carefully regularized objective will capture ground-truth directions. We further strengthen this local convergence analysis by incorporating early-stage feature learning analysis. Our results demonstrate that feature learning not only happens at the initial gradient steps, but can also occur towards the end of training.

papers.title: Extending a Mathematical Theory of the Emergence of Knowledge from the Experience to Capture Learning Dynamics in Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers' learning dynamics emerge from the structure of training data, and how does this relate to human semantic development?
papers.core_contribution: Extends a mathematical theory of learning dynamics to minimal transformers, demonstrating that learning trajectories are predictable from data structure and mirror human semantic development.
papers.conclusion: The work provides initial steps toward understanding how transformers learn, demonstrating that experience guides learning in a way that mirrors human semantic development, and the mathematical theory helps capture these dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Learning occurs in two phases: fast reduction of loss-between via relation information, and slower reduction of loss-within via item information through attention.
Learning dynamics follow sigmoidal trajectories for dataset dimensions, as predicted by deep linear network theory.
The model exhibits progressive differentiation of concepts, learning broader categories before finer ones.
The model shows U-shaped learning for certain features, such as overgeneralization of properties.
Embeddings from the minimal transformer correlate with those from larger LLMs, suggesting relevance to scaled-up models.
papers.limitation: The study uses a simplified toy dataset and minimal transformer architecture, which may not fully capture complexities of natural language and larger models.
future_direction: Extending models and training sets to more natural language datasets.
Exploring how attentional strategies emerge for handling longer contextual dependencies.
papers.abstract: The Transformer architecture used in LLMs has garnered widespread attention due to these model's human-like conceptual knowledge and language understanding, yet understanding how these models' capabilities result from experience-guided learning, and connecting this learning process with the structure in their training data, can seem intractable. Here we present preliminary steps to characterizing the developmental trajectory of a minimal Transformer trained on a next-token prediction task, using a simple dataset with quantifiable uncertainty and a simple, intuitively characterizable structure that captures some aspects of natural semantic structure learned by LLMs from large datasets. We show how the dynamic learning process of this model is a predictable consequence of the structure of the training data, exhibiting attested features of human semantic development, as captured in a theory of neural network learning dynamics (Saxe et. al. 2019) previously used to capture such dynamics in a network originally introduced by Rumelhart & Todd (1993).

papers.title: Secret mixtures of experts inside your LLM
papers.research_question: Can MLP layers in trained transformer language models be well approximated by sparsely-activating Mixture of Experts (MoE) layers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper hypothesizes and empirically validates that dense MLP layers in pretrained transformers secretly implement a sparse Mixture of Experts (MoE) structure, which can be uncovered via distillation and depends crucially on the structure of the activation distribution.
papers.conclusion: MLP layers in trained transformers exhibit a latent sparse MoE structure, which explains the success of explicit MoE architectures and suggests new directions for efficient MoE design via distillation-based experimentation.
papers.key_findings:
MLP layers in pretrained LLMs can be effectively approximated by sparsely-activating MoE layers with fewer active parameters than a dense MLP.
This secret MoE structure is dependent on the distribution of internal activations and does not hold for Gaussian data with matched statistics.
Including a shared expert in the MoE student model improves distillation performance.
Using a low-rank router in the MoE gating function improves distillation performance and reduces computational cost.
The results provide an explanation for the effectiveness of modern MoE-based transformer architectures.
future_direction: Using distillation as a fast and cheap test-bed for architecture design experimentation.
Further testing of MoE architectures with low-rank routers.
papers.abstract: Despite being one of the earliest neural network layers, the Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) is arguably one of the least understood parts of the transformer architecture due to its dense computation and lack of easy visualization. This paper seeks to understand the MLP layers in dense LLM models by hypothesizing that these layers secretly approximately perform a sparse computation -- namely, that they can be well approximated by sparsely-activating Mixture of Experts (MoE) layers. Our hypothesis is based on a novel theoretical connection between MoE models and Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) structure in activation space. We empirically validate the hypothesis on pretrained LLMs, and demonstrate that the activation distribution matters -- these results do not hold for Gaussian data, but rather rely crucially on structure in the distribution of neural network activations. Our results shine light on a general principle at play in MLP layers inside LLMs, and give an explanation for the effectiveness of modern MoE-based transformers. Additionally, our experimental explorations suggest new directions for more efficient MoE architecture design based on low-rank routers.

papers.title: Editing Conceptual Knowledge for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs possess the capability to modify concepts (conceptual knowledge) and how to evaluate such modifications.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the task of conceptual knowledge editing for LLMs, constructs a benchmark dataset ConceptEdit, and establishes a suite of evaluation metrics including Instance Change and Concept Consistency.
papers.conclusion: Concept editing is a challenging task for LLMs, and existing editing methods have limitations in modifying conceptual knowledge without distorting related instances. This work provides a benchmark and metrics to inspire further research.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing methods (FT, ROME, MEMIT, PROMPT) can achieve high reliability in modifying concept-level definitions in LLMs.
These methods perform poorly on concept-specific metrics like Instance Change and Concept Consistency, indicating they distort related instance knowledge.
There is a gap between reliability (token-level accuracy) and concept consistency (semantic similarity of generated definitions).
Concept editing is easier when the replacement definition comes from the same superclass (intra module) compared to a different superclass (inter module).
Causal tracing reveals that conceptual knowledge is stored differently from instance knowledge, with attention mechanisms in earlier layers playing a key role.
papers.limitation:
The experiments are limited to models up to 7B parameters; larger models may exhibit different behaviors.
The generalization of edited concepts to unseen instances or related concepts is not fully explored.
The mechanisms of how LLMs learn and represent concepts and concept hierarchies are not fully understood.
future_direction: Exploring concept editing in larger-scale language models.
Improving the generalization of edited concepts to related knowledge.
Studying the mechanisms of concept learning and representation in LLMs.

papers.title: Inversion dynamics of class manifolds in deep learning reveals tradeoffs underlying generalisation
papers.research_question: How does the optimization dynamics balance segregation and entanglement of class manifolds during training, and what is the role of 'stragglers' in this tradeoff and generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals a non-monotonic dynamics in class manifold segregation during training, characterized by an inversion point where manifolds become more entangled, and identifies 'stragglers' as a subset of training examples that drive this inversion and are crucial for generalization.
papers.conclusion: The inversion dynamics reveals a tradeoff between segregation and entanglement of class manifolds, with stragglers playing a key role in shaping the learning dynamics and influencing generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Class manifold dynamics is non-monotonic: an initial segregation phase is followed by an inversion where manifolds expand and become more entangled.
The training error at the inversion point is stable across different optimizers, data subsets, and initializations.
The inversion is caused by 'stragglers', a set of misclassified examples at the inversion point, which are conserved across initializations and data shuffles.
Removing stragglers from the training set eliminates the inversion and leads to worse generalization.
The fraction of stragglers is an invariant property of the dataset, weakly dependent on architecture, and related to dataset complexity.
papers.limitation:
The phenomenology may not be as clear in state-of-the-art deep convolutional neural networks or transformers.
The analysis focuses solely on the internal representations at the first layer, even in deeper architectures.
The sensitivity of the test error under pruning to architecture choice is not fully explored.
future_direction: Exploring the relation between stragglers and other metrics of task difficulty, such as intrinsic dimensions of the dataset.
Investigating the potential role of stragglers in data pruning strategies and curriculum learning.
More systematic exploration of the behavior in different architectures, especially convolutional neural networks.
papers.abstract: To achieve near-zero training error in a classification problem, the layers of a feed-forward network have to disentangle the manifolds of data points with different labels, to facilitate the discrimination. However, excessive class separation can bring to overfitting since good generalisation requires learning invariant features, which involve some level of entanglement. We report on numerical experiments showing how the optimisation dynamics finds representations that balance these opposing tendencies with a non-monotonic trend. After a fast segregation phase, a slower rearrangement (conserved across data sets and architectures) increases the class entanglement.The training error at the inversion is stable under subsampling, and across network initialisations and optimisers, which characterises it as a property solely of the data structure and (very weakly) of the architecture. The inversion is the manifestation of tradeoffs elicited by well-defined and maximally stable elements of the training set, coined ``stragglers'', particularly influential for generalisation.

papers.title: Invertible Neural Networks for Understanding Semantics of Invariances of CNN Representations
papers.research_question: How can we understand the semantic concepts and invariances learned by deep neural networks (specifically CNNs) by recovering the invariances and translating the representations into an interpretable form without modifying the original model?
papers.core_contribution: An invertible neural network (INN) approach that recovers the invariances a deep model has learned and bijectively translates the model representation and its invariances into a semantically accessible encoding without compromising the original model's performance.
papers.conclusion: The invertible approach provides a powerful, post-hoc diagnostic pipeline for explaining deep representations by recovering invariances and enabling semantic interpretation without retraining the model.
papers.key_findings:
The method visualizes representations and their invariances without artifacts, outperforming existing network inversion methods.
Analysis of FaceNet shows that invariances (e.g., to pose) increase with layer depth, while some features (e.g., glasses) remain identity-relevant across layers.
The approach can quantify how much of a semantic concept (e.g., texture vs. shape) is captured by a model's representation, revealing biases like texture bias in ImageNet-trained CNNs.
Semantic modifications in the interpretable space correctly alter the original representation and can be visualized, enabling diagnostic probing of model sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Abstract To tackle increasingly complex tasks, it has become an essential ability of neural networks to learn abstract representations. These task-specific representations and, particularly, the invariances they capture turn neural networks into black-box models that lack interpretability. To open such a black box, it is, therefore, crucial to uncover the different semantic concepts a model has learned as well as those that it has learned to be invariant to. We present an approach based on invertible neural networks (INNs) that (i) recovers the task-specific, learned invariances by disentangling the remaining factor of variation in the data and that (ii) invertibly transforms these recovered invariances combined with the model representation into an equally expressive one with accessible semantic concepts. As a consequence, neural network representations become understandable by providing the means to (i) expose their semantic meaning, (ii) semantically modify a representation, and (iii) visualize individual learned semantic concepts and invariances. Our invertible approach significantly extends the abilities to understand black-box models by enabling post hoc interpretations of state-of-the-art networks without compromising their performance. Our implementation is available at https://compvis.github.io/invariances/ .

papers.title: Break It Down: Evidence for Structural Compositionality in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Do neural networks implement compositional solutions by decomposing tasks into modular subnetworks, or do they learn non-compositional templates?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks often implement compositional tasks via modular subnetworks, suggesting they can learn compositionality without symbolic mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks exhibit structural compositionality, indicating they can learn compositional representations internally.
papers.key_findings:
Many models implement subroutines in modular subnetworks, which can be ablated while maintaining other functionalities.
Pretraining leads to more consistently compositional structure in language models.
Evidence of structural compositionality varies across tasks and architectures, with some showing strong modularity and others more diffuse implementations.
Control experiments with randomly initialized models show that the discovered subnetworks are not epiphenomenal artifacts.
papers.abstract: Though modern neural networks have achieved impressive performance in both vision and language tasks, we know little about the functions that they implement. One possibility is that neural networks implicitly break down complex tasks into subroutines, implement modular solutions to these subroutines, and compose them into an overall solution to a task - a property we term structural compositionality. Another possibility is that they may simply learn to match new inputs to learned templates, eliding task decomposition entirely. Here, we leverage model pruning techniques to investigate this question in both vision and language across a variety of architectures, tasks, and pretraining regimens. Our results demonstrate that models often implement solutions to subroutines via modular subnetworks, which can be ablated while maintaining the functionality of other subnetworks. This suggests that neural networks may be able to learn compositionality, obviating the need for specialized symbolic mechanisms.

papers.title: Can LLMs Predict Their Own Failures? Self-Awareness via Internal Circuits
papers.research_question: Can LLMs predict their own failures by inspecting internal states during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Gnosis, a lightweight self-awareness mechanism that enables frozen LLMs to perform intrinsic self-verification by decoding signals from hidden states and attention patterns with negligible inference overhead.
papers.conclusion: Gnosis provides a highly efficient framework for self-evaluation and sibling modeling, enabling early error detection and compute-aware control, demonstrating that intrinsic self-verification is both scalable and cost-effective.
papers.key_findings:
Gnosis consistently outperforms strong internal baselines and large external judges (e.g., 8B reward models, Gemini 2.5 Pro) in accuracy and calibration across math reasoning, QA, and academic knowledge benchmarks.
Gnosis generalizes zero-shot to partial generations, enabling early detection of failing trajectories and compute-aware control.
A Gnosis head trained on a small backbone transfers effectively to judge larger sibling models without fine-tuning.
Gnosis adds only ~5M parameters and operates with negligible inference cost, independent of sequence length.
Results show that reliable correctness cues are intrinsic to the generation process and can be extracted efficiently without external supervision.
papers.limitation: Gnosis is designed as a self-awareness mechanism rather than a general-purpose reward model; it transfers robustly to siblings but is not capable of acting as a general reward model.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) generate fluent and complex outputs but often fail to recognize their own mistakes and hallucinations. Existing approaches typically rely on external judges, multi-sample consistency, or text-based self-critique, which incur additional compute or correlate weakly with true correctness. We ask: can LLMs predict their own failures by inspecting internal states during inference? We introduce Gnosis, a lightweight self-awareness mechanism that enables frozen LLMs to perform intrinsic self-verification by decoding signals from hidden states and attention patterns. Gnosis passively observes internal traces, compresses them into fixed-budget descriptors, and predicts correctness with negligible inference cost, adding only ~5M parameters and operating independently of sequence length. Across math reasoning, open-domain question answering, and academic knowledge benchmarks, and over frozen backbones ranging from 1.7B to 20B parameters, Gnosis consistently outperforms strong internal baselines and large external judges in both accuracy and calibration. Moreover, it generalizes zero-shot to partial generations, enabling early detection of failing trajectories and compute-aware control. These results show that reliable correctness cues are intrinsic to generation process and can be extracted efficiently without external supervision.

papers.title: Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens (CORAL): Transferrable and Calibration-Aware Inference-Time Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve both accuracy and calibration of LLMs during inference by directly steering using correctness signals from internal activations, rather than optimizing proxies?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CORAL, a lightweight inference-time steering method that uses regularized MLP probes on residual activations to improve accuracy and calibration in MCQA tasks, with demonstrated transferability across benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CORAL provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference by extracting distributed correctness signals via regularized probes.
papers.key_findings:
CORAL consistently improves accuracy and calibration across three 7B models and multiple MCQA benchmarks.
CORAL's learned steering directions transfer without retraining to four held-out benchmarks, averaging 14% accuracy and 49% ECE improvements.
Correctness signals are distributed across many neurons and require supervised aggregation; sparse methods like SAE fail to capture them.
Middle layers (17-21) contain the most useful correctness signals for steering.
Regularized probes capture distributed correctness signals that sparse methods miss.
papers.limitation:
Limited to multiple-choice question answering; generalization to free-form generation is open.
Requires labeled data to train probes, which may not be available for all domains or languages.
Adds inference latency due to activation extraction and probe prediction.
Transfer performance depends on similarity between source and target tasks; dissimilar tasks yield smaller improvements.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit persistent miscalibration, especially after instruction tuning and preference alignment. Modified training objectives can improve calibration, but retraining is expensive. Inference-time steering offers a lightweight alternative, yet most existing methods optimize proxies for correctness rather than correctness itself. We introduce CORAL (Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens), a regularized inference-time steering method that captures distributed correctness signals from model internal activations using weight-decay MLP probes. We evaluate CORAL across three 7B-parameter models and find that it consistently improves accuracy by 10\% and expected calibration error (ECE) by 50\% on average. We additionally demonstrate that these gains transfer without retraining to the complete published test sets of four held-out benchmarks (ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, Math-MC, OpenBookQA), averaging 14\% accuracy improvements and 49\% ECE improvements. Our results support the hypothesis that distributed information in model internals can be extracted using regularized probes when individual neurons are insufficient. CORAL thus provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference.

papers.title: Representation Learning: A Review and New Perspectives
papers.research_question: What makes one representation better than another? Given an example, how should we compute its representation, i.e. perform feature extraction? Also, what are appropriate objectives for learning good representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reviews recent advances in representation learning and deep learning, and discusses open questions about the objectives for learning good representations, computing representations, and the connections between representation learning, density estimation, and manifold learning.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that representation learning is a key component for advancing AI, and identifies open questions about the objectives for learning good representations, inference, and the connections to manifold learning and density estimation.
papers.key_findings:
Representation learning is crucial for AI because it can disentangle the underlying explanatory factors in data.
Deep architectures promote feature re-use and abstraction, leading to more expressive and invariant representations.
Unsupervised pre-training and deep learning have led to breakthroughs in speech recognition, object recognition, and natural language processing.
There are many open questions about the appropriate objectives for learning good representations and for performing inference (computing representations).
The geometrical perspective of manifold learning connects representation learning to density estimation and provides insights into the structure of data.
future_direction: Determine appropriate objectives for learning good representations.
Develop methods for computing representations (inference).
Explore the geometrical connections between representation learning, density estimation, and manifold learning.
papers.abstract: The success of machine learning algorithms generally depends on data representation, and we hypothesize that this is because different representations can entangle and hide more or less the different explanatory factors of variation behind the data. Although specific domain knowledge can be used to help design representations, learning with generic priors can also be used, and the quest for AI is motivating the design of more powerful representation-learning algorithms implementing such priors. This paper reviews recent work in the area of unsupervised feature learning and deep learning, covering advances in probabilistic models, auto-encoders, manifold learning, and deep networks. This motivates longer-term unanswered questions about the appropriate objectives for learning good representations, for computing representations (i.e., inference), and the geometrical connections between representation learning, density estimation and manifold learning.

papers.title: PMET: Precise Model Editing in a Transformer
papers.research_question: How can we achieve more precise model editing in transformers by optimizing the hidden states of individual components (MHSA and FFN) rather than the combined transformer layer hidden states?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes PMET, a model editing method that optimizes hidden states of both MHSA and FFN but only updates FFN weights, based on the finding that MHSA acts as a knowledge extractor with general patterns.
papers.conclusion: We reveal that MHSA works as a knowledge extractor and encodes certain general knowledge extraction patterns. Based on this finding, we propose PMET, which simultaneously optimizes the TC hidden states of both MHSA and FFN while only uses the optimized TC hidden states of FFN to perform precise updates of FFN weights. Our experiments on zsRE and COUNTERFACT demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of PMET.
papers.key_findings:
MHSA works as a knowledge extractor and encodes certain general knowledge extraction patterns.
PMET achieves state-of-the-art performance on COUNTERFACT and zsRE datasets.
Simultaneously optimizing the TC hidden states of MHSA and FFN improves editing reliability compared to optimizing only FFN hidden states.
Updating MHSA weights slightly improves generalization but harms specificity.
Square root spread of residuals enhances reliability but leads to larger model changes, affecting specificity.
papers.limitation:
The partial opacity of LLMs’ internal mechanisms poses challenges for direct weight modification; edited models might not truly internalize knowledge and cannot reason using edited knowledge.
Benchmark and dataset construction have not strictly adhered to the subject-centric definition of model editing.
future_direction: Devise more sophisticated editing methods and evaluation metrics (e.g., MQuAKE, RIPPLEEDITS) to advance model editing.
papers.abstract: Model editing techniques modify a minor proportion of knowledge in Large Language Models (LLMs) at a relatively low cost, which have demonstrated notable success. Existing methods assume Transformer Layer (TL) hidden states are values of key-value memories of the Feed-Forward Network (FFN). They usually optimize the TL hidden states to memorize target knowledge and use it to update the weights of the FFN in LLMs. However, the information flow of TL hidden states comes from three parts: Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA), FFN, and residual connections. Existing methods neglect the fact that the TL hidden states contains information not specifically required for FFN. Consequently, the performance of model editing decreases. To achieve more precise model editing, we analyze hidden states of MHSA and FFN, finding that MHSA encodes certain general knowledge extraction patterns. This implies that MHSA weights do not require updating when new knowledge is introduced. Based on above findings, we introduce PMET, which simultaneously optimizes Transformer Component (TC, namely MHSA and FFN) hidden states, while only using the optimized TC hidden states of FFN to precisely update FFN weights. Our experiments demonstrate that PMET exhibits state-of-the-art performance on both the COUNTERFACT and zsRE datasets. Our ablation experiments substantiate the effectiveness of our enhancements, further reinforcing the finding that the MHSA encodes certain general knowledge extraction patterns and indicating its storage of a small amount of factual knowledge. Our code is available at https://github.com/xpq-tech/PMET.

papers.title: Grokking as a First Order Phase Transition in Two Layer Networks
papers.research_question: How can grokking in deep neural networks be understood as a first-order phase transition in representation learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper establishes a mapping between grokking and first-order phase transitions in representation learning, providing analytical predictions for two teacher-student models and identifying distinct feature learning phases.
papers.conclusion: Grokking is a result of a first-order phase transition in representation learning, and the proposed framework provides a way to classify feature learning effects and make analytical predictions.
papers.key_findings:
Grokking in two-layer networks corresponds to a first-order phase transition in the internal representations.
Three phases of feature learning are identified: Gaussian Feature Learning (GFL), Gaussian Mixture Feature Learning I (GMFL-I), and GMFL-II.
For the cubic teacher and modular addition models, the learning problem reduces to solving a non-linear equation involving one or two order parameters.
For the modular addition model, the location of the phase transition is determined analytically.
Grokking can reduce sample complexity compared to the Gaussian Process (GP) limit by leveraging feature learning.
papers.limitation:
The equivalent kernel approximation washes out generalization phenomena associated with Grokking, focusing only on underlying feature learning mechanisms.
The analysis is limited to two-layer networks, though the formalism may generalize to deeper architectures.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to deeper networks and varying architectures.
Developing measures to predict when a model is close to grokking by tracking outliers in weight or pre-activation distributions.
Exploring novel pruning and regularization methods based on latent kernel eigenvalues.
papers.abstract: A key property of deep neural networks (DNNs) is their ability to learn new features during training. This intriguing aspect of deep learning stands out most clearly in recently reported Grokking phenomena. While mainly reflected as a sudden increase in test accuracy, Grokking is also believed to be a beyond lazy-learning/Gaussian Process (GP) phenomenon involving feature learning. Here we apply a recent development in the theory of feature learning, the adaptive kernel approach, to two teacher-student models with cubic-polynomial and modular addition teachers. We provide analytical predictions on feature learning and Grokking properties of these models and demonstrate a mapping between Grokking and the theory of phase transitions. We show that after Grokking, the state of the DNN is analogous to the mixed phase following a first-order phase transition. In this mixed phase, the DNN generates useful internal representations of the teacher that are sharply distinct from those before the transition.

papers.title: Representing Deep Neural Networks Latent Space Geometries with Graphs
papers.research_question: How can we enforce desirable properties on intermediate representations of deep neural networks? The paper proposes to represent latent space geometries with graphs (LGGs) and constrain them to address knowledge distillation, latent embedding design, and robustness.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a methodology to represent latent space geometries with similarity graphs (LGGs) and shows how constraining these graphs can address knowledge distillation, latent embedding design, and robustness in deep neural networks.
papers.conclusion: The proposed formalism of Latent Geometry Graphs (LGGs) is effective for knowledge distillation, latent embeddings, and robustness, and could be applied to other problems such as predicting generalization and understanding decisions in deep learning architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Graph Knowledge Distillation (GKD) using LGGs outperforms relational knowledge distillation (RKD) and baseline in compressing a teacher network to a student network.
Using label variation as an objective function for latent embeddings yields test accuracy comparable to cross-entropy and improves robustness to corruptions.
Using label variation as a regularizer to enforce smooth evolution of geometries across layers improves robustness to adversarial attacks and corruptions.
The proposed graph-based formalism is dimension-agnostic and can compare latent spaces of different dimensions.
The methodology is demonstrated on standard vision benchmarks (CIFAR-10) with ResNet and WideResNet architectures.
papers.limitation: The graph construction method (using cosine similarity or RBF kernel) may be influenced by the curse of dimensionality, and graph normalization is not ideal but helps.
future_direction: Applying the LGG formalism to more problems, such as predicting generalization, improving performance in data-thrifty settings, and understanding how decisions are taken in deep learning architectures.
Improving graph construction methods to better handle the influence of dimension on graph comparison.
Using graph convolutional networks in domains that are not typically supported by graphs.
papers.abstract: Deep Learning (DL) has attracted a lot of attention for its ability to reach state-of-the-art performance in many machine learning tasks. The core principle of DL methods consists of training composite architectures in an end-to-end fashion, where inputs are associated with outputs trained to optimize an objective function. Because of their compositional nature, DL architectures naturally exhibit several intermediate representations of the inputs, which belong to so-called latent spaces. When treated individually, these intermediate representations are most of the time unconstrained during the learning process, as it is unclear which properties should be favored. However, when processing a batch of inputs concurrently, the corresponding set of intermediate representations exhibit relations (what we call a geometry) on which desired properties can be sought. In this work, we show that it is possible to introduce constraints on these latent geometries to address various problems. In more detail, we propose to represent geometries by constructing similarity graphs from the intermediate representations obtained when processing a batch of inputs. By constraining these Latent Geometry Graphs (LGGs), we address the three following problems: (i) reproducing the behavior of a teacher architecture is achieved by mimicking its geometry, (ii) designing efficient embeddings for classification is achieved by targeting specific geometries, and (iii) robustness to deviations on inputs is achieved via enforcing smooth variation of geometry between consecutive latent spaces. Using standard vision benchmarks, we demonstrate the ability of the proposed geometry-based methods in solving the considered problems.

papers.title: Make Haste Slowly: A Theory of Emergent Structured Mixed Selectivity in Feature Learning ReLU Networks
papers.research_question: How do finite-width ReLU networks learn features, and what inductive biases do they exhibit in contextual tasks requiring nonlinearity?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Rectified Linear Networks (ReLNs) as a tractable analytical framework for ReLU networks and demonstrates that ReLU networks have an inductive bias towards structured mixed-selectivity representations that are reused across contexts.
papers.conclusion: ReLU networks exhibit emergent structured mixed-selectivity in their latent representations due to a bias for node-reuse and learning speed, providing a step towards a theory of feature learning in finite ReLU networks.
papers.key_findings:
Establishes an equivalence between ReLU networks and Gated Deep Linear Networks (GDLNs) via ReLNs, enabling full training dynamics analysis.
Shows that ReLU networks adopt nonlinear decision boundaries even when a problem is linearly separable, transitioning at a predictable margin.
In a contextual task, ReLU networks exhibit an implicit bias towards structured mixed-selectivity and node reuse, which minimizes loss fastest.
The bias towards node reuse and mixed selectivity is amplified with the addition of more contexts and hidden layers.
papers.limitation: The analysis relies on assumptions of mutually diagonalizable dataset correlation matrices and network weight alignment to singular vectors (Assumption 2.1).
papers.abstract: In spite of finite dimension ReLU neural networks being a consistent factor behind recent deep learning successes, a theory of feature learning in these models remains elusive. Currently, insightful theories still rely on assumptions including the linearity of the network computations, unstructured input data and architectural constraints such as infinite width or a single hidden layer. To begin to address this gap we establish an equivalence between ReLU networks and Gated Deep Linear Networks, and use their greater tractability to derive dynamics of learning. We then consider multiple variants of a core task reminiscent of multi-task learning or contextual control which requires both feature learning and nonlinearity. We make explicit that, for these tasks, the ReLU networks possess an inductive bias towards latent representations which are not strictly modular or disentangled but are still highly structured and reusable between contexts. This effect is amplified with the addition of more contexts and hidden layers. Thus, we take a step towards a theory of feature learning in finite ReLU networks and shed light on how structured mixed-selective latent representations can emerge due to a bias for node-reuse and learning speed.

papers.title: A mathematical theory of semantic development in deep neural networks
papers.research_question: What are the theoretical principles governing the ability of neural networks to acquire, organize, and deploy abstract knowledge by integrating across many individual experiences?
papers.core_contribution: Provides a mathematical theory of semantic development in deep linear networks, showing how hierarchical differentiation and other semantic phenomena emerge from the interaction of statistical structure and nonlinear learning dynamics.
papers.conclusion: The simple neural model qualitatively recapitulates many diverse regularities underlying semantic development, providing analytic insight into how statistical structure interacts with nonlinear deep learning dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Deep linear networks exhibit hierarchical differentiation of concepts through rapid developmental transitions.
The model accounts for semantic illusions during periods of developmental stasis.
Item typicality and category coherence emerge as factors controlling semantic processing speed.
Patterns of inductive projection change over development.
The similarity structure of internal representations is conserved across networks trained optimally.
papers.limitation: The linear model cannot capture complex nonlinear semantic phenomena such as context dependence, theory of mind, causal reasoning, and event structure binding.
future_direction: Theoretical analysis of more complex neural circuits to explain higher-level cognitive computations.
papers.abstract: An extensive body of empirical research has revealed remarkable regularities in the acquisition, organization, deployment, and neural representation of human semantic knowledge, thereby raising a fundamental conceptual question: What are the theoretical principles governing the ability of neural networks to acquire, organize, and deploy abstract knowledge by integrating across many individual experiences? We address this question by mathematically analyzing the nonlinear dynamics of learning in deep linear networks. We find exact solutions to this learning dynamics that yield a conceptual explanation for the prevalence of many disparate phenomena in semantic cognition, including the hierarchical differentiation of concepts through rapid developmental transitions, the ubiquity of semantic illusions between such transitions, the emergence of item typicality and category coherence as factors controlling the speed of semantic processing, changing patterns of inductive projection over development, and the conservation of semantic similarity in neural representations across species. Thus, surprisingly, our simple neural model qualitatively recapitulates many diverse regularities underlying semantic development, while providing analytic insight into how the statistical structure of an environment can interact with nonlinear deep-learning dynamics to give rise to these regularities.

papers.title: Constructing Benchmarks and Interventions for Combating Hallucinations in LLMs
papers.research_question: What are the optimal strategies for intervening in LLMs to mitigate hallucinations, and how can we construct benchmarks to evaluate such interventions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the WACK method for constructing per-LLM hallucination benchmarks and performs a comprehensive investigation of intervention strategies, including a novel dynamic intervention that intervenes only when needed.
papers.conclusion: The WACK framework provides a way to create knowledge-based hallucination datasets and offers insights into effective intervention strategies, with attention intervention and pre-answer vectors being particularly effective.
papers.key_findings:
Intervening using pre-hallucination inner states for the steering vector is better than post-hallucination.
Intervention on the residual stream compromises the model's language modeling capability, which is mitigated to some extent by dynamic intervention.
Intervening on the attention component is preferred over the MLP component.
Model preference between answers (classification accuracy) is not a good approximation for whether the model will generate the grounded answer (generation accuracy).
Fine-tuned models (Goat-7B) are more amenable to intervention than base models (Llama2-7B).
papers.limitation:
Only focused on one model (Llama2-7B) and one fine-tuned variant (Goat-7B), and only one open-book dataset (DisentQA) and one closed-book dataset (TriviaQA).
Modified one variable at a time instead of checking across all options.
future_direction: Investigate additional settings and models.
Address hallucinations in cases where the model has no clear preference for the golden answer (type-2 knowledge).
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are prone to hallucinations, which sparked a widespread effort to detect and prevent them. Recent work attempts to mitigate hallucinations by intervening in the model's generation, typically computing representative vectors of hallucinations vs. grounded generations, for steering the model's hidden states away from a hallucinatory state. However, common studies employ different setups and do not properly separate different possible causes of hallucinations, making interventions misguided. In this work, we introduce a method for categorizing examples based on the model's prior knowledge, named WACK. We construct WACK benchmarks that support interventions in two settings: open-book and closed-book question answering. Using the benchmarks, we perform an extensive investigation of the effect of different choices for intervention, such as the intervened components, and how often and how strongly to intervene. We find that intervention success varies depending on the component, with the attention blocks performing well and the residual stream proving detrimental to language modeling capabilities. We also show that interventions can benefit from representative vectors collected before, rather than after, a hallucination occurs. Finally, we introduce a new dynamic intervention, which intervenes only if needed, and thus is more robust than standard static interventions. The code is available at https://github.com/technion-cs-nlp/hallucination-mitigation .

papers.title: Steering Knowledge Selection Behaviours in LLMs via SAE-Based Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: How can we detect and resolve knowledge conflicts in LLMs by steering their internal activations at inference time?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SPARE, a training-free representation engineering method that uses pre-trained sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to identify and edit functional features in LLM activations, effectively steering knowledge selection behavior during inference.
papers.conclusion: SPARE offers an effective and efficient way to control knowledge selection in LLMs at inference time, without significant computational overhead.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge conflicts can be detected in the residual stream of LLMs, especially in mid-layers.
SPARE effectively controls knowledge selection, outperforming existing representation engineering and contrastive decoding methods.
SPARE requires only a small set of SAE features (e.g., <0.05% for Gemma2-9B) for effective control.
The residual stream shows skewed representations when models use contextual knowledge compared to parametric knowledge.
Middle layers are more steerable for knowledge selection behavior.
papers.limitation:
Relies on pre-trained SAEs, which may not be available for all models.
Generalization to other types of tasks or conflicts (e.g., complex reasoning, multi-hop questions) is unclear.
Control is evaluated primarily in binary terms (contextual vs. parametric knowledge), while real-world decisions may require more nuance.
papers.abstract: Yu Zhao, Alessio Devoto, Giwon Hong, Xiaotang Du, Aryo Pradipta Gema, Hongru Wang, Xuanli He, Kam-Fai Wong, Pasquale Minervini. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: Structure and Representation in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we find modular structure in neural networks, and does this structure have functional relevance in terms of local specialization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that trained neural networks exhibit clusterability (modular structure) and that clustering can find locally specialized groups of neurons. It also shows that interpretability tools reveal shortcomings in reward models' feature representation and generalization.
papers.conclusion: The dissertation advances understanding of neural network structure and representation, and highlights the need for better interpretability tools to understand generalization behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Trained neural networks are more clusterable than randomly initialized networks.
Clustering finds groups of neurons that are important and coherent, indicating local specialization.
Interpretability tools applied to reward models show they do not adequately represent relevant features and mispredict reward out of distribution.
These tools do not reveal a clear picture of the computation the networks are performing.
There is a need for better interpretability tools to understand generalization behavior.
papers.limitation: Interpretability tools do not reveal a clear picture of what computation the networks are performing.
future_direction: Applying the methods to larger networks.
Studying the dynamics of clusterability during training.
Developing better interpretability tools for understanding generalization.
papers.abstract: Since neural networks have become dominant within the field of artificial intelligence, a sub-field of research has emerged attempting to understand their inner workings. One standard method within this sub-field has been to primarily understand neural networks as representing human-comprehensible features. Another possibility that has been less explored is to understand them as multi-step computer programs. A seeming prerequisite for this is some form of modularity: for different parts of the network to operate independently enough to be understood in isolation, and to implement distinct interpretable sub-routines.To find modular structure inside neural networks, we initially use the tools of graphical clustering. A network is clusterable in this sense if it can be divided into groups of neurons with strong internal connectivity but weak external connectivity. We find that a trained neural network is typically more clusterable than randomly initialized networks, and often clusterable relative to random networks with the same distribution of weights as the trained network. We investigate factors that promote clusterability, and also develop novel methods targeted at that end.For modularity to be valuable for understanding neural networks, it needs to have some sort of functional relevance.The type of functional relevance we target is local specialization of functionality. A neural network is locally specialized to the extent that parts of its computational graph can be abstractly represented as performing some comprehensible sub-task relevant to the overall task. We propose two proxies for local specialization: importance, which reflects how valuable sets of neurons are to network performance; and coherence, which reflects how consistently their neurons associate with features of the inputs. We then operationalize these proxies using techniques conventionally used to interpret individual neurons, applying them instead to groups of neurons produced by graph clustering algorithms. Our results show that clustering succeeds at finding groups of neurons that are important and coherent, although not all groups of neurons found are so.We conclude with a case study of using more standard interpretability tools, designed to understand the features being represented by directions in activation space, applying them to the analysis of neural networks trained on the reward function of the game CoinRun. Despite our networks achieving a low test loss, the application of interpretability tools shows that networks do not adequately represent relevant features and badly mispredict reward out of distribution. That said, these tools do not reveal a clear picture of what computation the networks are in fact performing. This not only illustrates the need for better interpretability tools to understand generalization behaviour, but motivates it: if we take these networks as models of 'motivation systems' of policies trained by reinforcement learning, the conclusion is that such networks may competently pursue the wrong objectives when deployed in richer environments, indicating a need for interpretability techniques to shed light on generalization behaviour.

papers.title: Feature contamination: Neural networks learn uncorrelated features and fail to generalize
papers.research_question: What is the fundamental difficulty of out-of-distribution generalization with deep neural networks? The paper investigates a new failure mode, 'feature contamination', where networks learn uncorrelated features alongside predictive ones.
papers.core_contribution: Identifies 'feature contamination' as a novel inductive bias of SGD-trained neural networks, where they learn uncorrelated background features together with predictive core features, leading to out-of-distribution generalization failure.
papers.conclusion: Feature contamination is a fundamental yet unexplored feature learning proclivity of neural networks that causes OOD generalization failure, and large-scale pre-training may help by learning more linearized representations.
papers.key_findings:
Even when a student network is explicitly trained to fit good representations from a teacher network that generalizes OOD, the student still fails to generalize OOD.
Theoretically, two-layer ReLU networks trained by SGD learn both core and uncorrelated background features, causing feature contamination and OOD failure.
Feature contamination arises from asymmetric neuron activation for different classes, leading to non-zero gradient projections onto background features.
Linear models do not exhibit feature contamination, showing a separation between linear and non-linear models.
Pre-trained models like CLIP have more linearized representations and denser neuron activation, which may alleviate feature contamination.
papers.limitation: Theoretical analysis is limited to two-layer ReLU networks and a structured feature model.
future_direction: Extending the theoretical analysis to deeper neural networks and more general data models.
Studying how large-scale pre-training alleviates feature contamination and leads to linearized representations.
Exploring algorithmic interventions to mitigate feature contamination.
papers.abstract: Learning representations that generalize under distribution shifts is critical for building robust machine learning models. However, despite significant efforts in recent years, algorithmic advances in this direction have been limited. In this work, we seek to understand the fundamental difficulty of out-of-distribution generalization with deep neural networks. We first empirically show that perhaps surprisingly, even allowing a neural network to explicitly fit the representations obtained from a teacher network that can generalize out-of-distribution is insufficient for the generalization of the student network. Then, by a theoretical study of two-layer ReLU networks optimized by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) under a structured feature model, we identify a fundamental yet unexplored feature learning proclivity of neural networks, feature contamination: neural networks can learn uncorrelated features together with predictive features, resulting in generalization failure under distribution shifts. Notably, this mechanism essentially differs from the prevailing narrative in the literature that attributes the generalization failure to spurious correlations. Overall, our results offer new insights into the non-linear feature learning dynamics of neural networks and highlight the necessity of considering inductive biases in out-of-distribution generalization.

papers.title: Uncovering Layer-Dependent Activation Sparsity Patterns in ReLU Transformers
papers.research_question: How does token-level sparsity evolve over training in ReLU Transformers, and how do sparsity patterns differ across layers and between token, sequence, and batch levels?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that sparsity patterns in ReLU Transformers are layer-dependent, with the first and last layers exhibiting inverted sparsity behaviors, and that neuron death is driven by training dynamics rather than random outliers.
papers.conclusion: Sparsity in ReLU Transformers varies systematically across layers, with the first and last layers being inverses in sparsity behavior, and that one can prune a significant fraction of hidden units without affecting accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Different layers in a ReLU Transformer exhibit distinct sparsity patterns, with the first layer using few hidden units per batch but using them frequently, and the last layer using many hidden units per batch but infrequently per token.
Sparsity patterns at token, sequence, and batch levels often anticorrelate, with layers that use few hidden units per token using many over a batch.
Neuron death (hidden units that never activate) is driven by training dynamics and occurs in specific regimes, rather than randomly.
A significant fraction of hidden units (about 5%) are never used from initialization, suggesting potential for better initialization methods.
Pruning hidden units that are never used after a point in training does not harm model performance, indicating potential for compute savings.
papers.limitation: The study focuses exclusively on small models and ReLU activation functions, which limits immediate applicability to modern foundation models.
future_direction: Investigate changes to initialization functions or model structure to allow more effective use of capacity in both ReLU and more competitive activation functions.
Study the underlying similarities in features learned between ReLU and smoothly-activated networks.
papers.abstract: Previous work has demonstrated that MLPs within ReLU Transformers exhibit high levels of sparsity, with many of their activations equal to zero for any given token. We build on that work to more deeply explore how token-level sparsity evolves over the course of training, and how it connects to broader sparsity patterns over the course of a sequence or batch, demonstrating that the different layers within small transformers exhibit distinctly layer-specific patterns on both of these fronts. In particular, we demonstrate that the first and last layer of the network have distinctive and in many ways inverted relationships to sparsity, and explore implications for the structure of feature representations being learned at different depths of the model. We additionally explore the phenomenon of ReLU dimensions "turning off", and show evidence suggesting that "neuron death" is being primarily driven by the dynamics of training, rather than simply occurring randomly or accidentally as a result of outliers.

papers.title: Large Language Models Do NOT Really Know What They Don't Know
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs' internal states reflect truthfulness or merely the process of recalling parametric knowledge.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs' internal states encode the process of knowledge recall, not truthfulness, making hallucination detection challenging for associated hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: Hidden states encode whether models rely on their parametric knowledge rather than truthfulness, so detection methods succeed for unassociated hallucinations but struggle for associated hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Associated Hallucinations (AHs) and Factual Associations (FAs) share similar internal processes and representational geometries.
Existing hallucination detection methods struggle to distinguish AHs from FAs, performing near random guessing.
